label: Department status review
human_steps: Stand at the captain's chair and read the status board lamps left to right: engineering, medical, security, ops, science.
Tap the department key on the chair console to open engineering's one-line state and read the warp core efficiency figure.
Turn to the comm and ask chief engineering for one sentence on the department's state, then wait for the answer.
Write each red or amber department on the paper pad clipped to the chair arm, beside a short note of the cause.
Repeat for medical, security and ops, and compare each answer with its lamp, since a green lamp can hide a stale report.
Mistake: copying a lamp colour without asking, or missing an amber because the lamp is dim against the bright screen.
what_makes_it_hard: Judging whether a head's one-line answer agrees with the lamp, and noticing when a department's report is stale.
ideal_interaction: Player reads each department lamp, opens it, then picks a question to send to the head; a reply that contradicts a green lamp flags a discrepancy the player must mark on the pad before the review closes.
fit_note: A trend graph shows numbers over time; the real job is verbal one-line reports from heads and spotting contradictions with the lamps.

label: Captain's log and standing orders
human_steps: Sit at the ready room desk and pick up the log recorder, a small handheld with a foam windscreen on its mic.
Speak the date, stardate and ship's position into the recorder, then pause and repeat any line that stumbled.
Pull the standing orders binder from the drawer and turn to the current posture section, reading each order aloud to confirm the wording.
Tap the posture selector on the desk pad to match the alert state the orders now require.
Scroll the saved log back, listen to the playback, and delete any sentence that names a crew member without cause.
Mistake: leaving an order on the old posture, or a log entry that contradicts the orders page.
what_makes_it_hard: Keeping the log accurate and consistent with the orders in force, and resisting the temptation to write what sounds good instead of what happened.
ideal_interaction: Player holds the recorder button and speaks a short entry, then compares the orders page against the posture selector and corrects any mismatch before saving the log.
fit_note: A sign action is a single approval; dictating, listening back and matching orders to posture is the real work.

label: Walk the ship
human_steps: Leave the captain's chair, hand the chair to the XO, and walk out through the lounge doors into the main corridor.
Walk aft toward engineering, looking at faces in the corridor and stopping to greet anyone carrying a PADD.
Enter engineering through the sliding doors and stand at the warp core rail for a moment, listening to the pitch of the coolant pumps.
Continue to sickbay, pausing at the ward doors to see who is resting and whether the staff look exhausted.
Stop at the mess hall and sit at a table for a short talk with two crew, noting any complaint they raise.
Mistake: walking straight through a department without speaking, or turning around too early and missing the corridor drift.
what_makes_it_hard: Reading morale from faces and short talk without pretending to care, and choosing which spaces to visit so the walk is not just a tour.
ideal_interaction: Player walks the route with the stick, stopping at each department door to press Greet; the crew's expression and reply shows morale, and the player logs one note per stop before the loop ends.

label: Decide on requests from departments
human_steps: Sit in the captain's chair and listen to the department head's report on the chair comm, watching their face on the small screen.
Ask the head for two or three options and write each one on the pad with its cost in power, time or people.
Weigh the options against the current mission posture and the cost of delay, and point at the one you pick.
Say the decision in one plain sentence on the comm so the head hears exactly what they have been given.
Mark the request closed on the chair console and press confirm, which sends the decision to the department's board.
Mistake: approving without options, or giving a decision that leaves the head guessing about the next step.
what_makes_it_hard: Weighing competing options against cost and posture and committing to one plainly, rather than just clearing the request.
ideal_interaction: Player receives a request, opens its options card, and assigns a cost weight to each; choosing one and speaking it aloud closes the request, and a vague decision leaves it open.
fit_note: A queue processes requests in order; the real job is weighing options against cost and posture before committing.

label: Announce quiet watch and set green alert
human_steps: Stand at the captain's chair and press the ship-wide PA key on the arm console.
Speak the announcement: quiet watch in force, green alert, watch officer named, and read it back from the card in your hand.
Reach to the alert switch on the chair arm and turn it to green, watching the bridge lamp change colour.
Confirm the alert lamp and the status board both show green before lifting your hand.
Tap the watch bill on the console to confirm the named officer has logged on.
Mistake: announcing green while the lamp still reads amber, or leaving the PA key held down so the announcement loops.
what_makes_it_hard: Making sure the spoken order, the alert switch and the status board all agree before the ship relaxes.
ideal_interaction: Player holds the PA key to speak the announcement, then turns the alert switch to green and waits until the lamp and board both confirm before the quiet watch starts.

label: Mid-run walk of departments
human_steps: Leave the chair and walk the corridor from the lounge toward the main departments, carrying the departments checklist card.
At each department door, read its checklist row aloud to yourself: power, staffing, open faults, and the watch officer's name.
Look inside the room and count the staff at their stations, comparing the count to the checklist's staffing line.
Tick the row on the card only when the staffing count and the open-fault list match, and flag any row that does not match.
Hand the card to the XO at the end of the walk, noting which departments needed a word.
Mistake: ticking a department without going in, or missing a fault listed on the bulkhead panel.
what_makes_it_hard: Matching the staffing count and open faults on the card to what is physically in each room, and not ticking a row unseen.
ideal_interaction: Player walks to each department door on the checklist, enters it to count the stations, then ticks the row only if the count matches; a wrong count leaves the row marked for follow-up.

label: Sign the log and review reports
human_steps: Sit at the ready room desk and pull the day's reports from the in-tray, reading the first page of each.
Check the sickbay and engineering reports for the figures that differ from yesterday, marking them in pencil.
Ask the XO by comm about any marked figure that the report does not explain.
Read the log entry for the watch and correct any sentence that misstates the orders in force.
Pick up the stylus and sign the log, pressing firmly so the signature registers on the pad.
Mistake: signing without reading the marked figures, or signing a log entry that still names last shift's posture.
what_makes_it_hard: Spotting the figure that has changed without a reason and refusing to sign until the explanation is on paper.
ideal_interaction: Player opens each report, marks any figure that moved beyond its band, and must resolve every mark by asking the XO before the sign control unlocks.
fit_note: A sign control is a bare approval; the real work is finding and questioning changed figures before signing.

label: Brief the bridge on survey objective
human_steps: Stand at the captain's chair and take the survey brief form from the arm slot, reading the objective line.
Write the target body, the expected duration and the sensor priority on the form, in that order.
Turn to the bridge crew and read the objective aloud, then ask the science officer to repeat the target back.
Point at the status board where the survey route will appear, so each station knows its role.
Initial the form and drop it into the bridge tray so the ops and helm stations can read the same brief.
Mistake: leaving duration blank, or reading an objective that names a body that is not on the sensor plot.
what_makes_it_hard: Writing an objective specific enough that science and helm agree on the target and the time, without padding it.
ideal_interaction: Player fills the brief form's target, duration and priority fields from the sensor plot and must match them to the plotted body before the form can be sent to the bridge tray.

label: Approve approach and sensor power
human_steps: Lean toward the helm display and read the approach vector: distance, closing speed and the planned stop point.
Read the sensor power budget on the chair console, noting how much of the eps reserve the array would draw.
Ask the helm and science officers by comm whether the approach holds at the planned power, and listen for hesitation.
If the reserve drops below the safe line, lower the sensor power setting with the chair dial before approving.
Press the approve key only after both numbers sit inside their limits, then watch the helm acknowledge.
Mistake: approving the vector without checking the power line, or approving a stop point that sits inside the target's gravity well.
what_makes_it_hard: Checking that the approach and the sensor draw both stay within limits together, since trimming one can break the other.
ideal_interaction: Player reads the approach vector and power budget, adjusts the sensor dial until the reserve stays above the safe line, then presses approve only when both gauges are green.
fit_note: A sign action approves without any numbers to check; the job is balancing approach distance against sensor power draw.

label: Decide whether to extend the survey
human_steps: Read the sensor summary on the chair screen, scanning the finds list from the top and noting the two most promising.
Read the remaining time and fuel figures, which sit in a bar under the summary, and note how many hours each option costs.
Ask the science officer one question about the strongest find: is it a repeat sample or a new reading?
Weigh the extra hours against the fuel margin and the mission's return deadline, writing both numbers on the pad.
Press extend or depart on the chair console, and say the decision aloud so the helm can set the course.
Mistake: extending on the strength of one find while the fuel bar is already in the amber band.
what_makes_it_hard: Trading a possible find against fuel margin and the return deadline, and recognising when the data is not yet strong enough to justify the hours.
ideal_interaction: Player reviews the finds list and the time and fuel bars, then chooses extend or depart; extending while the fuel bar is in the amber band triggers a warning the player must acknowledge.
fit_note: Classify sorts items into bins; the real decision is weighing extra time and fuel against the value of what has been found so far.

label: Order departure and debrief
human_steps: Walk from the bridge to the ready room desk, carrying the survey log card in your left hand.
Open the PA on the desk panel and announce the departure, naming the heading and the time it will take.
Sit down and collect the debrief notes from the science and flight officers as they come in on the desk tray.
Read each note's finding line and mark the ones that need follow-up with a red star on the card.
Initial the debrief sheet once every department has delivered its note, then drop it in the outgoing tray.
Mistake: announcing departure before the science officer has filed the data, or leaving a starred note unanswered.
what_makes_it_hard: Holding departure until the data is safe and ensuring every starred follow-up is answered before the sheet closes.
ideal_interaction: Player makes the departure announcement from the desk panel, then sorts incoming debrief notes into the tray, starring each follow-up that must be answered before the sheet can be initialled.
fit_note: A PA alone does not capture collecting and following up debrief notes.

label: Confirm cargo manifest and route
human_steps: Sit in the captain's chair and take the cargo manifest from the arm tray, reading the container count at the top.
Compare the count to the bay tally figure on the chair console, reading both numbers aloud.
Trace the planned route on the nav plot with a finger on the screen, stopping at each waypoint named on the manifest.
Check that each waypoint's dock is free on the traffic board before accepting the route.
Initial the manifest on the top line and return the tray to the arm slot.
Mistake: approving a count that is off by a container, or a route through a dock already marked busy.
what_makes_it_hard: Matching container counts and waypoints exactly, since a single missing crate or busy dock delays the whole run.
ideal_interaction: Player compares the manifest count to the bay tally, then traces the route waypoints on the nav plot; a waypoint whose dock is busy must be swapped before the route can be confirmed.

label: Authorise transfer and docking
human_steps: Read the docking request from the chair screen, noting the station's clearance code and the planned berth number.
Confirm the berth number matches the one on the traffic board by looking across the bridge to the board.
Read the transfer conditions: time window, escort requirement and the sealed-container count.
Speak the clearance code to the helm and wait for the helm to read it back exactly.
Press the authorise key on the chair arm once the readback matches, and watch the docking lamp turn amber.
Mistake: authorising before the readback, or a berth number that does not match the board.
what_makes_it_hard: Confirming that the clearance code and berth match exactly before authorising, since a misread code can send a ship into the wrong bay.
ideal_interaction: Player reads the clearance code and berth, checks the traffic board, then speaks the code to the helm and waits for a matching readback before pressing the authorise key.
fit_note: A sign action does not involve reading back a code or checking a berth against the board.

label: Sign receipt and close out
human_steps: Walk to the ready room desk and collect the receipt from the outgoing tray, reading the item count and the signatures above the line.
Check the received count against the bay tally card on the desk, reading each row aloud to yourself.
Note any row where the received count is below the manifest, writing the gap in red on the receipt.
Ask the quartermaster by comm whether the gap is a loss or a late item, and wait for the answer.
Sign the receipt on the signature line with the stylus, pressing until the ink registers.
Mistake: signing a receipt that is short without the quartermaster's explanation, or signing on the wrong line.
what_makes_it_hard: Reconciling received counts with the tally row by row and holding the signature until shortages have an explanation.
ideal_interaction: Player compares each receipt row to the tally card; any short row must be marked and explained by the quartermaster before the signature line becomes active.
fit_note: A sign action skips the row-by-row reconciliation that makes a receipt meaningful.

label: Set course and priority for relief
human_steps: Stand at the helm rail and take the relief route card from the chair arm, reading the destination and the arrival deadline.
Set the course heading on the nav plot by dragging the route line to the destination marker.
Read the warp factor the route needs and set it on the helm dial, watching the power gauge for overdraw.
Choose the priority level on the chair console, selecting between routine, urgent and emergency for the relief run.
Confirm the route on the plot and listen for the helm to read back the heading and the factor.
Mistake: setting urgent priority with a warp factor the engines cannot hold, or a heading that cuts through a debris field.
what_makes_it_hard: Balancing arrival time against engine load and avoiding hazards on the route, since urgent priority with too high a warp can strain the warp core.
ideal_interaction: Player drags the route line on the nav plot, sets the warp dial while watching the power gauge, and picks a priority; an overdraw or hazard crossing forces a route change before confirm.

label: Authorise medical stores and surge staff
human_steps: Walk to the sickbay biobed and pick up the stores inventory clipboard from the foot of the bed.
Read the supply counts for drugs, dressings and blood, marking any line below its reorder level in pencil.
Walk to the staff board on the wall and read which medics are free and which are on rest.
Assign the free medics to the surge rota by tapping their names on the board, one shift at a time.
Sign the stores requisition on the clipboard, specifying the quantities for each marked line.
Mistake: assigning a medic already on rest, or signing a requisition that leaves a marked line unfilled.
what_makes_it_hard: Matching the requisition to actual shortfalls and the real staff hours available, without overloading any one medic.
ideal_interaction: Player reads each marked stores line and picks free medics from the staff board to fill the surge rota; assigning someone on rest is refused and the requisition only signs once every marked line has a quantity.

label: Check on triage in person
human_steps: Walk from the biobed into the main ward, stopping at the first bed and reading the triage tag clipped to the frame.
Look at the patient's colour and breathing, and listen for any change in the monitor's tone at the bedside.
Read the tag's priority colour and compare it to the bed's current status card on the wall above it.
Speak briefly to the patient or the attending nurse, asking one question about the wound or the pain.
Move to the next bed and repeat until every red tag has been seen by you in person.
Mistake: skipping a red tag because the monitor looks steady, or moving on before the nurse answers.
what_makes_it_hard: Matching a tag's priority colour to what the patient actually looks like and not letting a steady monitor hide a deteriorating patient.
ideal_interaction: Player walks the ward and stops at each bed, reading its tag and looking at the patient; a red tag whose patient looks worse than its colour triggers a re-triage the player must confirm.

label: Declare relief complete
human_steps: Stand at the captain's chair and read the relief checklist on the arm screen, scanning down to each completed line.
Check the sickbay bed count on the status board against the number of patients the relief was sent to treat.
Tap the complete line on the chair console once the count and the checklist agree.
Press the PA key and announce the relief complete, naming the number of patients and the ship's new posture.
Watch the status board update to show medical back on routine, and confirm the lamp changes.
Mistake: declaring complete while a bed count is still short, or announcing before the lamp updates.
what_makes_it_hard: Waiting until the bed count and the checklist truly agree, rather than declaring relief to end the pressure.
ideal_interaction: Player compares the relief checklist to the bed count on the status board; declaring complete is blocked until the count matches, then the PA announcement and the lamp update finish the job.
fit_note: A PA covers the announcement but not the comparison of checklist against bed count that justifies it.

label: Announce shakedown plan and yellow alert drills
human_steps: Stand at the captain's chair and pick up the shakedown plan card from the arm slot, reading the trial order.
Press the PA key and announce the shakedown plan, naming the trial sequence and the drill window.
Turn the alert switch on the chair arm to yellow and watch the bridge lamp change to amber.
Confirm on the status board that each department's lamp has moved to yellow before lifting your hand.
Read the first drill's name off the card and set the drill timer on the chair console.
Mistake: announcing a sequence that differs from the card, or setting yellow without the lamps following.
what_makes_it_hard: Making the spoken plan and the alert state agree on every station before the drill starts.
ideal_interaction: Player reads the plan card, holds the PA key to announce it, then turns the alert switch to yellow and sets the drill timer only after every department lamp has followed.

label: Order system trials one by one
human_steps: Stand at the captain's chair and read the first system name off the trial list on the arm screen.
Press the trial key for that system and wait for the department to report ready on the comm.
Watch the system's readout on the status board while its trial runs, noting any spike or drop.
When the trial passes, tick its line on the list and move to the next system in order.
If a trial fails, hold the list at that line and call the chief engineer to explain the fault.
Mistake: starting the next trial before the previous one has finished, or skipping an out-of-order system to save time.
what_makes_it_hard: Holding the trial order and waiting for each result rather than rushing into the next system.
ideal_interaction: Player steps through the trial list in order, sending each trial and watching its readout; a system started before the previous one passes is refused, and a failure locks the list until the player calls the chief.

label: Review trial results with heads
human_steps: Walk to the ready room desk and pick up the trial results sheets from the tray, one per department.
Read each sheet's measured column and set it beside the spec column, running a finger down each pair.
Mark any measured value outside its spec band with a red circle, and write the value in the margin.
Call each chief by comm in turn and ask about each circled value, listening for whether the fault is known.
Write the fix and its date next to each fault that has an owner, and leave an open box for any that do not.
Mistake: accepting a circled value because the chief says it is minor, or closing a fault with no date beside it.
what_makes_it_hard: Comparing measured values to spec line by line and not accepting a known defect as fine just because a chief says so.
ideal_interaction: Player compares each measured value to its spec band on the sheets, circling out-of-band values, then calls the chief for each; a fault closes only when a fix and date are entered.
fit_note: A trend graph shows values over time; the real work is checking measured values against spec bands line by line.

label: Accept or reject ship readiness
human_steps: Stand at the captain's chair and read the readiness checklist on the arm screen, scrolling to the open-fault count.
Read the total fault count and the count of faults closed with a fix date from the ready room log.
Compare the two totals; the ship is ready only if every fault has a closed status or a logged waiver.
Press accept or reject on the chair console, depending on the comparison.
If rejecting, speak the reason on the PA so the crew knows which systems hold the ship back.
Mistake: accepting with open faults that have no waiver, or rejecting without naming the system responsible.
what_makes_it_hard: Accepting only when every open fault has either a fix or a waiver, and naming the system when rejecting.
ideal_interaction: Player reads the open-fault count against closed and waived faults; accepting is locked while any fault is open without a waiver, and rejecting requires choosing the responsible system before the PA announcement.
fit_note: A sign action is a single approval; the job is reconciling open faults against waivers before choosing accept or reject.

label: Read the bridge status board
human_steps: Stand at the bridge console and scan the alert lamp at the top of the board, noting its colour.
Read the system lights below it left to right, marking each amber or red one on the pad.
Tap the amber department on the console to open its short state line and read the cause.
Speak to that department's senior person on the comm and ask what is failing and how long it has been so.
Write the answer beside the amber light on the pad, with the time you asked.
Mistake: reading only the alert lamp and missing a dim amber system light lower down the board.
what_makes_it_hard: Scanning every system light instead of the one loud alert lamp, and asking the right question when an amber light appears.
ideal_interaction: Player scans the alert lamp then each system light in order, tapping any amber light to open its cause and asking the department; a missed amber light is flagged on the board before the loop completes.
fit_note: A trend graph shows numbers over time; the job is scanning discrete lights and asking departments about each amber one.

label: Walk the decks
human_steps: Leave the stores hatch and walk the main corridor, looking into each open door as you pass.
Stop at the department door you have chosen and find the senior person on shift, looking for the one who seems busiest.
Ask that person what is failing on their deck, and listen for the specific item and when it started.
Write the item and the time in the log book that hangs on the corridor bulkhead.
Walk on to the next deck, repeating the question at each station.
Mistake: asking a general question and getting a general answer, or leaving a deck without writing its item in the log.
what_makes_it_hard: Asking precise questions that surface the one failing item rather than accepting a reassuring general answer.
ideal_interaction: Player walks decks by corridor, stops at a department and asks the senior person a chosen question; a specific answer is written in the bulkhead log, and a vague one prompts the player to ask again.

label: Run a readiness drill
human_steps: Stand by the armory locker and press the PA key on the wall panel to announce the drill.
Start the stopwatch on the locker panel the moment you finish the announcement.
Watch the crew arrive at their lockers, reading the arrival time off each name on the sign-in board.
Check each person's kit against the locker checklist, opening the locker door and counting the items inside.
Stop the stopwatch when the last station reports manned and write the total time on the board.
Mistake: starting the timer after the announcement ends, or accepting a station as manned when its kit is missing.
what_makes_it_hard: Timing the response honestly and refusing to pass a station with a missing item, even when the crew is quick.
ideal_interaction: Player presses the drill key to start timing, then opens each arriving station's locker to count kit items; a locker with a missing item keeps that station unmanned until the item is supplied.
fit_note: A checklist walks kit items but does not time the response, which is half of what a drill measures.

label: Rebalance rosters
human_steps: Sit at the ready room desk and open the duty roster on the screen, scrolling to the fatigue flag column.
Note each person flagged with more than the allowed consecutive hours, writing their name on the pad.
Find a swap partner for each flagged person by reading down the free list and matching their rating.
Drag the two names across each other on the roster to swap their shifts, then confirm the new hours.
Write a short note for each affected department head and send it on the desk comm.
Mistake: swapping someone into a shift that would give them the same fatigue flag, or leaving a department head uninformed.
what_makes_it_hard: Finding swap partners whose ratings fit the role and whose own hours stay inside the fatigue limit.
ideal_interaction: Player selects each flagged name and drags it onto a qualified free partner; a swap that trips the partner's fatigue flag is refused, and the swap only commits after a note is sent.

label: Stand officer of the watch; keep log
human_steps: Step into the command chair and read the alert lamp and the watch bill on the console before saying anything.
Speak the watch log entry aloud into the recorder: time, alert state, and the names of stations manned.
Scan the bridge stations in turn, checking each one has a person seated and a comm light lit.
Write any station without a person on the log pad, and call the XO if one of them is a key post.
Read the log entry back to yourself and correct any time or station name that does not match the board.
Mistake: logging a station as manned from its light alone, or leaving the chair without signing the entry.
what_makes_it_hard: Keeping the log accurate about who is actually at each station and noticing an empty post before it becomes a gap.
ideal_interaction: Player reads the watch bill and scans each station's seat and comm light, then speaks the log entry; a station with a lit light but no seated officer is flagged, and the entry cannot close while it is unresolved.
fit_note: A trend graph does not capture logging who is at each station; the real work is checking seats and writing a verified log.

label: Walk the decks and spot-check logs
human_steps: Walk out of the stores into the corridor and head to the first department on your list, carrying the log clipboard.
Open the department's log book on its wall stand and read the last three entries, looking for any gap in the times.
Compare the most recent entry to the status board lamp for that department, reading both aloud to yourself.
Note any entry that is missing, late, or contradicts the lamp, writing the department name in pencil beside it.
Initial the log book's spot-check line if the entries are complete, then move to the next department.
Mistake: initialling a log that has an hour-long gap, or treating a lamp colour as proof that the entries are current.
tools: department log books on wall stands
what_makes_it_hard: Reading logs for gaps and contradictions with the lamps, and not initialling a book that only looks tidy.
ideal_interaction: Player walks to each department's log stand, reads the last entries for time gaps and compares to the lamp; an unexplained gap blocks the initial stamp until the player marks it.

label: Assign watch officers so sensors stay manned
human_steps: Sit at the bridge console and open the sensor watch bill, reading the current shift and the next one.
Count the sensor posts still needing a watch officer and note each post's required rating on the pad.
Scroll the officer list and pick a rated officer with rest hours left, checking their last rest time on the card.
Drag the officer onto the post on the watch bill, then confirm the assignment with the console key.
Repeat for each open post until none is empty, watching the fatigue meter for the scans that run into the night watch.
Mistake: putting a fatigued officer on a long scan, or leaving a sensor post empty because the rating looked close enough.
what_makes_it_hard: Filling every sensor post with a qualified, rested officer without overloading anyone across a long scan.
ideal_interaction: Player drags each rated officer onto an open sensor post; placing an officer over their rest limit or under the required rating is refused, and the bill only closes when every post is manned.

label: Visit lab and check data handling
human_steps: Walk into the science lab and go to the data console, where the survey logs are stored.
Open the newest survey data file and read its header, checking the instrument ID and the date of capture.
Compare the file's record count on the header with the count of entries listed below, counting the rows aloud.
Check the storage checksum shown in the corner against the one on the data handling sheet taped to the console.
Ask the science officer which records were copied to the archive, and confirm the archive count matches.
Mistake: accepting a file whose record count differs from its header, or a checksum copied from an earlier file.
what_makes_it_hard: Verifying the data itself, not just the file name, and catching a short or corrupted record before it spreads into the archive.
ideal_interaction: Player opens a survey file, compares its record count and checksum to the header and the handling sheet, and confirms the archive index; a mismatched checksum flags the file as corrupted before it can be archived.

label: Brief a landing party if a site is chosen
human_steps: Walk to the transporter pad and stand where the team will assemble, reading the site card taped to the console.
Call each team member forward by name and hand them their kit list, reading each item aloud as they take it.
Point at the site map on the pad's screen to show the route, the rendezvous point and the time to recall.
Ask each member to repeat their role and the recall time back to you, correcting any answer that is wrong.
Check each member's comm badge by asking them to speak, watching the badge light turn green.
Mistake: sending someone with a dead badge, or letting the team leave without a repeated recall time.
what_makes_it_hard: Making sure every person knows their role, kit, and recall time, and that no badge is dead before they beam down.
ideal_interaction: Player calls each team member, hands them their kit list, and asks them to repeat the recall time; a member who answers wrong or has a dead badge is held back until corrected.
fit_note: A roster assigns names to slots; the real briefing is verbal, with repeated recall times and badge checks.

label: Verify manifest against the stowage plan
human_steps: Walk into the cargo bay and stand at the first stowage locker, holding the manifest on a clipboard.
Open the locker and count the crates inside, saying each count aloud while touching each crate once.
Read each crate's label and match it to the manifest line for that locker, marking the line with a tick.
Look at the stowage plan on the bulkhead for that locker's mass limit and note whether the load is inside it.
Move to the next locker and repeat, writing any crate missing from the manifest or in a locker it does not belong to.
Mistake: counting the crates from the doorway, or ticking a manifest line when the label does not match the crate.
what_makes_it_hard: Counting every crate and matching labels exactly, since one misfiled crate becomes a delivery delay at the far end.
ideal_interaction: Player opens each stowage locker, taps each crate to count and read its label, and ticks the matching manifest line; a crate with no manifest line or a wrong label is flagged before the locker closes.

label: Check shuttlebay readiness for transfers
human_steps: Walk to the shuttlebay door and stand where you can see the pad, reading the shuttle's ready board on the frame.
Walk to the pad and check each transfer shuttle's hatch seal by pressing the seal and listening for the click.
Read the shuttle's fuel gauge and the lift-jack pressure on the gauge panel beside the pad.
Check the bay door's status light and the tractor beam lock on the control panel, reading the lock line aloud.
Mark the readiness board line for each shuttle that passes, and note any seal that does not click.
Mistake: marking a shuttle ready with a seal that did not click, or ignoring a low fuel gauge.
what_makes_it_hard: Confirming each seal and gauge physically rather than trusting the board, since a bad seal in vacuum is a serious failure.
ideal_interaction: Player walks the bay pad, presses each shuttle's hatch seal and waits for the click, then checks the fuel and lift-jack gauges; a seal that does not click keeps that shuttle's board line open.

label: Sign off the transfer log
human_steps: Sit at the bridge console and open the transfer log, scrolling to the newest unsigned entry.
Read the entry's shuttle, time, and cargo count, comparing them to the manifest count you verified earlier.
Confirm the entry lists a receiving station and a signed transfer order from the captain.
Type your initials into the officer field and press the sign key on the console.
Watch the log entry change to signed status and confirm the time stamp is correct.
Mistake: signing an entry with no receiving station, or initialling before reading the cargo count.
what_makes_it_hard: Checking that the log truly matches the verified cargo and the authorised transfer before putting your name to it.
ideal_interaction: Player reads the newest transfer entry, compares its cargo count to the verified manifest, and confirms the receiving station before typing initials; a missing receiving station blocks the sign key.
fit_note: A sign key alone skips comparing the logged count and receiving station to the verified manifest.

label: Clear priority transport and berths for patients
human_steps: Sit at the bridge console and open the berth board showing free and occupied sickbay beds.
Read the patient transport list for the arriving casualties, noting each one's priority and bay.
Assign each priority casualty to a free berth on the board, starting with the most critical.
Open the lift routes panel and clear the route from the transporter to sickbay, tapping each blocked corridor to release it.
Confirm the lift is free by reading the lift status lamp and then notify sickbay on the comm.
Mistake: assigning a casualty to an occupied berth, or clearing a route that another team is still using.
what_makes_it_hard: Matching casualties to berths by priority and clearing routes without blocking a team already in the corridor.
ideal_interaction: Player assigns each casualty to a free berth in priority order and then clears the lift route; clearing a corridor where a team is still present is refused until the team's lamp goes clear.
fit_note: A schedule orders events in time; the job is assigning bodies to berths and clearing physical routes.

label: Help sickbay with crowd control and logistics
human_steps: Stand at the sickbay door and look at the queue of people waiting outside, counting how many are visitors and how many are patients.
Check each person's badge against the visitor list on the door panel, reading the name and the reason for entry.
Let through anyone with a patient or medic badge, and direct visitors to the waiting bench in the corridor.
Carry a stack of linen from the door cupboard to the nearest ward, stopping at the bed numbers to drop each set.
Speak to the queue at the door about the wait, giving a time estimate from the bed board.
Mistake: letting in a visitor on a patient badge, or leaving the door clear while the ward is full.
what_makes_it_hard: Turning people away kindly while keeping the ward clear enough for medics to work.
ideal_interaction: Player stands at the door and scans each arriving badge against the visitor list, admitting patients and medics and sending visitors to the bench; a patient badge used by a visitor triggers a refusal.

label: Rebalance rosters to cover medical staff leave
human_steps: Sit at the ready room desk and open the medical roster, reading the names marked on leave this week.
List each shift with an empty medical post, noting the rating required for the post.
Find a rated officer from another department whose rest hours allow an extra shift, reading their fatigue flag.
Drag the officer onto the empty medical post on the roster and confirm the shift.
Send a note to the affected department head on the desk comm so they know the cover is in place.
Mistake: covering a post with an officer who lacks the medical rating, or pushing someone past their fatigue limit.
what_makes_it_hard: Covering every empty medical post with a qualified officer who still has rest hours, across several shifts.
ideal_interaction: Player drags a rated officer from another department onto each empty medical post; a post that lacks the required rating or overruns fatigue is refused until another officer is chosen.

label: Run the system test checklist with each department
human_steps: Sit at the bridge console and open the system test checklist, reading the first department's test line.
Call that department on the comm and ask them to start the test, then watch its status light on the board.
Read the test result they report and write it on the checklist beside the line, marking pass or fail.
If a test fails, ask the department what reading they got and write the number next to the fail mark.
Move to the next department in the list and repeat until every line has a result.
Mistake: marking a test passed because the department said so without the status light changing, or skipping a line.
what_makes_it_hard: Waiting for the real reading rather than accepting a verbal pass, and recording the number when a test fails.
ideal_interaction: Player calls each department to start a test, watches its status light change, then marks pass or fail on the checklist; a pass is refused while the light has not changed.
fit_note: A queue processes tests in order; the real job is confirming each result against the status light and recording failing numbers.

label: Run a damage-control drill
human_steps: Walk to the engineering junction and stop by the emergency locker, reading the drill card taped to its door.
Call out the simulated breach on the PA, naming the deck and compartment written on the card.
Open the locker and pull out the fire extinguisher and seal kit, checking each is full and the seal kit's pins are present.
Walk to the junction's pressure door and test the manual seal wheel, turning it until the seal lamp goes green.
Check the extinguisher's pressure gauge reads in the green band and that its safety pin is in place.
Mistake: sealing the wrong door, or turning the seal wheel with a fault that the drill card did not mention.
what_makes_it_hard: Doing the seal and extinguisher steps in the right order and correctly, under time pressure, without skipping the pin check.
ideal_interaction: Player walks to the locker, pulls the extinguisher and seal kit, then turns the junction's seal wheel until the lamp goes green; sealing the wrong door or skipping the extinguisher pin check resets the drill step.

label: Compile the shakedown report
human_steps: Sit at the ready room desk and open the shakedown report template, reading each heading in order.
Fill the first section with the trial dates, pulling each date from the trial log card on the desk.
Copy each failing test from the checklist into the faults section, with its reading and the department that ran it.
Read the previous shakedown's report and mark any fault that appears in both, writing the repeat count beside it.
Add the sign-off line at the end with your initials and the date, then save the report to the archive folder.
Mistake: leaving out a repeated fault, or copying a test result without its reading.
what_makes_it_hard: Recording every failing test and every repeat so the report tells the next crew which faults keep returning.
ideal_interaction: Player fills the report's sections from the trial log and checklist, and the report flags any fault that matches the previous archive so the player must enter a repeat count before saving.

label: Command the bridge watch
human_steps: Step into the command chair and take the watch from the officer of the watch, reading the handover note on the console.
Read the alert board and the system board, noting any amber or red light and the time it changed.
Speak to each chief by comm in turn and ask for their current status, listening for anything they hedge on.
Filter the reports into two piles on the pad: items for the captain now, and items that can wait for the next shift.
Brief the captain on the first pile in two or three sentences, then turn to the status board while they reply.
Mistake: passing on a hedged status without checking it, or briefing the captain with a long list instead of the urgent items.
what_makes_it_hard: Sorting reports so the captain hears the few things that matter now, without filtering out a worry a chief hedged on.
ideal_interaction: Player speaks to each chief, sorts the replies into captain-now and can-wait piles, then briefs the captain; a hedged reply that is dropped from the brief triggers a follow-up request from a chief.
fit_note: A queue processes items in order; the real work is sorting reports by urgency and briefing the captain on the few that matter.

label: Department walk-round
human_steps: Stand at the engineering console and read the open-fault list, then walk to the first department with a fault.
Walk the engineering corridor, touching each bulkhead panel and reading its status lamp as you pass.
Stop at the coolant junction and look at the pipe joints for drips, listening for a hiss from the valve.
Walk to the cargo corridor and look at the stores seal and the lashing on the nearest pallet, pulling each strap by hand.
Walk to sickbay and the mess, checking the air vent grilles for dust and the galley hood for grease.
Mistake: reading the console's fault list without looking at the joint, or walking past a loose lashing because the lamp is green.
what_makes_it_hard: Finding real faults by touch and sight in each room, rather than trusting the console's summary.
ideal_interaction: Player walks the route, touches each panel and joint, and pulls each strap; a dripping joint or loose strap that the console did not list adds a deficiency that the player must log.

label: Duty roster and deficiency review
human_steps: Sit at the ready room desk and read each chief's report from the tray, noting the deficiencies they list.
Open the duty roster and find the gaps, marking each empty post on the screen with the required rating.
Assign a repair priority to each deficiency by writing 1, 2 or 3 beside it, with 1 meaning the ship cannot run without it.
Match each priority-one deficiency to a qualified officer with free hours, dragging their name onto the repair task.
Sign each requisition on the desk for any part the repair needs, checking the quantity against the stores list.
Mistake: assigning a repair to an officer without the rating, or signing a requisition for more parts than the repair needs.
what_makes_it_hard: Ranking deficiencies by their real risk and matching each one to a rated officer with time to do it.
ideal_interaction: Player reads each chief's report, assigns priority numbers to deficiencies, then drags a rated officer onto each priority-one repair; an unrated or overloaded officer is refused.
fit_note: A roster covers the staffing half; the job also ranks deficiencies and signs requisitions, which the roster alone does not model.

label: Alert and comm net check
human_steps: Sit at the bridge console and press the test key for the red alert relay, watching the relay lamp for a green flash.
Pick up the comm badge on the console and speak a test phrase, then listen for the echo from the badge's speaker.
Press the test key on each department comm in turn and confirm each station answers with its name.
Note any relay that does not flash or any station that does not answer, writing its name on the pad.
Walk to the nearest comm panel on the bulkhead and test it by hand, since a fault there can hide behind the console test.
Mistake: counting a station as answering when only its light came on, or skipping the bulkhead panel.
what_makes_it_hard: Confirming each relay and station with a real spoken response rather than trusting a lit lamp.
ideal_interaction: Player presses each relay test key and each department comm, then speaks into the badge to confirm a station's answer; a station whose lamp lights but gives no spoken reply is marked unanswered.
fit_note: A decode game deciphers messages; the real check tests relays and confirms each station speaks back.

label: Confirm watch bill and brief chiefs
human_steps: Sit at the bridge console and open the watch bill, reading each post and its named officer for the coming shift.
Count the posts with no officer or a name marked absent, writing the post on the pad.
Call each chief on the comm and tell them who is covering their department on the next watch, reading each name.
Ask each chief to confirm the named officer is awake and has their handover, and wait for a yes or a correction.
Correct any post where the chief names a different officer, updating the bill on the console.
Mistake: confirming a bill with an empty post because the chief did not answer, or accepting a name without the chief's confirmation.
what_makes_it_hard: Getting every chief to confirm the names on the bill, and not treating silence from a chief as agreement.
ideal_interaction: Player reads each post's name and calls its chief to confirm; a chief who does not answer keeps the post flagged, and the bill only confirms once every chief has given a yes.

label: Walk-round of all departments
human_steps: Stand at the cargo corridor entrance and read the walk-round list on the pad, starting with the cargo bay.
Walk into the cargo bay and check the lashings on the nearest pallets by pulling each strap by hand.
Walk on to shuttlebay, then the mess, reading each department's status lamp and looking at its floor for spills.
Stop at each department door and count the staff at their stations, noting any post left empty.
Return to the bridge by the deck corridor, checking each bulkhead panel you pass for lit fault lamps.
Mistake: walking past a loose strap because the lamp is green, or not entering a room to count staff.
what_makes_it_hard: Covering every department in one walk and finding the small faults that accumulate, without losing track of the route.
ideal_interaction: Player walks the list route from cargo to shuttlebay, mess and back to the bridge, pulling straps and entering each room to count staff; a loose strap or empty post found on the walk must be logged before the route closes.

label: Clear deficiency list with chiefs
human_steps: Sit at the ready room desk and open the deficiency list, reading the oldest open item first.
Call the chief responsible for the oldest item and ask for the repair status, listening for a date.
Mark the item as fixed, deferred or blocked, writing the date or the blocking part on the line.
Move to the next open item and repeat with its chief until the list has no unmarked lines.
Read the deferred items aloud to yourself and confirm each one has a reason and a new date.
Mistake: marking an item fixed on the chief's word alone, or deferring a line with no new date.
what_makes_it_hard: Pressing each chief for a real status and a date, and refusing to let an item drift into deferred with no end.
ideal_interaction: Player works down the deficiency list, calling each chief for status; an item marked fixed without a date or deferred without a reason is refused until the entry is complete.
fit_note: A queue processes items in order; the job is pressing each chief for a dated status and rejecting vague entries.

label: Assign survey priorities to science and flight
human_steps: Sit at the bridge console and read the survey target list, noting each target's window and its sensor needs.
Read the flight schedule on the helm display, marking the times the ship can hold a steady heading.
Open the science schedule and find the overlaps where a target's window falls inside a steady-heading period.
Drag each overlapping target onto its time slot on the shared plan, assigning science and flight the same slot.
Call the science officer and the helm to read each slot back, listening for any disagreement on the time.
Mistake: scheduling a target inside a turn, or letting science and helm read different times for the same slot.
what_makes_it_hard: Matching each target's window to a steady heading and making sure both stations hold the same time.
ideal_interaction: Player drags each target onto a slot where its window overlaps a steady heading; placing a target inside a turn is refused, and the plan only closes once science and helm both read the same slot back.
fit_note: A queue processes targets in order; the real job is matching target windows to steady-heading periods and aligning two stations.

label: Check sensor power draw with engineering
human_steps: Stand at the engineering console and read the eps reserve gauge, noting the current draw and the safe line.
Read the sensor array's planned draw from the survey plan on the screen beside the console.
Add the planned draw to the current draw and compare the total to the reserve, writing both numbers on the pad.
Ask the chief engineer on the comm whether the grid can hold that total for the planned scan length.
Adjust the sensor duty cycle on the console dial if the total crosses the line, and watch the gauge settle.
Mistake: comparing the planned draw alone without the current draw, or accepting a duty cycle that still crosses the safe line.
what_makes_it_hard: Adding the planned draw to what the grid is already carrying and trimming the duty cycle until the total stays under the safe line.
ideal_interaction: Player reads the reserve gauge and the planned draw, then turns the duty-cycle dial until the combined draw sits under the safe line; the scan is refused if the gauge stays in the red band.

label: Keep the watch bill covered for long scans
human_steps: Sit at the ready room desk and open the watch bill for the scan's full length, reading the posts that must be manned throughout.
Find each post whose officer finishes their shift before the scan ends, marking the gap on the bill.
Pick a rested officer with the right rating for each gap, reading their rest hours from the roster card.
Drag each chosen officer onto the gap and confirm the post, then read the bill's new coverage line.
Send a note to each affected officer on the desk comm telling them their shift and the handover time.
Mistake: leaving a gap because the officer was almost rested, or sending a note without the handover time.
what_makes_it_hard: Keeping every post covered across a long scan, with rested officers who have the right ratings for each gap.
ideal_interaction: Player drags a rested, rated officer onto each gap in the long-scan bill; an officer whose rest hours do not cover the gap is refused, and the bill closes only with no gaps left.

label: Approve cargo manifest and transfer schedule
human_steps: Stand at the cargo console and open the manifest, reading the total mass line at the top.
Compare the mass line to the mass limit on the console's side panel, and read the stowage plan's trim figure.
Check each pallet row on the manifest against the stowage plan's position for it, tracing the position with a finger on the screen.
Set the transfer schedule by dragging each pallet's slot onto the transfer window, starting with the heaviest pallet.
Read the trim figure again after the schedule is set and confirm it sits inside the trim band.
Mistake: approving a manifest whose trim sits outside the band, or scheduling the heavy pallet last, where it upsets the trim.
what_makes_it_hard: Keeping total mass and trim inside their limits while scheduling pallets in an order that does not unbalance the ship.
ideal_interaction: Player drags pallets into the transfer schedule, watching the trim readout; a schedule that pushes trim outside the band is refused until the player moves a pallet to balance it.

label: Check shuttlebay and transporter readiness
human_steps: Stand at the shuttlebay console and read the transporter and shuttle ready lamps on the panel.
Walk to the transporter pad in the corridor and check the pad's alignment marks by looking at the floor grid.
Step onto the pad and look at the transporter's status board, reading the power and lock lines aloud.
Return to the shuttlebay and check each shuttle's pressure gauge through the door window.
Write any lamp that is not green and any pad mark that is out of line on the pad.
Mistake: reading the console lamps without visiting the pad, or passing a shuttle with a low gauge.
what_makes_it_hard: Checking the physical pad and each shuttle's gauge rather than trusting the console's ready lamps.
ideal_interaction: Player reads the console lamps, walks to the transporter pad to check the floor marks and status board, then checks each shuttle's gauge; a misaligned mark or low gauge keeps readiness from being confirmed.

label: Inspect lashings and stores seal
human_steps: Walk to the cargo locker and open its door, reading the seal number on the frame against the stores log.
Check the seal's wire and clamp by pulling on it and reading the clamp's stamp for the matching number.
Walk to the pallets beside the locker and pull each lashing strap, checking its tension by how far it gives.
Tighten any strap that gives more than a finger's width by turning its ratchet until the strap stops moving.
Write each loose or broken strap and each seal that does not match the log on the pad.
Mistake: calling a strap tight by eye, or closing a locker whose seal number differs from the stores log.
what_makes_it_hard: Feeling the difference between a tight and a loose strap by hand, and catching a mismatched seal before the locker moves.
ideal_interaction: Player pulls each strap to test its give and turns the ratchet on any loose one; a seal whose number differs from the stores log blocks the locker from closing until the player logs it.

label: Confirm sickbay needs and clear the route
human_steps: Stand at the sickbay biobed and read the needs list clipped to its frame, noting the supplies and beds requested.
Walk the main ward and count the free beds, writing the count on the pad beside the needs list.
Walk from sickbay to the transporter corridor, checking that no crate or cart blocks the route with a hand on each one.
Move any blocking cart by pushing it to the storage alcove, and listen for the lock click on the alcove door.
Ask the chief medical officer on the comm whether the route and beds now meet the needs list.
Mistake: counting only the beds shown on the board, or calling the route clear without walking it end to end.
what_makes_it_hard: Walking the actual route and counting beds by eye, so the needs are met before the team arrives.
ideal_interaction: Player walks the ward counting free beds, then walks the route to the transporter and pushes any blocking cart aside; a route still blocked when the player reaches the corridor keeps the needs list open.
fit_note: A form records confirmations on paper; the real job is walking the route, counting beds and moving blocking objects.

label: Reassign hands to sickbay support
human_steps: Sit at the ready room desk and open the crew list, reading each department's headcount and the names on light duty.
Find the officers with no critical post on their shift, marking each name on the pad.
Pick the free officers whose ratings include first aid or orderly duty for sickbay support.
Drag each chosen officer onto a sickbay support post on the roster, reading the post's required task.
Send each reassigned officer a short note on the desk comm telling them the post and the handover time.
Mistake: moving an officer off a critical post, or assigning a support post to someone with no first-aid rating.
what_makes_it_hard: Moving only truly free hands, and matching each one's rating to the support task.
ideal_interaction: Player drags free, rated officers onto sickbay support posts; an officer taken off a critical post is refused, and a rating mismatch is flagged before the note can be sent.

label: Pre-brief transporter and shuttlebay
human_steps: Walk to the transporter pad and stand by the console, reading the patient transfer plan taped beside it.
Call the transporter chief and the shuttlebay chief in turn, reading the transfer's route and time window to each one.
Ask each chief to repeat the handover time and the number of patients, listening for any disagreement.
Point at the pad's floor marks and the shuttle's bay door on the plan, confirming which spot each patient lands on.
Initial the plan and drop it in the transporter tray so both teams read the same brief.
Mistake: briefing one chief without the other, or letting a chief leave without repeating the time.
what_makes_it_hard: Making sure transporter and shuttlebay teams repeat the same time, route and patient count back to you.
ideal_interaction: Player reads the transfer plan to the transporter chief, then the shuttlebay chief, and requires each to repeat the time and count; a chief who gives a different number is corrected before the plan is initialled.
fit_note: A form captures the brief on paper; the job is a verbal brief with read-backs from two teams.

label: Check quarantine readiness with life support
human_steps: Stand at the life support console and read the quarantine airflow setting, noting the pressure difference the ward needs.
Walk to the quarantine door in the corridor and feel the air at the seal with a hand, checking for a draught.
Check the quarantine pressure gauge on the wall beside the door and read its number against the required difference.
Ask the life support chief on the comm to run the seal test, and watch the pressure gauge move during it.
Mark the quarantine as ready only when the gauge holds the difference through the full test, and log the time.
Mistake: taking the console's airflow setting as proof without feeling the seal, or ending the test early before the gauge settles.
what_makes_it_hard: Seeing the seal hold under test rather than trusting the setting, since contamination spreads if the seal fails.
ideal_interaction: Player reads the airflow setting, feels the door seal for draught, then runs the seal test while watching the pressure gauge; a gauge that drops below the required difference keeps quarantine marked not ready.

label: Brief chiefs on test sequence
human_steps: Sit at the ready room desk and open the test sequence card, reading each system in its order.
Call each chief in turn and read them the systems that fall under their department, in the sequence order.
Ask each chief to repeat their system's position and what the test checks, listening for any wrong order.
Write the order number beside each chief's name on the desk sheet, and note any chief who asks to test out of order.
Hold any out-of-order request and tell the chief the order must stand, giving the reason from the card.
Mistake: letting a chief start early because their system seemed ready, or briefing the sequence without asking for a read-back.
what_makes_it_hard: Holding the sequence firm when a chief wants to jump ahead, and confirming each chief has the order right.
ideal_interaction: Player reads the sequence card to each chief and requires a read-back of their position; a chief who requests an out-of-order start is refused until the sequence reaches their system.
fit_note: A queue processes items in order; the job is a verbal brief that needs read-backs and firm refusal of early starts.

label: Observe reactor and eps trial
human_steps: Walk to the warp core rail and stand where you can see the core's glow and the coolant gauge at once.
Read the reactor output gauge, then the eps distribution panel, noting the load each one carries during the trial.
Listen to the core's pitch and the coolant pump's hum, noting any rise or stutter as the trial load increases.
Watch the eps load gauge climb in steps, and stop the trial with the emergency cut key if it passes the red line.
Read the final load and output figures aloud to the chief engineer, asking whether the reading is within spec.
Mistake: watching only the output gauge and missing a coolant stutter, or letting the load climb past the red line.
what_makes_it_hard: Watching several gauges and the sound of the core together, and cutting the trial at the first sign of an unsafe load.
ideal_interaction: Player stands at the warp core rail, watches the output, coolant and eps gauges as the load climbs, and presses the cut key the moment a gauge crosses the red line; a late cut causes the core to alarm.
fit_note: A trend graph shows the load over time; the real observation covers several gauges, the sound of the core and a cut decision.

label: Collect fault list from all departments
human_steps: Sit at the ready room desk and pick up the fault slips from the in-tray, one slip per department.
Read each slip's fault line and its location, marking any slip that gives no location.
Call the department on the comm and ask them to read the fault back, listening for any fault they forgot to write.
Write each new fault on the master fault list in the department's column, with its location and severity.
Send back any slip with no location to the department for a second slip, noting the time it was returned.
Mistake: copying a slip without its location, or accepting a department's verbal fault that is not on a slip.
what_makes_it_hard: Getting every fault onto the list with a location, including the ones a department did not think to write down.
ideal_interaction: Player reads each fault slip and calls the department to read it back; a slip missing its location is returned, and a fault mentioned on the call but not on a slip must be written before the list closes.
fit_note: A queue processes slips in order; the real job is collecting faults with locations and catching faults departments mention but did not write.

label: Verify alert drill and station times
human_steps: Sit at the bridge console and open the drill record, reading each station's recorded response time.
Start a second timer and trigger the alert drill from the console, watching each station's lamp turn on.
Stop the second timer as each station's lamp lights, noting the time against its name on the pad.
Compare each station's time to the recorded time, marking any station more than a few seconds off.
Ask the station's officer by comm why their time differed, and write the reason beside the mark.
Mistake: trusting the recorded times without retiming, or stopping the second timer when the officer speaks instead of the lamp.
what_makes_it_hard: Timing each station from its lamp rather than from the officer's voice, and noticing when a recorded time is not credible.
ideal_interaction: Player triggers the alert drill, stops the timer as each station's lamp lights, and compares to the recorded time; a station whose recorded time is far off the measured time is flagged as not credible.
fit_note: A form records times on paper; the job is measuring each station's lamp response against the recorded value.

label: Flight deck walk-round
human_steps: Enter the bay by the aft door and walk the floor pad to pad, clipboard in hand, scanning the deck plating for oil sheen and loose bolts.
Crouch at each shuttle's landing gear and press a thumb against the tie-down clamps, feeling for any play in the joint.
Run a gloved hand around the hatch seal and look at the rubber for cracks, flattening, or grit caught in the gasket.
Read the fuel gauge on the external port, checking the needle against the red band, and write the figure on the pilot log.
Look up at the bay doors and overhead rails to confirm nothing is hanging, leaking or left unsecured.
Sign the pilot log with the time only after every pad has been touched and read.
what_makes_it_hard: Judging a seal or clamp by feel and sight in a noisy bay, and refusing to sign until every craft is physically checked; failure is a signed log for a shuttle that leaks on launch.
ideal_interaction: Walk the bay pad to pad with a torch in hand, holding the light on each seal and clamp for a set dwell and tapping any flagged spot, and sign only when every craft is covered.

label: Review helm and nav status
human_steps: Stand at the forward console and read the heading and bearing readouts against the course figures on the ops slate.
Compare the displayed numbers line by line, noting any heading that differs from the orders by more than half a degree.
Lean over the helm station and ask the helmsman by voice for the current trim and throttle setting.
Ask the navigator to read back the next waypoint and its estimated time of arrival.
Circle any mismatch on the slate and say the correction aloud to the helm.
Press confirm only after both stations have read back the same numbers.
what_makes_it_hard: Spotting a small heading drift between two sources of numbers and getting honest read-backs from crew; failure is an unnoticed drift that takes the ship off course.
ideal_interaction: Hold the heading and bearing against the orders on a split display and step through each read-back as a call and response, pressing confirm only when every figure agrees within tolerance.
fit_note: A trend view is passive graph-reading; the real job is comparing figures to orders and taking spoken read-backs.

label: Check inertial dampers and sensors
human_steps: Walk to the damper panel beside the helm and read the three damper bank gauges, noting each needle's band.
Flag any bank reading outside its green band and lift the reset cover to see whether the needle settles.
Move to the nav sensor console and select the forward sensor array diagnostic.
Run the sensor self-check and watch the return count against the expected baseline.
Scan the status lamp for amber or red; if amber, pull the fault code from the sensor log.
Enter the readings in the damper log, because logging nominal while a bank still drifts is the classic error.
what_makes_it_hard: Telling a settling needle from a stuck one and separating a real sensor fault from a reading that is actually fine; failure is an amber lamp logged as nominal.
ideal_interaction: Turn the damper reset dial and watch the three needles settle inside their bands within a set time, then start the sensor self-check and confirm the baseline count matches before the log can close.

label: Update flight schedule and sign-offs
human_steps: Walk to the readyroom desk and lift the pending pilot requests from the request tray.
Check each request against the shuttle availability board and the pilots' rest log.
Write each pilot's name into the schedule grid, one row per shuttle per shift.
Hand each pilot a sign-off slip and wait while they initial it.
Compare the initialled slips against the grid to catch any name written in the wrong shift.
Carry the completed sheet to the XO's out tray and file a copy in the schedule folder.
what_makes_it_hard: Matching pilot qualifications and rest limits to shuttle assignments under shift pressure without a double-booking; failure is a pilot flying a craft they are not cleared for.
ideal_interaction: Drag each pilot card onto a shuttle slot in the grid, where the card refuses to drop into a slot that breaks the pilot's rest timer or qualification, then send the finished sheet to the XO.

label: Confirm helm and nav staffing
human_steps: Walk the bridge rail and count the helm and nav seats against the watch bill pinned to the wall board.
Read each seated officer's name tag against the roster line for that seat.
Ask the duty officer to confirm any empty seat and whether a relief is on the way.
Check the crew fatigue flags on the status panel at the rear of the bridge.
Write any gap in the watch log with the time it was found.
Mark the seat staffed only after the name tag, roster and fatigue flag all agree.
what_makes_it_hard: Reconciling the printed watch bill with who is physically seated, including relief arrivals; failure is an unstaffed console that nobody notices until a heading goes wrong.
ideal_interaction: Tap each seat on the bridge layout to match its name tag against the watch bill; empty or mismatched seats flash until the roster is corrected, and the watch closes only when every seat is green.

label: Deck walk-round
human_steps: Enter the bay and walk the floor from the aft door to the far shuttle, watching the deck for debris or fluid.
Stop at each pad and look under the craft for drips and note any pool shape.
Thump each shuttle's landing strut with the flat of a hand and feel for give or a rattle.
Read the fuel level on the pad post and flag any shuttle under the half-full mark.
Lift stray tools off the bay rail and shelf and carry them to the locker.
Log the pad numbers with defects, and mark the rest ready only after each pad has been seen.
what_makes_it_hard: Spotting a small leak or loose strut among many similar craft in a dim bay; failure is a shuttle that is not ready when it is called.
ideal_interaction: Walk the bay with a torch, tapping each strut and holding the beam on each seal for a count of three, then mark a pad ready only after both checks pass.

label: Hold course and report
human_steps: Stand at the helm console and read the drift figure on the course line across a full minute.
Watch the heading number tick and note whether it creeps in one direction.
Turn the course trim knob one notch against the drift, then wait and re-read.
Repeat the trim and re-read until the drift stays inside its band for three readings.
Write the final heading and the trim setting on the watch sheet.
Speak the heading and drift figure to the bridge so the record is not silent.
what_makes_it_hard: Holding a steady heading against slow drift and recognising when a correction is overshooting; failure is drift that builds across a whole watch unreported.
ideal_interaction: Keep a course pointer centred by dialling trim against a drifting line on a station-keeping screen, with a timer scoring how long the pointer stays in its band before the watch ends.
fit_note: A generic station screen does not obviously include reading the drift trend or making the spoken report.

label: Plot survey course
human_steps: Pull the survey target list from the ops slate and note each target's bearing and range.
Walk to the chart table and lay out the sensor arc templates for the probe pass.
Trace a route on the chart that keeps each target inside its arc at closest approach.
Slide the plot cursor along the nebula and debris markers to check the route for hazards.
Enter the waypoints into the helm plotter and read back the total burn time.
Re-check each target's angle against the arc before signing the course, since a wrong angle wastes the pass.
what_makes_it_hard: Balancing sensor geometry against hazards and burn time so every target is covered in one pass; failure is a survey that misses targets and must be flown again.
ideal_interaction: Drag waypoints across the chart so each target sits inside its sensor arc at closest approach, with hazard zones turning red and the route refusing to commit if it crosses one.

label: Brief helm and nav on slow approach
human_steps: Walk to the helm station and wait for the helmsman to look up from the console.
Point at the approach line on the chart and state the target bearing and the closing speed aloud.
Tell the navigator the cut-off distance at which speed must drop to a crawl.
Ask both officers to read back the bearing, speed and cut-off in their own words.
Correct any read-back that differs from the chart by pointing to the exact line.
Confirm the helmsman has the same cut-off distance on his console before stepping away.
what_makes_it_hard: Getting an exact, unambiguous approach brief into two people's heads and verifying it through read-backs; failure is an overshoot caused by a misheard figure.
ideal_interaction: Speak the three approach figures into the comms panel and have each station pick the matching value from a short list under time pressure, with mismatched picks scored as a misheard brief.
fit_note: A form cannot capture a spoken brief or the read-back check that makes it safe.

label: Prep a survey shuttle
human_steps: Walk to the survey shuttle on its pad and read the probe request tag on the pilot's chalkboard.
Climb the access ladder and check the probe pod mount bolts by hand.
Seat the probe pod on the mount and pull the locking lever down until its click is felt.
Watch the lock indicator and confirm it shows locked, not just seated.
Fill the shuttle's fuel from the pad hose to the survey line on the gauge.
Walk round the craft checking the pod's wiring loom and sealing cap.
what_makes_it_hard: Confirming a probe pod is fully locked and the fuel level is right without a second pair of hands; failure is a pod lost in flight or a short survey.
ideal_interaction: Pull the pod's locking lever until it clicks, then hold the lock indicator under the torch until it turns green before the fuel hose unlocks for filling to the survey line.

label: Report pass complete
human_steps: Walk to the bridge comms panel and open the survey log on its screen.
Read each target line and compare its sweep count against the planned count.
Note any target with a missing sweep or a poor-quality return.
Say the pass summary aloud to the bridge: targets covered, sweeps missed, and the time.
Attach the data pack reference to the report.
Send the report to science and wait for their acknowledgement before leaving the panel.
what_makes_it_hard: Counting every target's sweep against the plan without glossing over a missing one; failure is science receiving a clean report that hides a gap.
ideal_interaction: Walk down each target line in the survey log, tapping it to match the recorded sweep count, and send the report only once every line is either matched or flagged.
fit_note: The form is text entry only; the job is also spoken reporting and checking sweep counts against the plan.

label: Plot efficient route
human_steps: Open the cargo manifest and read the origin, destination and total cargo mass.
Pull up the lane chart and find the quickest lane that avoids the known debris field.
Drag the route across the lane chart and read the fuel and time estimate at each leg.
Check the running fuel total against the shuttle's reserve on the side panel.
Mark the chosen lane and note which alternates were rejected and why.
Send the plan to the helm and wait for the helm's confirmation.
what_makes_it_hard: Weighing fuel reserve, lane hazards and arrival time together and choosing a lane that is both safe and quick; failure is a route that strands cargo short of its destination.
ideal_interaction: Drag route legs across the lane chart while the fuel bar and arrival clock update per leg, with lanes through debris turning red and locking the route until it is detoured.

label: Assign shuttle and deck crew
human_steps: Walk to the crew board by the shuttle pad and read which craft the route plan calls for.
Check the pilot's status tag on the board for rest and fitness.
Walk to the deck crew's bunk room and read off names for the loading shift.
Tap each name onto a station slot on the board, one crew member per station.
Walk the pad to confirm each crew member is standing at the station they were given.
Tell the pilot the crew list and wait for the pilot to nod before the load starts.
what_makes_it_hard: Balancing rest, skill and station coverage so loading never has a gap; failure is a load that stalls at the first unmanned station.
ideal_interaction: Drag crew tokens onto the loading stations on a bay layout, where a token refuses to drop onto a station already filled or onto a pilot who is off rest.

label: Confirm docking approach
human_steps: Walk to the helm station and read the range to the dock on the approach display.
Read the closing speed and compare it with the approach profile on the chart.
Look out the forward viewport and check the dock's alignment lights against the marker.
Call the helmsman for a burn to bring closing speed down to the profile.
Watch the range counter until it reaches the stop mark.
Confirm the dock lock light and report the docking complete.
what_makes_it_hard: Judging closing speed against range and cutting the burn early enough; failure is a hard dock that damages the cargo in the hold.
ideal_interaction: Hold a burn slider down and release it at the moment the closing-speed curve meets the approach profile, timing the release so the range counter lands on the stop mark.

label: Report arrival
