human_steps: Walk to the comms panel and open the arrival form on its screen.
Read the dock time from the chronometer on the bulkhead.
Read the cargo count from the manifest and compare it with the crates seen in the hold.
Enter the actual arrival time and crate count in the form fields.
Note any damaged or missing crate on the damage line.
Speak the arrival to the bridge and wait for the acknowledgement tone.
what_makes_it_hard: Reporting actual times and counts rather than planned ones; failure is a bridge working from arrival data that never happened.
ideal_interaction: Type the actual dock time and crate count into the arrival form while a side checklist lights each field only when its value matches the manifest.
fit_note: Only text entry; the real report is spoken and depends on checking the hold.

label: Plot fastest safe route
human_steps: Open the casualty pick-up request and read the coordinates aloud to confirm them.
Look at the chart for the shortest lane toward the pick-up point.
Check the candidate lane against the hazard list for radiation, nebula and debris.
Trace the route on the touch chart and read the travel time at each leg.
Compare the total time with the patient's timing window on the medical board.
Commit the route only after every hazard on the lane has been checked.
what_makes_it_hard: Trading speed against hazards while the clock runs; failure is a route that looks fast on paper but cuts through a radiation band.
ideal_interaction: Trace a route with a finger-drag on the touch chart, where a hazard flashes and the line snaps back to the last safe waypoint, while the arrival countdown is held against the patient window.

label: Ready the medical shuttle
human_steps: Walk to the medical shuttle on its pad and open the hatch by its handle.
Check the litter mounts inside, tugging each strap to confirm it holds.
Read the oxygen and power gauges by the rear locker.
Refill any low oxygen bottle from the rack and screw each seal cap until it stops.
Stow the medical kit into its floor clip so nothing shifts in flight.
Close the hatch and check its seal lamp before walking away.
what_makes_it_hard: Verifying every life-support fitting by hand, not by the gauge alone; failure is an oxygen seal that leaks mid-evacuation.
ideal_interaction: Work down the list of straps and seal caps, turning each cap until it clicks and pulling each strap, and mark the craft ready only when every fitting passes.
fit_note: A bench activity does not cover moving around the pad and checking the craft's fittings in situ.

label: Clear the approach with nav
human_steps: Walk to the nav station and ask the navigator for any obstacles on the approach.
Look at the sensor sweep for each obstacle's range and bearing.
Mark a safe corridor on the chart overlay with the grease pencil.
Check the corridor against the traffic board to confirm no ship is in it.
Tell the helm the corridor and speed limit, then wait for a read-back.
Confirm the corridor is clear again if the sweep picks up anything new.
what_makes_it_hard: Confirming that obstacles are real, not stale returns; failure is a corridor drawn through debris that the sweep had already flagged.
ideal_interaction: Sweep the sensor cone across the approach while blips flag any obstacle the corridor touches, and the player draws the corridor only after every blip is cleared.

label: Report ETA to the bridge
human_steps: Read the current time and the route's remaining travel from the helm display.
Add the dock time and the transfer allowance for the medical team.
Write the total estimate on the ETA card.
Walk to the comms panel and read the ETA into the channel.
Ask sickbay to confirm the receiving time.
Note the sickbay confirmation on the card before filing it.
what_makes_it_hard: Adding travel and transfer time correctly and sending a figure medics can plan around; failure is sickbay unready when the shuttle lands.
ideal_interaction: Enter the travel, dock and transfer times into the ETA form, and the send button unlocks only when the total matches the sum shown beside it.
fit_note: Form entry omits the spoken report and the receiving confirmation from sickbay.

label: Brief helm on test manoeuvres
human_steps: Walk to the helm station and tell the helmsman which tests run and in what order.
Name each manoeuvre with its speed and turn figures.
Ask for a read-back of each manoeuvre before any test starts.
Confirm the emergency stop call and who gives it.
Hand the helm the test sheet with the manoeuvres listed.
Watch the helmsman's first input to confirm the read-back was understood.
what_makes_it_hard: Getting every manoeuvre understood before any engine is lit; failure is a test run out of order or without a stop call.
ideal_interaction: Walk the test sheet line by line, and the helm console locks each test until the player has confirmed the read-back wording shown on screen.
fit_note: Text entry does not capture the spoken brief or the stop-call check.

label: Run helm and damper checks
human_steps: Stand at the helm and call for the first manoeuvre to be run.
Watch the damper gauges through each turn and note any needle that lags.
Set the throttle to each stage and listen for the engine note to change.
Read the damper load values after each test and write them on the sheet.
Call a halt if any bank reads past its band.
Repeat the cycle for each manoeuvre on the sheet.
what_makes_it_hard: Catching a transient needle lag during a manoeuvre; failure is a hidden fault that only shows under load and is missed.
ideal_interaction: Push the throttle through its stages while the damper needles show live, and press halt the moment a needle crosses its band during a turn.

label: Test shuttle launch
human_steps: Walk to the shuttle on its pad and climb into the pilot seat.
Run the pre-launch panel and read each lamp in order.
Signal the bay crew to clear the pad, then start the engine.
Watch the thrust gauge through the lift and note the figure at hover.
Set the craft back down on the pad.
Check the landing gear lamps and hatch seal after touchdown before marking the test done.
what_makes_it_hard: Reading several gauges during a short lift and catching a fault that appears only once the craft moves; failure is an in-flight abort.
ideal_interaction: Ease the lift slider up, reading thrust as the needle settles at hover, then set the craft down and check the post-landing lamps before the test can close.
fit_note: A burn covers only the lift; the pre-launch panel reading and post-landing checks are missing.

label: Report results
human_steps: Collect the test sheets from the helm and the shuttle pilot.
Compare each test's readings against the pass band on the sheet.
Write a pass or fail mark beside each test.
Walk to the comms panel and send the results to the XO.
Read the failures aloud with their gauge values.
Wait for the XO to acknowledge before filing the sheets.
what_makes_it_hard: Judging edge values against the pass band honestly; failure is a fault sent to the XO as a pass.
ideal_interaction: Check each test row's readings against the pass band, and any row sitting on the edge stays flagged until the player marks it pass or fail.
fit_note: Text entry does not capture the spoken failure report or the edge-value judgement.

label: Shuttle walkaround and FOD sweep
human_steps: Walk from the bay door to the first shuttle pad, scanning the floor for loose bolts, rags or metal shavings.
Kneel and sweep the pad with the brush into the debris pan, lifting anything over a thumbnail in size.
Check each shuttle's tie-down clamps by pulling on them with both hands.
Run a hand around each hatch seal and feel for a tear or dent.
Look under the craft for fluid drips and note their colour.
Log each defect on the pad tablet against its pad number.
what_makes_it_hard: Finding a bolt or shaving in the scatter of the floor and feeling a clamp that is only slightly loose; failure is debris drawn into an engine or a clamp that gives under thrust.
ideal_interaction: Sweep the pad with the brush, dragging debris into the pan, while a counter tallies each piece collected against a hidden target count for the pad.

label: Fuel and stock shuttles
human_steps: Walk to the fuel locker and lift the fuel hose off its hook.
Couple the hose nozzle to the shuttle's fuel port and turn the collar until it seats.
Watch the tank gauge on the craft's side and stop the flow near the mark.
Uncouple the nozzle, cap the port and wipe the nozzle with a rag.
Count out replacement suits and tool kit items from the locker shelf.
Check each count against the stores sheet and tick it off.
what_makes_it_hard: Stopping the flow at the right level by eye and never leaving a port open; failure is a spill on the pad or a tank that runs dry before launch.
ideal_interaction: Hold the nozzle on the fuel port and tilt the handle to pour while watching the level; release at the mark, then tick the stores sheet as each suit is counted.

label: Bay door and forcefield check
human_steps: Walk to the bay door control and read the door status light.
Cycle the door open and closed on the test switch while watching the track.
Read the seal pressure on the gauge beside the door.
Walk to the forcefield emitter post and check its indicator light.
Push a test tag on a pole through the field line and see whether the field stops it.
Confirm the pressure needle held steady through the whole cycle.
what_makes_it_hard: Reading pressure and field status together and noticing when the field light is green while the seal is failing; failure is a bay that holds pressure only on paper.
ideal_interaction: Cycle the door on the panel, then push a test tag through the field line; the field should catch it, and the pressure needle should hold steady through the whole cycle.

label: Move cargo sleds
human_steps: Walk to the cargo sled bay and read the manifest tag on the first sled.
Check the sled's load straps and balance each crate on its deck.
Push the sled onto the lift plate and step back to the controls.
Ride the lift to the shuttle deck with the sled.
Lift the sled off the plate and wheel it to its stow point.
Strap the sled down before leaving it.
what_makes_it_hard: Balancing weight across a sled deck by feel while pushing it; failure is a sled that tips on the lift and spills crates.
ideal_interaction: Slide each crate across the sled deck until the balance marker sits centred, then push the loaded sled onto the lift plate, which tilts if the load sits off-centre.
fit_note: The balance step is there, but the physical push, lift ride and strapping are not.

label: Routine deck walk and tie-down check
human_steps: Walk the pad row and look at each shuttle for loose tie-downs.
Pull each strap and clamp end to confirm it does not slide.
Look for oil or fuel sheen under each craft and note its position.
Check the drip trays on the bay floor for any that are full.
Record a loose strap on the pad board by its craft number.
Walk back along the row to confirm the straps you re-tensioned are still tight.
what_makes_it_hard: Telling a strap that is truly tight from one that only looks tight; failure is a loose craft in thrust-wash on the next launch.
ideal_interaction: Walk the pad row and pull each strap end; a strap that gives shows a red mark and must be re-tensioned into its groove before the row can clear.

label: Inventory suits and tool lockers
human_steps: Open the suit locker and take each suit off its hook, checking its seal ring.
Count the suits against the register, one tick per suit, pointing with a pen.
Open each tool drawer and lift the tools out to count them.
Check each tool for cracks or missing grips and set bad ones aside.
Log the counts and set-aside items on the register.
Re-hang each suit on its own numbered hook before closing the locker.
what_makes_it_hard: Counting accurately without double-counting or skipping a hook; failure is a missing suit that is only discovered in an emergency.
ideal_interaction: Tap each suit on the locker rail to tally it, with the counter rising only when the suit's hook number matches the register, and empty hooks flagged in red.

label: Prep survey shuttle with probe pods
human_steps: Walk to the survey shuttle on its pad and read the probe request tag.
Carry a probe pod from the rack to the shuttle's pod mount.
Align the pod's guide pins with the mount holes and push it home.
Tighten each mount bolt with a wrench, working in a star pattern.
Plug the pod's signal lead into the shuttle socket and wiggle it to confirm it is seated.
Walk round the pod and check each bolt head once more.
what_makes_it_hard: Seating a heavy pod square and torquing bolts evenly without a second person; failure is a pod that shifts during launch.
ideal_interaction: Lift the probe pod onto the mount and seat its pins, then tighten each bolt with the wrench in a star pattern, the wrench clicking at its torque mark.

label: Clear bay and cycle doors for launch
human_steps: Walk to the bay console and read the launch call on its screen.
Walk the bay floor, moving crates and sleds out of the launch lane.
Stand at the door and call the bay clear to the console by voice.
Press the bay door open on the console and watch the track clear.
Confirm the forcefield is up before the shuttle moves.
Stand clear of the lane as the craft taxis out.
what_makes_it_hard: Making sure the whole lane is truly clear, not only the parts you can see; failure is a craft launched into a stacked sled.
ideal_interaction: Drag crates and sleds off the launch lane on the floor plan, and keep the door control disabled until the lane reads clear and the field line is up.
fit_note: A PA announcement is a broadcast; the job is physically clearing the lane and watching the doors.

label: Stand by for recovery and wash down probes
human_steps: Stand at the pad with the wash hose and wait for the shuttle hatch to open.
Take each probe pod from the pilot and check it for scoring.
Hose each pod down in the wash bay and turn it to rinse the seams.
Set each pod on the drying rack with its sample port facing down.
Bag the contaminated residue and tag it for science.
Log the pod count received against the count on the survey sheet.
what_makes_it_hard: Rinsing contamination out of seams without spreading it across the bay; failure is contaminated samples crossing into the bay.
ideal_interaction: Sweep the hose across each pod's seams, where a contamination meter drops only when every seam is clean, then rack the pod.

label: Stage cargo sleds at cargo bay
human_steps: Walk to the cargo bay and read the sled order on the staging board.
Pull the first sled from the rack onto the floor.
Push it onto the lift plate, lining its wheels with the floor marks.
Stow the crates on the sled deck, heaviest at the bottom.
Lock the sled brake and fasten the lift strap.
Check the brake lamp is lit before stepping off the plate.
what_makes_it_hard: Lining sled wheels to the plate marks and stowing heavy crates low; failure is a sled that rolls on the lift.
ideal_interaction: Push the sled onto the lift plate and line its wheels to the marks, then lock the brake when the wheels show green.

label: Load and strap shuttle hold
human_steps: Walk to the shuttle's hold hatch and open it.
Take each crate off the sled and set it on the hold floor, heaviest at the centreline.
Run a strap over each crate and cinch it at the ratchet.
Pull each strap sideways against its crate to test it.
Check the hold door seal and close the hatch.
Walk the hold's length once more to confirm no crate is unstrapped.
what_makes_it_hard: Strapping crates so nothing shifts under thrust; failure is a load that moves in flight and upsets the shuttle's trim.
ideal_interaction: Loop each cargo strap over its crate and pull the ratchet until the tension gauge reaches its line, then tug the crate to confirm it stays put.

label: Unload returning crates
human_steps: Stand at the hold hatch as the shuttle lands and open it on the pilot's signal.
Unstrap each crate and check it for dents or a leaking seal.
Lift the crate onto a sled and roll the sled off the pad to the cargo bay.
Tick each crate off the arrival list as it leaves the pad.
Walk the pad to make sure no crate sits in the recovery path.
Report the pad clear to the pilot.
what_makes_it_hard: Lifting heavy crates safely and clearing the pad fast without dropping one; failure is a crate blocking the recovery path.
ideal_interaction: Place each crate onto the sled grid, where it turns green once counted, and the pad lane stays closed until the last crate is cleared.

label: Ready the shuttle for casualty transport
human_steps: Walk to the shuttle's cabin and open the cabin door.
Fold down each stretcher berth and lock it into its slot.
Pull each berth's strap clip until it holds.
Wipe the berth surface with a sanitiser cloth.
Set the cabin lamp and check it lights.
Tilt the cabin slightly to see whether any berth shifts.
what_makes_it_hard: Locking every berth and clip so it holds under a bump, not just looks latched; failure is a patient sliding off a berth in flight.
ideal_interaction: Fold each berth down and turn its lock until the tab clicks, then tilt the cabin and watch each berth hold; a berth with an unset lock slides visibly.

label: Clear a stretcher lane to sickbay
human_steps: Walk from the bay door toward the corridor and note the stretcher route to sickbay.
Lift and carry any loose crate, locker or tool off the stretcher path.
Push each sled out of the lane and against the bay wall.
Stand at the bay door and check the opening is a full stretcher width.
Set a cone at the start of the lane.
Walk the lane end to end looking for cable trips at knee height.
what_makes_it_hard: Judging clearance for a stretcher through a door and spotting low trip hazards; failure is a stretcher snagged at the door.
ideal_interaction: Hold-and-carry each obstacle to the wall, with a width gauge on the lane turning green only once the stretcher gap and trip-free status both read clear.

label: Meet returning shuttle with medical team
human_steps: Walk to the pad and wait with the medical team at the hatch.
Open the shuttle hatch when the pilot calls it, and take the patient log.
Help bring the stretcher down the ramp and hold its foot end steady.
Check the patient's straps are secure as the stretcher goes onto the medic's trolley.
Say the handover aloud: patient, injury and time.
Hand the patient log to the lead medic and wait for a signature.
what_makes_it_hard: Carrying a stretcher down a ramp without tilting it and giving a clear handover; failure is a patient dropped or handed over unclear.
ideal_interaction: Hold the stretcher's foot end on the ramp and keep the level bubble centred while the vitals screen reads steady, then call the handover once the trolley takes the weight.
fit_note: A monitor screen covers the readings but not the physical carry or the spoken handover.

label: Run full pre-launch checklist on all craft
human_steps: Walk the pad row with the checklist and go craft by craft.
At each craft, read the fuel, pressure and battery gauges and write the readings down.
Open each access panel and look for loose wiring or fluid.
Move the control stick through left, right and back to check its free travel.
Tick the craft's line only when every item is read or physically touched.
Initial the sheet at the end of the row.
what_makes_it_hard: Doing every item on every craft rather than skipping the awkward ones; failure is a hidden fault that shows up at launch.
ideal_interaction: Work each craft's checklist on a tray of gauge readings, where each item stays locked until the reading falls inside its band, then move to the next craft.
fit_note: A tray of readings misses the walk along the pad and the access panels.

label: Test bay door, forcefield and fire suppression
human_steps: Walk to the console and read the test script for the doors, field and suppression.
Cycle the bay door and watch the track and light for smooth travel.
Walk to the forcefield emitter and test the field with a test tag.
Walk to the suppression head on the ceiling and check the nozzle is clear.
Trigger a test spray into the drain and check the pressure on the line gauge.
Restore each system to its normal state before signing the script.
what_makes_it_hard: Running the three tests in order without skipping the one nobody likes; failure is a fire system that works only on paper.
ideal_interaction: Run the test script step by step on the console, unlocking each test only in sequence, and the suppression test fires a timed burst that must be watched reaching the drain.

label: Drill emergency recovery with the pilot
human_steps: Walk to the pad and brief the pilot on the signal for a rough landing.
Stand at the recovery point and wave the landing paddles to guide the craft.
Watch the shuttle come in and read its angle against the signal lights.
Call the stop when the skid touches the pad.
Move in with the chocks and set one under each wheel.
Confirm the craft is fully chocked before the pilot shuts down.
what_makes_it_hard: Judging an approach angle through the signal and calling the stop in time; failure is a rough landing that skids into the bay.
ideal_interaction: Wave the paddles while the shuttle descends a glide path, then press stop and the chock button when the skid lands within its marker.
fit_note: A burn covers thrust but not the paddle signals, the stop call or the chocking.

label: Brief captain on schedule
human_steps: Walk to the readyroom desk and pull up the captain's day on the roster screen.
Scan the roster for double bookings and write each conflict on a sticky note.
Walk through the bridge door and cross to the captain's seat.
Stand beside the captain and read the next item aloud in three lines: time, subject, who is waiting.
Wait for a nod, then walk back to the desk.
Log the time of the brief on the desk slate.
what_makes_it_hard: Compressing conflicts into a three-line brief the captain grasps in seconds; failure is a captain walking into a double booking.
ideal_interaction: Walk to the captain's seat and deliver the three-line brief, choosing from a small panel which conflict to flag before the brief timer runs out.
fit_note: A calendar screen does not include the walk to the captain or the spoken three-line brief.

label: Relay messages and orders
human_steps: Walk to the bridge comms console and pick up the message queue printout.
Read each message header for its priority tag.
Sort the messages into three piles: urgent, routine and for-information.
Walk the urgent pile to the right department console and key in the routing code.
Confirm each delivery by reading the acknowledgement on the console.
Return to the queue and clear the routine pile by department.
what_makes_it_hard: Reading priority from a header and routing to the right department quickly; failure is a message landing with the wrong department.
ideal_interaction: Decode each incoming signal by matching its header to the routing list and sending it on the right channel before the signal decays.

label: Update log and duty roster
human_steps: Pull the watch rosters from the readyroom desk drawer.
Compare each watch's names against the sign-in sheet to find gaps.
Read any duty-swap request slips and check each swapper's rest times.
Write approved swaps into the roster in ink, initialling each change.
Draft a log entry for the day's changes in the captain's log template.
File the swap slips in the roster folder by date.
what_makes_it_hard: Reconciling names and rest times across several rosters without double-booking; failure is a crew member on two watches at once.
ideal_interaction: Fill the roster grid by placing names into watch slots, with a slot refusing a name already on another watch and showing the rest-hour gap beside it.

label: Captain's refreshment and comfort
human_steps: Walk to the mess replicator and ask for the captain's usual.
Watch the cup fill and touch its side to judge the temperature.
Carry the cup along the corridor, keeping it level through the corner.
Set the cup on the captain's desk coaster.
Ask the captain whether they have eaten.
If they have not eaten, return to the mess for the captain's usual tray.
what_makes_it_hard: Carrying a full cup through corridors without spilling and judging temperature by touch; failure is a scalded captain or a spill on the desk.
ideal_interaction: Hold the cup in both hands and tilt it along a corridor path, keeping the fill level inside its mark through every turn, with a spill breaking the carry.

label: Clear the paperwork backlog
human_steps: Walk to the readyroom desk and lift the backlog tray from the side shelf.
Sort each document by its due date into the order tray.
Read the first paragraph of the top document and decide: sign, file or send back.
Stamp the signed documents with the captain's stamp.
Walk the signed documents to the captain's desk.
File the rest in the cabinet by department code.
what_makes_it_hard: Making a quick sign, file or return call on each document without skipping due dates; failure is a backlog that the captain signs blind.
ideal_interaction: Drag each document in the queue to a sign, file or return bin, with a due-date timer turning red on any item left unsorted too long.

label: Walk the captain's deck round notes
human_steps: Walk the bridge corridor with the captain's notes in hand.
At each station, read the captain's note aloud to the officer on duty.
Wait for the officer to answer and write the answer beside the note.
Tick off each note once the officer confirms the item is done.
Look at the corridor lights for any dim panel and note its location.
Return the notes to the captain's folder.
what_makes_it_hard: Getting a real answer from each officer rather than a nod; failure is a small complaint that reaches the captain as a crisis.
ideal_interaction: Tap each station in the corridor in turn, and the note ticks only after the player selects the officer's answer from a spoken options list.

label: Log survey briefing and tasking
human_steps: Walk to the bridge desk and take the survey briefing sheet.
Read the targets and the bridge order line by line.
Copy each department's task beside its name in the tasking log.
Check the start and end times against the bridge order.
Read the finished log back to the first officer.
Hand the log to the first officer for a signature.
what_makes_it_hard: Copying tasks and times accurately from briefing to log; failure is departments working to inconsistent tasking.
ideal_interaction: Type each target and department into the tasking form, which flags any department name typed against the wrong task.

label: Route science requests to captain
human_steps: Walk to the science request tray and lift the top request.
Read the request title and the science officer's priority tick.
Place the request on the captain's review pile if urgent, or the next-day pile if not.
Clip the CSO's report page to the request.
Walk the review pile to the captain's desk.
Check the next-day pile has no urgent request left in it.
what_makes_it_hard: Ranking science requests by urgency without reading each one fully; failure is science waiting on a decision that was urgent.
ideal_interaction: Drag each science request into the urgent or next-day lane, where the lanes fill in urgency order and an alert fires if an urgent request sits unrouted.

label: Draft survey summary for the log
human_steps: Pull the survey results summary from the desk tray.
Read each target's result and write one line per target in the log template.
Note the completed pass count and any missed targets.
Check each line's timestamp against the survey log.
Read the finished summary aloud to the first officer.
Place the draft in the captain's log tray for review.
what_makes_it_hard: Summarising many results accurately and stating gaps plainly; failure is a log with gaps the debrief cannot explain.
ideal_interaction: Fill the log template one target line at a time, where the template refuses to close a line until its data status box is ticked.

label: Confirm manifest paperwork with Quartermaster
human_steps: Walk to the cargo desk and find the Quartermaster.
Take the manifest and read each crate's number and weight.
Walk the cargo floor and check each crate against its line.
Tick each line on the manifest as you reach its crate.
Count the crates against the total on the manifest's last line.
Ask the Quartermaster to initial the signed manifest copy.
what_makes_it_hard: Matching paperwork to physical crates one by one, including quantities; failure is a customs-style hold up at handover.
ideal_interaction: Walk the cargo floor and tap each crate on the manifest screen to match its number, with unmatched crates left unticked until they are counted.

label: Draft cargo status note for captain
human_steps: Pull the cargo status board and read the current crate tally.
Note the ETA and any delays on the status line.
Write a one-paragraph note covering cargo, ETA and risk.
Read the note back against the board to check each number.
Correct any figure that disagrees with the board.
Place the note in the captain's tray.
what_makes_it_hard: Writing a short status that says exactly what changed and when; failure is a captain surprised by a delay that was already known.
ideal_interaction: Fill the status form from the board, where each field pulls its number from the live board and any stale line turns amber.

label: Clear captain's calendar for relief op
human_steps: Walk to the desk and open the captain's calendar.
List the meetings in the next six hours, marking each as movable or fixed.
Call each attendee's department to move the movable meetings.
Note the new times on the calendar grid.
Block the relief operation window across the captain's day.
Confirm the block with the captain before the window starts.
what_makes_it_hard: Deciding which meetings truly move and getting each attendee to confirm; failure is the captain double-booked in the middle of a crisis.
ideal_interaction: Drag meetings off the relief window on the calendar grid; fixed meetings refuse to move, and the window only blocks once every conflict is resolved.
fit_note: Calendar clearing here means phone calls to attendees, which a calendar grid does not include.

label: Relay sickbay requests to captain and bridge
human_steps: Walk to the sickbay request panel and read each request.
Mark which requests need captain approval and which need bridge action.
Walk the captain's request slip to the ready room desk.
Walk the bridge request to the helm console and hand it to the duty officer.
Ask the receiver to read back each request.
Note the read-back on the request sheet before moving on.
what_makes_it_hard: Splitting medical requests correctly between captain and bridge and confirming receipt; failure is a medical ask lost in traffic.
ideal_interaction: Tap each request onto the captain or bridge lane on the routing board; a request turns green only after the receiver's read-back arrives.
fit_note: Decoding a signal does not cover the hand delivery of paper slips or the spoken read-back.

label: Track personnel reassignments to sickbay
human_steps: Pull the reassignment notices from the desk tray.
Find each named crew member on the duty roster.
Note the sickbay shift each one is moving to.
Write the new posting into the roster and cross out the old one.
Check that no reassignment leaves a watch short.
File the notices in the sickbay folder.
what_makes_it_hard: Matching names, cross-outs and shift gaps across the roster; failure is volunteers missing from the duty roster.
ideal_interaction: Drag each reassigned crew token from its watch slot to the sickbay slot; the old slot clears, and any watch left short shows a red gap.

label: Print drill checklist for captain
human_steps: Walk to the readyroom desk and open the drill template.
Fill in the drill name, date and station list.
Choose the checklist version from the template library.
Print the checklist sheet on the desk printer.
Read the printed sheet for any missing step line.
Clip the sheet into the captain's folder.
what_makes_it_hard: Picking the current checklist version and catching a missing step before it is printed; failure is the captain running drills from an old list.
ideal_interaction: Pick the checklist version from the library, drag the required steps onto the page, and send it to the printer; a stale version shows a dated watermark that blocks printing.
fit_note: Filling a form misses the printing, reading the sheet and handing it over in the captain's folder.

label: Time and note each drill result
human_steps: Walk to the bridge drill console and set the stopwatch to zero.
Press start on the stopwatch at the drill start lamp.
Press stop at the drill end lamp and read the elapsed time.
Write the time and the crew name on the drill sheet.
Compare the time with the target on the sheet and mark it pass or slow.
Move to the next drill and set the watch again.
what_makes_it_hard: Starting and stopping the watch exactly on the lamp signal; failure is a result with no reliable time for the post-run review.
ideal_interaction: Tap the stopwatch the instant the start lamp lights and again on the end lamp, with the reading judged against the target band.
fit_note: A trend view shows a graph; the job is timing a live signal and recording the figure.

label: Draft shakedown findings for the log
human_steps: Collect the drill sheets, test sheets and defect notes from the desk tray.
Read each defect and write a line for it in the findings draft.
Group defects by craft or system as the sheets show them.
Check each line's figure against its original sheet.
Read the margin notes on each sheet and transcribe any defect found there.
Send the draft to the captain's log.
what_makes_it_hard: Catching every defect, including margin notes, and quoting its figure exactly; failure is defects going undocumented.
ideal_interaction: Work through each defect card, with the findings line committing only when its figure matches the source sheet, and margin notes staying flagged until transcribed.

label: Hold course and log deviations
human_steps: Sit at the helm console and read the heading ring and the drift needle, noting how many degrees the ship is off its mark.
Rest two fingers on the attitude thruster trim lever and nudge it one click at a time until the needle sits on the centre tick.
Watch the needle for ten seconds to confirm it stays settled instead of creeping back.
Pick up the deviation log stylus, write the time, the heading error in degrees and the trim you applied in the next empty row.
Tap the comm key to ask nav for the ETA to the next waypoint and copy the reply into the log margin.
Mistake looks like trimming too hard so the needle overshoots, or logging a figure read off the wrong ring.
tools: helm console heading ring and drift needle
what_makes_it_hard: Judging how much trim will settle the ship without oscillating, and writing the true deviation; failure is overcorrection or a log that says holding while the needle has drifted.
ideal_interaction: Keep a drift needle centred by stepping a trim lever with the arrow keys, then press L to write the deviation once the needle has been still for a few seconds; overshooting or logging while off-centre is a fault.
fit_note: Station keeping holds a box against a current; it never asks for heading trim or a logged deviation.

label: Attitude thruster pre-check
human_steps: Go to the thruster bank cabinet below the helm rail and open the self-test panel with your key card.
Press the self-test button for quad one and watch the four response bars fill in turn.
Read each quad's response time off the digital counter and write it on the check sheet beside the rail.
Compare quad three against the other three; any figure over the printed limit gets a circle on the sheet.
Run a short dry puff on the suspect quad and listen at the valve housing for a hiss that means it is sticking.
Mistake looks like marking every quad green from the bar display without reading the counter, which hides a slow valve.
tools: thruster self-test panel and key card
what_makes_it_hard: Telling a slow valve that is within limit from one that is sticking needs the counter figures and the ear test together; failure is a sticky valve that passes the check and jams during a real burn.
ideal_interaction: Walk to the thruster cabinet, hold the self-test key per quad while reading its counter, then press the puff key on quad three while listening for the sticky click; a valve past the limit left unflagged is a fault.
fit_note: Braking burn is a timed approach to a marker; the real pre-check is a self-test read and a valve listen.

label: Align navigational deflector
human_steps: Stand at the deflector dish readout on the helm console and read the alignment offset in the top window.
Look at the debris density gauge below it and note whether the reading is light, medium or heavy.
Turn the dish alignment knob slowly toward the centre mark, stopping when the offset figure stops falling.
Set the density compensation dial one notch at a time to match the gauge, not the last figure you wrote.
Press the verify key so the sensors read back the deflector setting, and wait for the confirm light.
Mistake looks like chasing the offset past zero, so the dish now points into a dust cloud the sensors have just called clear.
what_makes_it_hard: Finding the true minimum of the alignment offset and matching compensation to the real density; failure is a dish aimed into dust or a verify that confirms a bad setting.
ideal_interaction: Sweep a faint hum on the deflector readout by turning the alignment knob with the hold keys, then press lock as the hum peaks; locking early or late on the peak is a fault.

label: Hold station and steady drift
human_steps: Stand at the helm console and read the drift meter to see which way the ship is sliding on the current.
Put both hands on the thruster stick and push it the opposite way in short bursts, never holding it hard over.
Watch the box on the mark display and count how long the marker stays inside its edges.
Ease the stick back as the marker reaches the centre so the next gust does not throw it past the far side.
Keep this going until the bridge order lamp changes, glancing at the hold indicator each time.
Mistake looks like full-deflection bursts that overshoot the box and leave the hull rocking slowly back and forth.
what_makes_it_hard: Making small, steady corrections against gusts you cannot predict without overshooting; failure is slow lurches as the drift builds up.
ideal_interaction: Nudge a marker back into a box against a steady drift with the arrow keys, tapping lightly for each correction while the hold meter fills; a marker that leaves the box resets the hold.

label: Thruster pre-check
human_steps: Walk to the thruster bank panel on the aft bridge wall and unlock its cover with the maintenance key.
Run the self-test cycle on all four quads in turn, watching each response counter settle.
Note the slowest quad's figure and compare it with the limit printed on the card taped to the panel.
Open the valve inspection window and look at the sticky-valve flag for each quad.
Press the flag reset only on a quad whose valve reads clear, then close the cover and turn the key.
Mistake looks like shutting the cover over a red flag because the counter bar looked fine.
tools: aft thruster bank panel and maintenance key
what_makes_it_hard: Judging whether a figure inside the limit still hides a valve that will stick; failure is a jam discovered only at burn time.
ideal_interaction: Hold the flag key on each quad while its counter runs, then reset only the clear ones; resetting a red flag or leaving the limit card unchecked counts as a fault.
fit_note: A timed braking approach does not represent a routine valve flag inspection.

label: Fly the survey grid at slow, steady speed
human_steps: Read the survey grid chart on the helm display and find the first line marked in amber.
Set the throttle lever to the slow notch and hold it there while watching the speed readout.
Steer along the grid line by nudging the yaw wheel, keeping the track on the thin amber line.
At each grid corner check the position dot, then ease the wheel to turn in a wide, even arc.
Glance at the speed readout after every turn to confirm you came back to the set notch.
Mistake looks like speed creeping up on the straights, or a jerky turn that smears the sensor sweep.
what_makes_it_hard: Holding a constant slow speed and a smooth arc at every corner so the sensor sweeps line up; failure is speed drift and jerky turns that smear the data.
ideal_interaction: Hold a throttle key at the slow notch and steer the ship round the grid with the arrow keys, keeping the track in the amber lane; leaving the lane or speeding up on a straight is a fault.
fit_note: Course plot steps through waypoints; the real work is holding a constant slow speed through smooth turns.

label: Hold station for deep scan
human_steps: Check the sensor officer's request chit for the scan heading and the hold time it asks for.
Switch the helm into station-hold mode and read the drift needle to see how hard the current pushes.
Ease the thruster stick against the drift in small pulses, keeping the marker in the centre ring.
Watch the scan status light; it turns amber as soon as the ship has moved too far for a clean scan.
Keep holding until the scan light goes green and the requested hold time has run out.
Mistake looks like a large correction that rocks the ship mid-scan and blurs the reading.
what_makes_it_hard: Keeping the ship still for the full requested time against a current that varies; failure is a scan that fails part way and a survey value that drops.
ideal_interaction: Pulse the arrow keys to keep a marker in a centre ring while a scan timer counts down; leaving the ring turns the scan light amber and the deep scan fails.

label: Realign deflector for dust
human_steps: Read the dust density figure on the bridge sensor panel and write the level in the survey log.
Go to the deflector alignment ring under the helm console and feel for the detent at each step.
Rotate the ring one detent at a time, reading the hull-pitting risk meter at each position.
Stop when the pitting meter drops into its lowest band and stays there for a few seconds.
Press the lock on the deflector panel so the harmonic stays set through the whole grid.
Mistake looks like locking at the first lower reading and missing a deeper dip one detent further on.
what_makes_it_hard: Finding the true lowest point among several dips instead of the first one that looks better; failure is a locked harmonic that leaves the hull exposed to pitting.
ideal_interaction: Sweep a tuner left and right across the deflector band with the hold keys, watch the strength meter climb, and press lock on the deepest dip so the pitting meter stays low.

label: Plot and fly the transit leg
human_steps: Take the waypoint list from the nav printout and check the first leg's start and end on the helm chart.
Enter the next waypoint's bearing on the course dial and confirm the plotted line on the screen.
Check the hazard overlay for debris or ion patches on the line, and move the waypoint if one is crossed.
Engage course hold and read the cross-track error on the strip beside the helm screen.
Trim the heading with the yaw wheel whenever the error rises above the printed tolerance.
Mistake looks like flying the old line without rechecking the hazard overlay after a waypoint change.
what_makes_it_hard: Keeping the ship on a plotted track while the hazards change, and noticing when the plan has gone stale; failure is flying into a hazard or arriving late at handoff.
ideal_interaction: Step the plot from waypoint to waypoint with the arrow keys and re-check each leg's hazard tiles before engaging hold; plotting through a flagged patch or skipping a waypoint is a fault.

label: Ease to a docking approach
human_steps: Read the docking port range and the closing speed on the approach board before the ship leaves the transit lane.
Bring the throttle to the approach notch and let the speed readout settle before braking.
Hold the brake key while watching the speed readout, releasing it as the speed enters the green band near the marker.
Glance at the cargo shift indicator; a rising shift warning means ease off right away.
Make small thruster corrections to line the ship up on the docking collar's centre line.
Mistake looks like holding the brake too long so the ship stalls short, or letting go early and missing the marker.
what_makes_it_hard: Timing the brake so the ship reaches the marker inside a narrow speed band while the cargo is already moving; failure is a rough approach that shifts the cargo.
ideal_interaction: Hold Space to brake so the ship reaches the dock marker inside the green speed band; too fast means go round and stalling short is a fault.

label: Confirm hold position for transfer
human_steps: Receive the deck's transfer request and read the hold window it gives on the transfer slip.
Look at the transfer collar's range display and note the offset in metres, front and side.
Use the lateral thrust keys to bring the offset into the printed box, one small press at a time.
Wait for the hold meter to fill, watching the offset stay inside the box for the full window.
Report hold confirmed to the pilot and the deck crew over bridge comms, giving the offset figure.
Mistake looks like confirming while the offset is still drifting, so the transfer starts against a moving collar.
what_makes_it_hard: Holding the offset steady for the whole window before calling it; failure is confirming too early, which aborts the transfer.
ideal_interaction: Use the lateral keys to centre a range marker, then press Enter to report hold confirmed only after the marker has sat centred for the full window; confirming early is a fault.

label: Best-speed run to the stricken site
human_steps: Read the casualty priority on the sickbay board and the distance to the stricken world on the chart.
Set the throttle to the full-cruise notch, then check the speed readout against the best-speed figure on the flight card.
Hold heading steady with the yaw wheel, keeping the ship inside the lane markers on the route screen.
Check the ETA counter every few minutes and tell the bridge if it slips past the requested time.
Ease off only when the hazard alarm sounds, reading the bearing to the obstacle before you move.
Mistake looks like pushing past best speed and tripping the warp limit alarm, or easing off with no hazard in sight.
what_makes_it_hard: Holding the highest safe speed for the whole run rather than just the start; failure is a late arrival or a limit alarm that forces a slowdown.
ideal_interaction: Keep a throttle key held at the cruise notch while steering down the lane with the arrow keys; easing off without a hazard, or exceeding the speed limit, is a fault.
fit_note: Route plotting is the current screen; the real job is sustaining top speed over a long run.

label: Smooth deceleration, minimal jolt
human_steps: Check the sickbay's casualty note for the jolt limit, and the handoff marker position on the helm display.
Start slowing early by feathering the retro-brake lever into a gentle first notch.
Keep one hand on the inertia bar and watch the casualty jolt meter as speed bleeds off.
Step the brake down in small increments, matching the meter so it stays below the printed jolt line.
Ease the ship onto the marker and stop with the speed readout inside the green.
Mistake looks like a fast final notch that spikes the jolt meter, which means a casualty was thrown on the sickbay deck.
what_makes_it_hard: Shedding speed gradually from a long way out so the final stop is gentle; failure is a jolt spike that injures patients during transfer.
ideal_interaction: Tap the brake key in short pulses that step the speed down gradually, keeping the jolt meter under its line until the marker is reached; a spike over the line is a fault.

label: Hold steady for transport
human_steps: Confirm with the transporter chief that the lock is ready, and read the transporter range on the console.
Set the station-hold toggle and check the drift readout for the current pushing the ship.
Use the attitude thruster pad in short taps to keep the ship centred on the transport beacon.
Watch the lock indicator; it flickers when the ship moves beyond the printed tolerance.
Hold position until the transporter chief calls transport complete over the comm.
Mistake looks like a sudden thrust that breaks the lock mid-transport and forces a restart.
what_makes_it_hard: Staying inside a tight tolerance for the whole transport without a single large correction; failure is a broken lock that drops the transport.
ideal_interaction: Keep a transport beacon inside a locking ring with light arrow taps, watching a lock lamp that must stay lit until the chief's call; a flicker that breaks the lock is a fault.

label: Run the helm maneuver test series
human_steps: Pick up the maneuver test card from the bridge table and read the list of tests in order.
Work through each test at the helm console: forward, reverse, port and starboard turns at the stated rate.
For each test, read the handling figure from the console and write the result against the test number.
Log any sluggish response, such as a yaw that lags the wheel or a thruster that fails to fire, as a handling fault.
Reset the console to baseline before the next test, and check the baseline light has come on.
Mistake looks like marking a test passed when its handling figure never left the normal band.
what_makes_it_hard: Telling a real handling fault from normal variation across a range of manoeuvres; failure is missing a sluggish response that shows up later in service.
ideal_interaction: Steer a sequence of turns with the arrow keys, one per test, logging each turn's response; a turn with a lagging response must be flagged rather than passed.
fit_note: A single braking approach; the real job is a sequence of manoeuvres each judged by its handling figures.

label: Hard turn and stop test
human_steps: Read the test card for the turn rate and the stop marker distance, then confirm the dampers are on standby.
Take the yaw wheel hard to one side and hold until the turn reaches the rate line.
Snap the wheel back to centre and pull the brake lever, watching the stopping distance readout.
Check the damper status light stays green through the stop; any amber means the dampers are working hard.
Stop on the marker and read the distance travelled off the stop ruler on the console.
Mistake looks like stopping short of the marker without logging it, or missing an amber damper light.
what_makes_it_hard: Stopping on the marker straight out of a hard turn without overshooting while watching the dampers for strain; failure is an untested damper and a stop that comes up short or long.
ideal_interaction: Hard-turn with the yaw keys, then hold the brake key until the ship stops on a marker; stopping short, or ignoring the damper light, is a fault.
fit_note: A straight braking approach only; the test has no hard turn and no damper check.

label: Submit maneuver report
human_steps: Collect the maneuver test log and the card with the handling figures from the helm console.
Open the report form on the console and fill in each test name from the top of its log line.
Copy each handling figure exactly, checking its unit, degrees or seconds, against the log line.
Set the status for each test, pass, marginal or fail, against the printed limit.
Read the completed form back and look for any blank field before filing.
Press Enter to file the report to the CFO's queue and confirm the filed lamp lights.
Mistake looks like copying the previous test's numbers into this form, or leaving a field blank so the CFO sends it back.
what_makes_it_hard: Copying every figure exactly and choosing the right status from the limit, with no blank field; failure is an incomplete report that has to go back to the CFO.
ideal_interaction: Fill each form field from the readings with the arrow keys, checking each value against its unit, then press Enter to file; a blank field or a figure from the wrong test is a fault.

label: Position fix against star references
human_steps: Take the star reference card from the nav table and find the three named stars for this watch.
Read the bearing for each of the three stars from the sensor star-bearing readout.
Draw a line from each star's bearing on the chart, using the parallel rule against the ruled edge.
Look at where the three lines meet, expecting a small triangle rather than a single point.
Measure the gap between the crossing and the dead-reckoning mark with the dividers.
Log the fix position and the drift correction in the nav log.
Mistake looks like using only two stars, or taking the middle of a wide triangle as the position.
what_makes_it_hard: Drawing three bearing lines accurately and reading their cross point, while rejecting a bad bearing; failure is a fix placed on a decoy line.
ideal_interaction: Press the marked point where three bearing lines cross; a decoy line that does not meet the others, or a fix taken from two lines, is a fault.

label: Plot and verify the next leg
human_steps: Pull the next leg's waypoint list from the chart tray and check the hazards marked in the chart margins.
Lay the leg on the chart with the plotting ruler, from the start point to the new waypoint.
Measure the leg length with the dividers and read the distance off the scale bar.
Work out the arrival time by dividing the distance by the cruise speed on the flight card.
Cross-check that arrival time against the helm's ETA, and flag any difference over five minutes.
Send the verified course to the helm and wait for its course laid in reply.
Mistake looks like laying a leg across a shaded hazard, or sending the course before the ETA check.
what_makes_it_hard: Checking the arrival time against an independent estimate and keeping clear of hazard margins; failure is a course that cuts a hazard or an ETA the helm does not trust.
ideal_interaction: Step the course through the waypoints with the arrow keys, avoiding shaded hazard tiles, then press Enter to send; plotting into a hazard or sending before the ETA check is a fault.

label: Deflector and damper readout check
human_steps: Walk from the bridge to the engineering junction with the damper sheet in your hand.
Read the deflector field values off the junction's three gauges and write each on the sheet.
Look at the damper bank indicator lights and note any that show amber or red.
Compare each damper reading with the value nav assumed and mark the difference in pencil.
Write any anomaly in the margin with the time, then walk back to the bridge.
Mistake looks like copying the nav's assumed figure instead of the gauge reading, which hides the drift.
what_makes_it_hard: Reading the gauge honestly and spotting the small gap from the assumed value; failure is hiding a drift because the reading looks close enough.
ideal_interaction: Walk to a pressure valve at the junction and press Space when its needle sits in the band, bleeding each gauge in turn; a bleed outside the band is a fault.
fit_note: Bleed-valve timing game; the real job is reading gauges and comparing them against nav's assumptions.

label: Maintain plot and fixes on the holding course
human_steps: At the nav table, pull the holding course plot and note the time of the last logged fix on the chart.
Every half hour, take a new bearing from the star sensor and write it in the chart margin.
Plot each fix against the holding line with the ruler, marking any offset from the line.
Move the dead-reckoning mark back to the fix position to correct the drift.
Tell the helm the current correction over the bridge comm so it can trim the heading.
Mistake looks like letting the dead-reckoning mark run for an hour unchecked, so the drift builds unseen.
what_makes_it_hard: Keeping a running plot honest as small errors pile up across a long watch; failure is slow drift that becomes a large correction later.
ideal_interaction: Keep a plot marker on the holding line by taking periodic bearing fixes with the star keys; letting the marker run unchecked for too long is a fault.
fit_note: A single three-star fix; the real job is a running plot kept up over a whole watch.

label: Update charts with the latest sensor data
human_steps: Go to the lab console and pull the latest sensor sweep log from the data tray.
Read each new contact's size, emission and motion on the printout.
Find the matching chart entry on the lab screen using the contact's grid reference.
Overwrite the entry's position and velocity with the new reading, replacing the stale value.
Mark any entry older than a day with a staleness flag so it gets rechecked.
Mistake looks like updating a contact's class but leaving its old position, so the chart still shows where it used to be.
what_makes_it_hard: Matching each new reading to the right chart entry and spotting which entries are out of date; failure is a chart that shows old positions as current.
ideal_interaction: Drag each contact's marker to its updated grid cell on the lab chart and type the new coordinates; a marker left at its old cell is a fault.
fit_note: Classify sorts contacts into classes; the real work is updating chart positions and staleness flags.

label: Plot survey grid and leg order
human_steps: Take the survey area brief from the science officer and read the grid size on the chart sheet.
Rule the grid on the chart: parallel lines at the spacing the brief prints.
Number the legs in order, planning each turn so the ship never doubles back over a leg.
Check the grid edges against the hazard markers and move any leg that touches one.
Write the leg order on a list and hand it to the helm with the chart.
Mistake looks like spacing lines too wide so sensors leave gaps, or too narrow so the legs overlap.
what_makes_it_hard: Spacing and ordering the legs so the sensor sweep covers the area with little overlap and no hazards; failure is gaps or overlaps that waste the survey.
ideal_interaction: Place each survey leg on the grid with the arrow keys, snapping its spacing to the brief; gaps or overlaps between legs, or a leg across a hazard, count as faults.

label: Hold station on each survey point
human_steps: Read the survey point's coordinates from the list and confirm them on the chart display.
Put the ship on station-hold and check the drift readout for which way the current is pushing.
Call thrust corrections to the helm over comm, saying which way and how much to push.
Watch the helm's marker sit inside its box and wait for the sensor officer's go-ahead.
Log the time the point was held and the largest drift seen during the hold.
Mistake looks like calling the hold done before the sensor officer's scan is complete.
what_makes_it_hard: Keeping a hold through the full scan window by talking the helm through corrections; failure is a blurred scan and a complaint from sensors.
ideal_interaction: Watch a drift marker on the mirror display and press the direction call-out keys to tell the helm which way to push, keeping the marker in the ring until the scan go-ahead; letting it leave the ring is a fault.
fit_note: The game has the player fly the thrust; the real job is calling corrections to the helm and logging the hold.

label: Merge survey fixes into the chart
human_steps: Take the survey fix log from the lab tray and count its entries against the grid's leg count.
Open the lab chart and find the first leg's row on the paper.
Transfer each fix onto the chart with a dot and a short label, writing its time beside it.
Look at where two legs meet and check that the overlapping fixes agree within the tolerance card.
Discard any duplicate fix, writing the reason in the margin so the next watch knows why.
Mistake looks like transferring a fix to the wrong leg because the grid labels were smudged.
what_makes_it_hard: Putting each fix in the right place and resolving overlapping points by the rule, not by eye; failure is a chart the cartographers cannot reuse.
ideal_interaction: Tap each survey fix onto the lab chart at its grid cell with a stylus, then hold the overlap key to reconcile duplicates; a fix tapped on the wrong leg or an unreconciled duplicate is a fault.
fit_note: A bearing-cross game; the real job is transferring and reconciling fix points onto a chart.

label: Plot the most economical route to the drop point
human_steps: Read the drop point position and the cargo's mass and power budget from the cargo sheet.
Lay out two or three candidate routes on the chart with the plotting ruler.
For each route, measure its length with dividers and multiply by the power cost per unit on the sheet.
Pick the route with the lowest total power cost that keeps clear of the shaded hazards.
Write the chosen route's waypoint bearings on the course sheet and check them twice.
Mistake looks like choosing the shortest line through a hazard shading, or forgetting the power cost of a detour.
what_makes_it_hard: Weighing distance against power cost and hazard clearance across several candidate routes; failure is a cheap-looking route that burns more power or crosses a hazard.
ideal_interaction: Compare candidate routes by stepping each plot through its waypoints and reading the power cost off the console; picking a route that crosses a hazard or costs more is a fault.

label: Compute arrival window with the cargo schedule
human_steps: Pull the cargo schedule from the ops board and read each handling block with its earliest and latest times.
Work out the transit time from the chosen route's total length and the cruise speed.
Mark the earliest and latest arrival on the schedule strip with a red pencil.
Check each cargo team's start window against the arrival window, moving any block that overlaps.
Write the final arrival window on the sheet and pass it to ops for the crew roster.
Mistake looks like forgetting the time spent slowing for the approach, so the window runs late.
what_makes_it_hard: Fitting the transit and every handling block into one window with the braking margin built in; failure is cargo teams who are not ready when the ship arrives.
ideal_interaction: Slide each cargo block along the timeline with the arrow keys so it fits inside its window, then press Enter to book it; a block booked outside its window or with no braking margin is a fault.

label: Final approach plot to the station
human_steps: Check the station's docking corridor on the chart, noting the entry bearing and the final range.
Plot the last three legs to the docking collar, keeping each one inside the corridor's walls.
Read the closing speed the helm will need on each leg and write it under the leg on the plot.
Check the station traffic schedule for any ship using the corridor, and shift your last leg if needed.
Send the final plot to the helm and wait for its approach plotted reply.
Mistake looks like an approach line that clips a corridor wall, which the helm would have to fight at the last second.
what_makes_it_hard: Holding the final legs inside a tight corridor with the right closing speed on each one; failure is a rough docking the helm has to rescue.
ideal_interaction: Step the plot through three approach waypoints with the arrow keys, keeping each leg between the corridor walls; a leg touching a wall or crossing a traffic lane is a fault.

label: Plot the fastest safe course to the stricken world
human_steps: Read the stricken world's position and the casualty urgency from the sickbay message on the console.
Lay the direct course on the chart, then check it against the hazard zones on the sensor overlay.
Where the direct line crosses a hazard, bend the route round it and measure the added distance.
Compare the fastest-looking route with the safe one and choose the one with the earlier safe arrival.
Write the course bearings on the relief sheet and read them back to the helm.
Mistake looks like taking the direct line through a hazard to save ten minutes, which costs far more if the hull is hit.
what_makes_it_hard: Trading the fastest line against hazard clearance under time pressure; failure is a fast route that puts the ship in a hazard.
ideal_interaction: Plot the fastest route with the arrow keys, then bend it around each hazard tile the sensor overlay lights up; a route entering a lit hazard tile is a fault.

label: Report revised arrival time as the plot changes
human_steps: When the course changes, recalculate the arrival time from the new route length and the current speed.
Open the arrival report form on the nav console and find the estimated arrival field.
Enter the new time, checking it against the urgency time written in the relief sheet's notes.
Set the revised status flag so sickbay knows the figure has changed, not just been copied.
Read back the time, the change and the reason you wrote before sending.
Press Enter to send it to the bridge and watch for the received light on the console.
Mistake looks like sending the old time because the new calculation was never done after the reroute.
what_makes_it_hard: Recalculating on every route change and sending promptly with the revised flag set; failure is sickbay staging supplies for the wrong time.
ideal_interaction: After each route change, fill the arrival form's time and status with the arrow keys and press Enter to send before the timer runs out; sending the old time or skipping the revised flag is a fault.

label: Plot orbit and transporter-range hold
human_steps: Read the orbit parameters on the transporter chief's sheet: the orbit height and the required transporter range.
Plot a circular orbit on the chart at the set height with the compass and ring template.
Shade in pencil the arc of the orbit that falls within transporter range.
Work out how long the ship can hold each range point at orbital speed.
Check that the hold windows match the times the transporter chief needs for the lock.
Send the orbit and hold windows to the chief and wait for its lock feasible reply.
Mistake looks like plotting an orbit that drops out of range at the exact moment the lock must be made.
what_makes_it_hard: Drawing an orbit whose range windows line up with the lock times; failure is a lock that slips when the ship leaves range.
ideal_interaction: Walk a marker round the orbit ring with the arrow keys, and hold the transporter key while it is inside the range arc; leaving the arc before the lock completes is a fault.
fit_note: Course plotting; the real job is an orbit with timed range windows rather than a route to a waypoint.

label: Run the full set of calibration courses
human_steps: Pull the calibration course list from the test card and set the first course's waypoints on the chart.
Plot each calibration course in turn, measuring its expected arrival time with dividers.
Record each course's planned time in the calibration log beside its test number.
Fly the course on the helm console while watching the ETA counter against the plan.
Note any arrival that differs from the plan by more than the card's tolerance.
Mistake looks like marking a course calibrated when its arrival was never compared with the plan.
what_makes_it_hard: Comparing each course's actual arrival with its plan and noticing when the gap matters; failure is helm errors that stay hidden until later.
ideal_interaction: Step each calibration course with the arrow keys, then check the ETA counter at the end of the leg; an arrival missing the planned time by more than the tolerance is a fault.
fit_note: Course plotting; the real job is a set of flown courses timed against plan.

label: Compare dampers and deflector against nav predictions
human_steps: Walk to the engineering junction with the nav predictions sheet and the damper log.
Read the damper and deflector values from the junction logger screen, one row at a time.
Compare each reading with its predicted value and mark any difference above the tolerance.
Look at how each difference changes across the last hour of the log, whether rising or falling.
Note the point where a reading first strays past its limit, with its timestamp.
Mistake looks like checking only the latest reading and missing a slow rise over the hour.
what_makes_it_hard: Spotting a slow rise across a long log that the latest reading does not show; failure is faults found later, under load.
ideal_interaction: Scroll a damper trace on the junction logger and press the segment where the reading first leaves its limit; choosing a later segment or missing the earliest drift is a fault.

label: Write up fix accuracy results
human_steps: Collect the fix log from the three shakedown runs and list the position error for each fix.
Measure each fix's error as its distance from the known test position, using the dividers.
Average the errors for each run, and note the worst single fix in the margin.
Write the results into the accuracy table on the report form, one row per run.
Add a note on whether each run met the accuracy the test card asks for.
Check the figures against the fix log once more, looking for a transposed digit.
Mistake looks like averaging the errors but dropping the worst fix, which hides the real accuracy.
what_makes_it_hard: Reporting the worst fix beside the average without dropping inconvenient points; failure is a report that overstates accuracy and leaves no baseline.
ideal_interaction: Enter each run's error values into the accuracy form with the arrow keys and press Enter to file; leaving out a run's worst error, or a transposed digit, is a fault.

label: Shuttle preflight walk-around
human_steps: Walk the hull of each shuttle on the pad, starting at the nose and going clockwise round the hull.
Crouch at each hatch seal and run a gloved finger round the gasket, feeling for cracks or lifting.
Look into each thruster nozzle for scorching or debris, and tap the housing to listen for a loose part.
Open the fuel access cover and read the level on the gauge against the card.
Check the battery indicator and the hull lights, noting anything dark on the card.
Sign the preflight card on the pad clipboard and tick the shuttle's box.
Mistake looks like signing a shuttle without walking the far side, so a loose seal is found at launch.
what_makes_it_hard: Spotting a small seal crack or loose part on the far side of a hull; failure is a defect found only when the shuttle is needed.
ideal_interaction: Walk the pad route with the movement keys, holding the inspect key at each seal and nozzle until its gasket shows; skipping a seal or signing before the walk is done is a fault.

label: Shuttlebay door and pressure check
human_steps: Walk to the bay door and read the pressure gauge on the door frame; both sides must show inside the band.
Check the interlock light on the door control, which should be amber when closed and green when sealed.
Press the interlock test button and watch the light change to confirm the lock engages.
Tug the manual release lever gently to confirm the mechanical latch holds.
Count the deck crew tethers on the rack by the door and compare the count with the stock sheet.
Mistake looks like passing the door on the gauge alone, without the interlock test or the tether count.
what_makes_it_hard: Confirming both the pressure band and the interlock on a door that can fail either way; failure is a door that opens onto vacuum or a bay short of tethers.
ideal_interaction: At the door control, press and hold the test key while the interlock lamp must change in the right order; a lamp that fails to change is a fault.

label: Fuel and flight log update
human_steps: Go to the shuttlebay console and read each shuttle's fuel figure from the gauge panel.
Type each gauge figure into the flight log against the shuttle's name and the time.
Read the defect list left by the preflight and record any defect in the defect field.
Write the fuel plan for the next launch in the notes, using the planned burn figure.
Tell the deck crew the fuel plan over bay comm, reading the figure back to them.
Mistake looks like logging a fuel figure from memory instead of the gauge, so the log and the tank disagree.
what_makes_it_hard: Entering the exact gauge figure and the real defects, then passing the fuel plan clearly to the crew; failure is a log that disagrees with the tank.
ideal_interaction: Copy each shuttle's fuel value into the flight log form, checking the figure against the gauge before pressing Enter; a value copied from the previous entry is a fault.

label: Routine preflight of both shuttles
human_steps: Go to the first shuttle on the pad and check each landing gear strut for a leak or sag.
Walk the underside and look for frost on the cold-side panels, which points to a coolant issue.
Run a gloved hand along the canopy edge to feel for a lifted seal, then check the wipers.
Move to the second shuttle and repeat the same checks in the same order, so nothing is skipped.
Compare the two shuttles' fuel gauges and write any mismatch in the pilot's log.
Mistake looks like skipping the underside of the second shuttle because the first one looked fine.
what_makes_it_hard: Running the same complete check on two shuttles so a small fault on the second is not missed; failure is a defect found only at launch.
ideal_interaction: Walk each shuttle's underside and canopy with the inspect key and press the log key to record that shuttle's check; a shuttle logged before its underside is inspected is a fault.

label: Stand ready for launch
human_steps: Stand at the launch console with the headset on and check the bay status board for both shuttles.
Hold position at the console and keep the bridge order lamp in view, ready to respond to a call.
Keep one hand near the launch key cover so you can open it without fumbling.
Confirm the bay pressure reading has not changed since the last check.
When the launch call comes in, acknowledge it over comm and start the launch sequence.
Mistake looks like looking away from the lamp too long, so the call goes unanswered and the launch is delayed.
what_makes_it_hard: Staying alert through a long stand-by with no visible work; failure is a slow answer when a launch is needed.
ideal_interaction: Keep watch on a lamp that flashes at random intervals and press the acknowledge key within two seconds of each flash; a missed flash is a fault.
fit_note: Bench is a pass or reject test rig; the real job is standing ready and reacting to a launch call.

label: Prep survey shuttle with sensor pod
human_steps: Collect the sensor pod from its cradle in the bay store and check its label against the survey brief.
Carry the pod to the survey shuttle's underside rack, holding it level by both handles.
Seat the pod's four lugs into the rack, feeling each one click into its socket.
Connect the power and data plugs at the pod's rear, twisting each collar until it locks.
Look at the pod's status light and confirm it shows steady green rather than blinking.
Mistake looks like seating the pod with one lug unclicked, which can shake loose in flight.
what_makes_it_hard: Seating and locking the pod so it stays fixed under flight loads; failure is a pod that works on the pad but shakes loose on launch.
ideal_interaction: Lift the pod into the rack with the grab key, then press each lug and twist each collar until its lock light shows; a lug left unlocked or a blinking status light is a fault.

label: Launch and fly survey pattern
human_steps: Strap into the survey shuttle's pilot seat and run the pre-launch check on the console.
Ask the bay for clearance, then release the clamps when the bay light goes green.
Lift off on the throttle with a steady climb, holding attitude against the bay's air draw.
Fly the survey pattern by steering along each leg and holding the speed the card gives.
Turn at each corner in a shallow bank, levelling out before the next leg.
Mistake looks like a steep bank that swings the sensor pod off its line and blurs the survey.
what_makes_it_hard: Holding a steady altitude and track along each leg in a constant bank; failure is a blurred survey or a pod knocked off its line.
ideal_interaction: Fly the survey route with the throttle and yaw keys, holding the leg marker inside the pattern lane; a steep bank that swings the pod out of the lane is a fault.
fit_note: Route plotting; the real job is flying a steady pattern with a sensor pod on board.

label: Recover shuttle and hand over data cores
human_steps: Bring the shuttle back toward the bay on approach, slowing as the bay mouth comes into view.
Brake with the reverse thrusters in steps, watching the closing speed on the approach board.
Set the shuttle down on the landing marks on the pad, feeling the gear take the deck.
Shut the engines down and wait for the pad crew to chock the wheels.
Open the data core bay and lift out each core, handing them to the science officer one at a time.
Mistake looks like landing with the core bay still open, so a core is lost when the bay is opened.
what_makes_it_hard: Bringing the shuttle to the marks at a safe speed and then removing every core without losing one; failure is a hard landing or a missing core.
ideal_interaction: Ride the reverse-thrust key down toward the pad's landing marker and hold it steady until the wheels-down light comes on; overshooting the marker or stalling short is a fault.

label: Clear and load cargo shuttle with cargo handlers
human_steps: Walk the cargo manifest with the handler lead, reading each crate's mass and label.
Lift each crate with the handler arm and set it on the shuttle deck, port or starboard as the manifest says.
Check the trim indicator on the shuttle's floor panel after every few crates.
Shift a heavy crate across when one side reads over the trim limit, then check the indicator again.
Pull each cradle strap tight until its clip clicks, once the crate is in place.
Mistake looks like loading the last heavy crate on one side, which pushes the trim past the limit before launch.
what_makes_it_hard: Keeping the mass balanced across the deck as crates go in, so the last ones do not tip the trim; failure is a mass-balance error at launch.
ideal_interaction: Stow crates on a trim board with the port and starboard keys, keeping the two sides inside the limit; letting one side exceed it is a fault.

label: Shuttle cargo across to rendezvous
human_steps: Take the rendezvous coordinates from the nav sheet and set them into the shuttle's flight computer.
Ask for launch clearance, then lift off and climb to the transit lane altitude.
Fly the plotted leg, watching the heading tape and the cross-track needle on the panel.
Check the hazard warning light as you pass each waypoint, turning early if it lights.
Slow for the final approach to the rendezvous ship, matching its speed on the radar.
Mistake looks like missing a waypoint and flying straight at the rendezvous, which takes the shuttle through a hazard.
what_makes_it_hard: Flying the plotted line accurately through each waypoint and matching the rendezvous ship's speed; failure is a missed waypoint or a rough meet.
ideal_interaction: Step the shuttle's route waypoint by waypoint with the arrow keys, holding heading inside the cross-track band; a missed waypoint or an ignored hazard light is a fault.

label: Return and secure shuttle
human_steps: Bring the shuttle into the bay on the door's guide light and stop at the marked spot.
Set the shuttle down and wait for the pad crew to fasten the clamps.
Check the bay door's seal light and the pressure gauge before closing the door.
Close the bay door using the control and watch the interlock lamp turn green.
Lock the shuttle's hatch, then set the security bar across the door's latch.
