Mistake looks like closing the door with the security bar left off, leaving the bay open and unsecured.
tools: door seal light and pressure gauge
what_makes_it_hard: Completing the whole lock-up in order, including the security bar that gets skipped; failure is a bay left open and unsecured.
ideal_interaction: Push and hold the door control until the interlock lamp turns green, then lift the security bar from its rack and hook it across; a door shut without the bar is a fault.

label: Ready casualty shuttle with biobeds
human_steps: Collect the biobed unit from the store and wheel it to the casualty shuttle's rear hatch.
Unfold the biobed frame and lock each leg until its stop clicks.
Plug the biobed into the shuttle's power socket and check its status panel shows green.
Set the restraints and check each strap buckle for a firm click.
Stock the medical kit beside the bed from the sickbay list, checking expiry dates.
Mistake looks like leaving one bed leg unlocked, so the bed tips when the shuttle banks.
what_makes_it_hard: Locking every bed part, the power and the restraints, and checking expiry dates against the list; failure is a bed that moves or fails with a patient on it.
ideal_interaction: Lock each biobed leg with the clamp key, then connect the power plug and wait for the status light to stay green; a leg left unlocked or a red status light is a fault.

label: Fast flight to patient site
human_steps: Load the patient site coordinates into the flight computer from the sickbay's urgent message.
Ask for launch clearance and lift off as soon as the bay light goes green.
Fly the direct route, watching the time-to-arrival counter and the route line on the panel.
Hold speed on the straight legs, but drop it before each waypoint turn.
Check the medic's comm light and tell the medics the ETA each time it changes.
Mistake looks like cutting a waypoint corner at speed, which puts the biobeds at risk of a jolt.
what_makes_it_hard: Balancing a fast route with speed drops at each waypoint so the patients are not jolted; failure is losing the golden hour or a rough ride.
ideal_interaction: Step the route with the arrow keys while holding a speed key on the straights, letting go before each waypoint turn; holding speed through a turn is a fault.

label: Smooth recovery with medics aboard
human_steps: Bring the shuttle over the patient site landing pad, reading the lowering rate on the altitude tape.
Ease the throttle back to a gentle descent, keeping the rate under the printed limit.
Touch down on the pad's marks, feeling for a soft settle rather than a bump.
Ask the medics to confirm the biobeds are secure before you open the hatch.
Shut down and hand the patients to the medics, checking each bed's straps are undone.
Mistake looks like a fast touchdown that jolts the biobeds, the injury the sickbay warned about.
what_makes_it_hard: Holding a gentle descent so every touchdown is soft; failure is a rough landing that injures patients.
ideal_interaction: Tap the descend key to bring the descent rate inside the landing band, then release it over the marker; a touchdown above the band is a rough-landing fault.

label: Full shuttle systems test
human_steps: Connect the test rig to the shuttle's diagnostic socket and power up the systems panel.
Run the engine, life support and navigation tests in the order on the test card.
Read each system's value on the rig and compare it with the spec printed beside it.
Pass a system whose value sits inside its spec, reject one outside it, and mark the card.
Check the battery and fuel sensor readings twice, since they drift between runs.
Mistake looks like passing a system from a reading taken before the warm-up finished.
what_makes_it_hard: Reading each system against its spec at the right point in warm-up, and rejecting ones that are only marginal; failure is a fault that surfaces in flight.
ideal_interaction: Work each system's reading against its printed spec with the pass and reject keys, after the warm-up timer runs out; passing a reading taken before warm-up is a fault.

label: Short test flight with launch and dock cycle
human_steps: Launch from the pad on the test card's climb profile and note the launch time.
Fly the short test leg, watching the flight recorder for each system's response.
Turn back toward the bay and set up for docking, lowering approach speed as the bay mouth grows.
Dock on the bay's marks, bringing speed into the green band before the final brake.
Check the dock clamp light and the recorder's end-of-cycle tally before shutting down.
Mistake looks like docking on a fast approach, which leaves no clean flight data for the report.
what_makes_it_hard: Completing a full launch and dock cycle with clean data for the report; failure is a rough dock or missing flight data.
ideal_interaction: On the dock approach, hold the brake key so the ship reaches the bay marker inside the green speed band, then release so the clamps seat; an approach outside the band is a fault.

label: File defect list
human_steps: Gather the defect notes from both shuttle walk-throughs and from the test flight recorder.
Open the defect form on the bay console and create one entry per defect.
For each entry, write the shuttle name, the system, and a one-line description of what was seen.
Set the severity to grounded, flagged or minor, according to the defect card's rules.
Attach the recorder reference number to any defect found in flight.
Read the list back against the test card and check nothing is missing.
Mistake looks like filing a grounded fault as minor, so the shuttle flies again with a known defect.
what_makes_it_hard: Classifying each defect's severity correctly against the card's rules; failure is a grounded fault filed as minor that reappears next time.
ideal_interaction: Type each defect's shuttle and system into the bay form, pick its severity with the arrow keys, then press Enter to file; a grounded fault filed as minor is a fault.

label: Test comm relays and PA zones
human_steps: Walk from the datacore door to the relay junction panel on the aft bulkhead, carrying a handheld noise probe clipped to a belt loop.
Open the junction cover with a hex key and read the status lamp on each relay card: green is seated, amber means it is drifting.
Clip the probe to the relay's noise port and watch the needle for hiss; a jump above the baseline mark is a fault.
Walk to the PA zone plate on the wall and press each zone key in turn, listening for a clean tone with no crackle.
Write latency and noise numbers into the junction logbook, one line per relay, in pencil.
If a relay card rocks in its slot, unplug it, check the edge connector for green corrosion, reseat it and re-test.
Mistake to avoid: ticking a zone as clean without listening to the tone through the speaker grille.
what_makes_it_hard: The officer must judge a faint hiss against baseline by ear and by needle, and a rushed tick hides a failing relay until the bridge goes deaf.
ideal_interaction: Carry the probe from relay to relay, press the matching zone key on the wall plate after each one, and reseat a card that reads noisy until the needle settles under the baseline mark.
fit_note: PA game covers zone pings only; the walk to junctions, probe reading and relay reseating are missing.

label: Monitor hails and ship traffic
human_steps: Sit at the comms console on the bridge and put on the headset, keeping one ear clear for the bridge.
Scan the incoming channel list top to bottom, looking for a flashing hail marker and its bearing readout.
Click the hail to open it and listen for the caller's ship name and channel code.
Note the bearing and channel number on the paper strip beside the console.
Route the call: a priority hail goes straight to the bridge handset, a routine one goes into the announcement queue.
Close the channel after the caller acknowledges, then return to the list.
Mistake to avoid: answering a hail on the wrong channel and cutting off a live caller mid-sentence.
what_makes_it_hard: The officer must triage several hails at once and route by priority without dropping a caller; a missed priority hail is the failure.
ideal_interaction: Watch the incoming list, click each flashing hail to open it, then drag it to the bridge handset or the queue before the caller's timer runs out.

label: Review the computer specialist queue
human_steps: Walk to the datacore console and sit down at the ticket terminal.
Scroll the fault queue, reading each ticket's system tag, severity and the specialist's name.
Open one ticket, read the error text and note which stack or network segment it names.
Pick the specialist whose shift is free and whose tag matches, then drag the ticket to their name.
Open a completed ticket and check the specialist's fix note against the error text before signing it off.
Send a fix back for rework if the note only says restarted without a cause.
Mistake to avoid: signing a ticket off with an empty fix note because the queue is long.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement comes from matching a fault to the right specialist and rejecting vague fix notes; a careless sign-off lets a fault recur unseen.
ideal_interaction: Read each ticket's error text, drag it onto the matching specialist, then open finished tickets and reject any whose fix note does not name a cause before stamping sign-off.

label: Align the subspace transceiver
human_steps: Walk to the transceiver cabinet and open the hatch with the access key.
Read the carrier lock lamp; if it is off, note that the array is out of phase.
Pick up the trim wrench and turn the first array trim screw in small clicks while watching the carrier meter.
Turn the trim in the opposite direction when the needle overshoots, stopping at the highest steady reading.
Read the signal margin dial and write its value in the alignment log.
Close the hatch and check the lock lamp again before leaving.
Mistake to avoid: over-turning a trim past the peak and losing lock on the link.
what_makes_it_hard: Finding the peak needs small, patient turns read against a needle that lags; overshoot drops the link and the officer must start again.
ideal_interaction: Hold the trim wrench on each array screw and turn it slowly, stopping when the carrier needle reaches its highest steady point, then lock the margin.

label: Open channels and test PA
human_steps: Stand at the bridge comms console as the bridge order comes in and confirm the channel list is empty.
Open the all-decks channel and select the PA test phrase from the card taped beside the console.
Speak the test phrase clearly into the headset mic at normal volume.
Listen through the bridge speaker for clipping or echo, and note the reply from one deck.
Open each remaining channel in turn and confirm its light turns green.
Close the test channel and log the time the announcement went out.
Mistake to avoid: speaking too quietly, so the test passes on a dead mic.
what_makes_it_hard: The officer must hear whether the announcement is clear, not just whether the light is green; a garbled first announcement is the failure.
ideal_interaction: Open each channel on the list in order, speak the test phrase into the mic, and listen for clipping before the channel light is allowed to turn green.

label: Routine relay sweep
human_steps: Walk to the relay junction on the datacore wall with the sweep card in hand.
Read each relay's status lamp and note any that are amber or dark.
Press the test button on each card and listen for the click that confirms the relay switched.
Wipe the dust off a card's lamp window with a cloth if the lamp looks dim.
Tick the sweep card for each relay and write the junction time at the bottom.
Carry the card to the ops officer's desk and hand it over.
Mistake to avoid: ticking every lamp green without pressing the test button on each one.
what_makes_it_hard: A drifting relay gives no alarm on its own; only a test press and a dim-lamp check catch it, and a skipped card hides the fault.
ideal_interaction: Walk the junction, press each relay's test button until it clicks, and wipe any dim lamp window before ticking that card off the sweep list.
fit_note: Physical sweep is inspection of relay lamps and test buttons; the current activity flips breakers, which is a different action.

label: Relay sensor data link to the bridge
human_steps: Sit at the datacore console and open the sensor relay feed screen.
Select the sensor data channel and confirm the packet counter is climbing.
Open the link route and check the hop list ends at the bridge node.
Send a test packet and watch it appear on the bridge node indicator.
If the packet stops at a hop, open that hop and re-enter its address from the routing card.
Confirm the bridge node shows full packet flow, then close the route screen.
Mistake to avoid: confirming the link from the local counter alone without seeing the packet arrive at the bridge.
what_makes_it_hard: The job is proving the data arrives end to end, not just leaving the datacore; a link that looks live locally but stalls at a hop is the failure.
ideal_interaction: Send a test packet down the route, then trace each hop on screen and retype a broken hop's address from the routing card until the packet lands on the bridge node.

label: Scan subspace bands for signals
human_steps: Sit at the bridge comms console and set the scanner to the lowest band.
Step the sweep up one band at a time, watching the waterfall display for bright streaks.
When a streak appears, lock the cursor on it and note its frequency and strength.
Listen on the audio monitor for a tone or pattern and compare it with the last log.
Log any contact that repeats across two sweeps as a possible signal.
Move to the next band and repeat until the top band is done.
Mistake to avoid: dismissing a faint streak as noise without checking whether it repeats.
what_makes_it_hard: Telling a real contact from noise means watching for repetition across sweeps; a faint real hail dismissed as static is the failure.
ideal_interaction: Step the sweep across each band, lock the cursor on every faint streak, and flag it only if it reappears on the next pass through the waterfall.

label: Keep the science team's comm channel clear
human_steps: Sit at the bridge console and open the science team's channel on the list.
Listen for crosstalk: a second voice or a tone bleeding in from a nearby channel.
Find the bleeding channel and open its patch panel view on the console.
Drag the faulty channel's input off the science feed to a clean spare slot.
Speak a test line on the science channel and confirm no bleed comes back.
Mute the spare slot so stray traffic does not reach the science team.
Mistake to avoid: patching the science feed onto a live bridge channel, which spreads the crosstalk instead of clearing it.
what_makes_it_hard: Clearing crosstalk means finding which channel leaks and re-patching it without cutting another crew's line; a wrong patch spreads the noise.
ideal_interaction: Listen for bleed on the science channel, drag the leaking input to a spare slot on the patch panel, then speak a test line to confirm the bleed is gone.
fit_note: Tuning a frequency does not match finding and re-patching a crosstalk source.

label: Hail the receiving station and confirm the schedule
human_steps: Sit at the bridge comms console and open a hail to the receiving station on the channel card.
Wait for the receiving station's operator to answer, listening for the station name and the call sign.
Read the planned docking window from the schedule sheet aloud, slowly, with the time zone.
Listen for the operator to read back the window; repeat any part they did not confirm.
Write the confirmed window and the operator's name in the schedule book.
Close the hail after both sides say the window is agreed.
Mistake to avoid: accepting a vague yes without the operator reading back the exact times.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is getting an exact, read-back confirmation of times over a noisy line; a slipped window makes the docking miss.
ideal_interaction: Open the hail, read the schedule sheet's window aloud, then wait for the operator's read-back and type only the times they actually confirmed into the book.
fit_note: Decoding a signal does not capture spoken schedule read-back and confirmation.

label: Link cargo and transporter channels
human_steps: Walk to the datacore junction with a patch lead and the cargo channel label card.
Find the cargo channel's jack on the junction board and unplug its lead gently.
Plug the lead into the transporter channel's jack and check the jack light turns on.
Run the continuity tester across both ends to confirm the link is closed.
Write the new patch pair on the junction board's label card.
Call the transporter chief on the handset and ask them to speak into the new line.
Mistake to avoid: unplugging the wrong jack, which silences a live channel for the cargo crew.
what_makes_it_hard: Patch errors are silent until someone talks; a wrong jack or a loose plug leaves cargo crews working blind.
ideal_interaction: Pull the cargo lead from its jack, seat it in the transporter jack, run the continuity tester across it, and confirm by voice with the chief before writing the label.

label: Send the delivery manifest confirmation
human_steps: Sit at the bridge console and open the manifest confirmation form.
Read the manifest number off the cargo clipboard and type it into the ID field.
Count the crates listed on the clipboard against the crate total field and enter the number.
Tick each seal number on the clipboard against the seal field, one at a time.
Check the receiving officer's name line matches the schedule book before submitting.
Press send and wait for the acknowledgement line to show the manifest was received.
Mistake to avoid: sending the form with a crate count copied from the last manifest.
what_makes_it_hard: A confirmation is only as good as the numbers typed in; a miscount or wrong seal number is accepted silently and causes mislabelled crates later.
ideal_interaction: Tick each seal on the clipboard against the form, check the crate count line by line, and submit only when the acknowledgement line confirms the manifest.

label: Open a priority channel to the destination
human_steps: Sit at the bridge comms console and open the destination list for medical traffic.
Select the destination's channel code from the list and confirm the priority flag is set.
Turn the frequency dial until the carrier lock light stabilises on the destination.
Listen for the handshake tone and confirm it sounds on both sides.
Log the handshake time in the medical traffic book.
Keep the channel open and set the priority flag as the active link.
Mistake to avoid: leaving the dial on a close neighbour frequency, which lets the link flicker.
what_makes_it_hard: The officer must lock the right carrier and keep it stable; a neighbouring frequency gives a link that looks open but drops during a patient handover.
ideal_interaction: Turn the frequency dial slowly until the carrier lock light holds steady on the destination, then wait for the handshake tone before logging the priority channel as open.

label: Keep the sickbay link prioritised
human_steps: Walk to the datacore junction board with the priority label card.
Find the sickbay line's jack and check its lamp shows priority, not routine.
If the lamp shows routine, move the lead from the routine bus jack to the priority bus jack.
Check the jack lamp changes to the priority colour and the bus count reads one.
Run the continuity tester across the lead to confirm no break.
Tick the priority card and note the time at the bottom.
Mistake to avoid: moving the sickbay lead to the priority bus without ticking the card, so the next officer undoes it.
what_makes_it_hard: Priority is a physical patch on a shared bus; a lead left on routine lets sickbay calls queue behind ordinary traffic during a crisis.
ideal_interaction: Check the sickbay jack's lamp, move the lead from the routine bus to the priority bus, then run the continuity tester and confirm the lamp turns priority before ticking the card.

label: Relay medical updates to the bridge
human_steps: Sit at the bridge console and pull up the sickbay update channel on the list.
Listen to the sickbay officer's update and write each patient's name and status on the pad.
Check each status term against the medical code sheet, for example stable, critical or in transit.
Type the coded update into the bridge report screen one patient per line.
Read the typed update back to the sickbay officer to confirm no name was wrong.
Send the report to the bridge handset and wait for the bridge officer's acknowledgement.
Mistake to avoid: passing a status word that the sickbay officer did not say, such as calling a patient stable when they said stabilising.
what_makes_it_hard: Accurate transcription under pressure is the skill; the bridge plans from these words, and a guessed status sends the wrong team.
ideal_interaction: Write each patient's status as the sickbay officer says it, check it against the code sheet, then read the typed line back to confirm before sending it to the bridge.
fit_note: Scanning signals does not capture transcribing spoken patient status from a voice update.

label: Full PA and relay test, every zone
human_steps: Walk to the relay junction with the shakedown checklist and the probe.
Check each relay lamp and clip the probe to its noise port.
Walk to each PA zone plate in turn, pressing its key and listening at the grille.
Speak the zone test phrase and listen for clipping, echo or a dead zone.
Mark each zone pass or fail on the checklist, and note the speaker number for any fail.
Walk back to the junction and re-test any failed zone after reseating its relay.
Mistake to avoid: testing only the zone nearest the junction and marking the rest as passed.
what_makes_it_hard: A full test means walking every zone and listening properly at each; skipping a zone leaves a dead speaker hidden until the ship needs an alert.
ideal_interaction: Walk each zone plate in turn, press its key, speak the test phrase and listen at the grille, marking pass or fail before moving to the next zone.
fit_note: Console-based PA game lacks the walk through every zone and the probe check at the junction.

label: Subspace transceiver range test
human_steps: Walk to the transceiver cabinet with the range card and the beacon case.
Take the beacon out of its case and check its battery light is on.
Walk along the corridor to the first distance mark and set the beacon down on the marker.
Return to the cabinet, set the transmit dial to the test carrier and read the margin.
Note the margin and distance in the range log, then repeat at each mark.
Stop at the mark where the margin falls below the minimum and record it.
Mistake to avoid: reading the margin at the cabinet without moving the beacon to the marks, which gives no range.
what_makes_it_hard: The range is only known by walking the marks and reading the margin at each; a short test gives a false sense of reach.
ideal_interaction: Carry the beacon to each distance mark, set it down, return to the transmit dial and read the margin before moving on until the margin drops below the minimum.
fit_note: Tuning at one console misses the walk to distance marks and the beacon placement.

label: Alert-tone and fault-warning drill
human_steps: Sit at the bridge console and open the alert panel from the drill card.
Press the first alert tone key and listen through the headset for the correct tone.
Check the tone matches the alert name on the card, such as red alert or fault warning.
Trigger the fault warning and confirm the bridge warning light and the speaker both respond.
Note any alert whose tone is missing, wrong or late on the drill sheet.
Reset each alert after it finishes and move to the next one.
Mistake to avoid: confirming an alert by its light alone without listening to the tone.
what_makes_it_hard: The drill must confirm each tone is right and audible; a warning that lights but sounds wrong fails in a real emergency.
ideal_interaction: Press each alert key, listen through the headset to match its tone to the card, and mark it wrong on the drill sheet if the tone or the light is missing.
fit_note: Decoding signals is not auditing alert tones and warning lights against a drill card.

label: Core diagnostic sweep
human_steps: Walk to the isolinear core stacks and stop at the first stack's diagnostic panel.
Press the integrity check key and watch the stack bar fill, noting any segment that shows amber.
Read the cache latency figure and the network latency figure on the readout beside the stack.
Open the error list and select each flagged error, reading its code before clearing it.
Clear the error only after the cause is fixed, then note the segment in the sweep log.
Repeat on each stack in turn, then write the sweep result in the log.
Mistake to avoid: clearing a flagged error without reading its code, which hides a repeating fault.
what_makes_it_hard: Reading an amber segment and a latency figure together tells a real fault from a passing blip; clearing without the cause lets faults recur.
ideal_interaction: Watch each stack's integrity bar and latency readout, open every flagged error to read its code, and clear it only after the cause is noted in the log.
fit_note: A trend chart shows the numbers but not the stack-by-stack integrity check and clearing of flagged errors.

label: Comm relay and data network check
human_steps: Sit at the ops console on the bridge and open the relay chain view.
Press the ping key on the first relay and watch the reply time appear.
Compare each reply time against the baseline card taped beside the console.
Ping each relay in the chain in turn, writing any reply that is above baseline.
If a relay is high, open its reroute menu and note the alternative route.
Report the high relay to the comms officer on the handset with its number and reply time.
Mistake to avoid: reporting a relay as high from a single slow reply instead of two pings.
what_makes_it_hard: A single slow reply is noise; the officer must compare against the baseline and confirm with a second ping before raising a fault.
ideal_interaction: Ping each relay, compare its reply time with the baseline card, re-ping any slow one to confirm, then pick the reroute and report it by handset.

label: Backup rotation and patch staging
human_steps: Walk to the backup tape rack in the datacore with the rotation card.
Pull the oldest backup cartridge from the rack and insert it into the reader slot.
Run the checksum verify key and watch the match line until it reads OK.
Snapshot the current log files onto a fresh cartridge and label it with the date.
Open the patch staging tray and place the pending patch file on the staging spot.
Run the cache purge on stale files and confirm the freed space figure.
Mistake to avoid: inserting a cartridge that failed verification, then rotating it back into the rack.
what_makes_it_hard: Rotation is careful sequencing of verify, snapshot and staging; a backup that fails checksum but is put back looks safe until a restore is needed.
ideal_interaction: Insert each cartridge, run checksum verify and wait for the OK line before rotating it into the rack, then stage the patch and purge stale cache in that order.

label: Routine core sweep and log review
human_steps: Sit at the datacore console and open the core log file from the list.
Scroll the log, reading each line's time and severity tag.
Pick out lines tagged warning or error and open each to read the stack ID.
Compare the stack ID against the stack map to find the physical stack.
Tick each reviewed stack on the sweep card and note any repeated error.
Save the sweep card and close the log.
Mistake to avoid: reviewing only the last page of the log and missing a warning from earlier in the shift.
what_makes_it_hard: Small cache errors repeat quietly in the log; the job is spotting a repeat pattern across lines, and missing it lets scan markers drop.
ideal_interaction: Scroll the core log, open each warning line to read its stack ID, match it on the stack map and tick the sweep card only for stacks you have read through.
fit_note: A door access log does not match reading core diagnostic logs and mapping stack IDs.

label: Backup rotation and cache purge
human_steps: Walk to the backup rack and pull the cartridge due for rotation.
Insert it into the reader and run the checksum verify until the OK line shows.
Return to the console and open the cache purge screen.
Select the stale cache folders from the list and confirm the purge.
Watch the freed-space figure rise and note it in the rotation log.
Put the verified cartridge in the rack slot marked with that day's date.
Mistake to avoid: purging cache before the snapshot is verified, losing the only good copy.
what_makes_it_hard: The order matters: verify the backup before purging anything, or the purge destroys the only copy.
ideal_interaction: Insert the cartridge, wait for checksum OK, then choose only the stale cache folders on the purge screen and confirm the freed-space figure before putting the cartridge in its rack slot.

label: Allocate core capacity to sensor data intake
human_steps: Sit at the datacore console and open the capacity allocation screen.
Read the sensor intake queue depth and its current share of the core.
Drag the intake share slider up in small steps while watching the queue depth fall.
Check the other departments' shares do not drop below their floor values.
Confirm the new share on the screen and note the change in the allocation log.
Wait a minute and re-read the queue to confirm scans are no longer backing up.
Mistake to avoid: giving sensors all capacity, starving the sickbay and bridge floors.
what_makes_it_hard: Balancing one department's need against the floors of others is a judgement call; too much to sensors starves other crews.
ideal_interaction: Drag the sensor intake slider in small steps while watching the queue depth, stopping once the queue clears and every other department still sits above its floor.
fit_note: Power budget game does not capture the queue-depth balance between departments' floors.

label: Index and archive survey data
human_steps: Sit at the datacore archive terminal and open the survey folder list.
Read each raw scan file's name and date, checking it matches the survey number on the card.
Tag each file with the survey code and the scan type in the index form.
Move the tagged files to the archive volume using the move command.
Open one archived file and confirm it opens and its size matches the original.
Write the index count and archive volume total at the bottom of the card.
Mistake to avoid: moving a raw scan before tagging it, so it cannot be found later.
what_makes_it_hard: Files that are moved untagged are lost to the next search; the job is careful tagging and a size check after each move.
ideal_interaction: Tag each raw scan with its survey code in the index form, move it to the archive, then open one archived file to confirm its size matches before the next file.
fit_note: Verification checks a file's integrity but not tagging files into an index before moving them to archive.

label: Back up results before mission end
human_steps: Walk to the backup cartridge rack and take a fresh cartridge from the spare tray.
Insert it into the reader and label it with the survey name in marker.
Open the survey results folder and select the full set for backup.
Run the backup and watch the progress bar until it reaches the end.
Run the checksum verify on the new cartridge and wait for the OK line.
Log the cartridge number and file count in the backup book.
Mistake to avoid: ending the mission after the progress bar hits the end without the checksum OK line.
what_makes_it_hard: A backup that has not been verified is only a hope; the checksum OK is the proof, and skipping it loses the results if the core faults.
ideal_interaction: Select the full results set, run the backup and wait for the progress bar, then do not sign off until the checksum verify shows OK on the labelled cartridge.

label: Load manifest database and seal records
human_steps: Sit at the datacore console and open the manifest database from the cargo list.
Load the current manifest and read its header for the manifest number and date.
Check each record against the paper manifest clipboard, line by line.
Correct any mismatched crate ID in the record field.
Press the seal key on each completed record to lock it.
Confirm the seal count on the screen matches the crate count on the clipboard.
Mistake to avoid: sealing a record with a crate ID that was not checked against the clipboard.
what_makes_it_hard: A sealed record is hard to reopen; a wrong crate ID sealed in place means handlers mislabel crates from then on.
ideal_interaction: Check each record's crate ID against the clipboard line by line, correct any mismatch, and press seal only after the seal count matches the clipboard's crate count.
fit_note: Verification checks integrity; the job is matching records to a paper clipboard and sealing them.

label: Keep transporter and cargo scanning links responsive
human_steps: Walk to the transporter room and sit at the scanner link console beside the pad.
Read the scanner link buffer and the lookup latency figure on the screen.
Clear the oldest entries in the buffer by selecting them and pressing purge.
Adjust the link priority dial toward cargo scans until the latency figure drops.
Watch a test pattern lookup complete within the time shown on the card.
Note the latency and buffer size in the transporter log.
Mistake to avoid: raising link priority so high that the transporter chief's own scans stall.
what_makes_it_hard: The officer trades cargo priority against the chief's scans; too much priority stalls the other side.
ideal_interaction: Purge the oldest buffer entries, then nudge the priority dial toward cargo until a test lookup finishes within the card's time, backing off if the chief's scans slow.

label: Prioritise medical records and sickbay database access
human_steps: Sit at the datacore console and open the sickbay database access screen.
Read the queue of pending record requests and their urgency tags.
Move the urgent patient requests to the top by dragging them above routine ones.
Open the first urgent record to confirm it loads within the expected time.
Grant access to the sickbay terminal ID shown on the request card.
Log the grant and the time on the access sheet.
Mistake to avoid: granting access to a terminal ID that is not on the request card.
what_makes_it_hard: The officer must rank urgent requests above routine ones and grant only the matching terminal; a wrong grant leaks records or delays treatment.
ideal_interaction: Drag urgent patient requests above routine ones, open the first record to confirm it loads, then grant access only to the terminal ID named on the card.

label: Hold clean relay link to the sickbay and bridge
human_steps: Sit at the bridge ops console and open the relay link screen.
Select the sickbay link and read its noise level and reply time.
Select the bridge link and read the same figures.
If either link shows noise, switch it to the backup route and re-read the figures.
Confirm both links read clean and the reply time is under the card's limit.
Log the link readings and the route used in the relay book.
Mistake to avoid: holding a noisy link because the reply time looks fine, which hides static on the line.
what_makes_it_hard: Reply time can look fine while the line is noisy; the officer must read both figures and switch routes before the relief team loses contact.
ideal_interaction: Read each link's noise level and reply time, switch a noisy link to the backup route, and hold until both show clean under the card's limit.

label: Keep the medical database mirrored
human_steps: Sit at the datacore console and open the mirror status screen.
Read the mirror lag figure and the last sync time.
If the lag is high, start a manual sync from the mirror menu.
Watch the sync bar until it reaches the end and the lag drops.
Open one patient record on the mirror and compare it with the live copy.
Log the sync time and lag figure in the mirror book.
Mistake to avoid: treating a finished sync bar as mirrored without comparing a record on the mirror.
what_makes_it_hard: A sync can finish with a stale record; comparing one live copy against the mirror is the only proof the mirror holds.
ideal_interaction: Start a manual sync when lag is high, wait for the bar to finish, then open a live patient record and compare it with the mirror copy before logging it.

label: Full core diagnostic and stress test
human_steps: Walk to the core stacks and open each stack's diagnostic panel in turn.
Set the load dial to the stress setting on the test card.
Start the stress run and read the temperature gauge on each stack as it climbs.
Watch for any segment that goes amber or any stack whose temperature passes the card's limit.
Stop the run when the time on the card runs out and note each stack's peak reading.
Read the error log for any error that appeared only under load.
Mistake to avoid: ending the stress run early because the first stack looks fine.
what_makes_it_hard: Hidden faults appear only under load; the officer must watch every stack's peak and not stop early.
ideal_interaction: Set the load dial to stress, watch each stack's temperature gauge climb while noting peaks, and stop only when the card's time runs out.
fit_note: A trend view shows numbers but not setting the load dial and watching each stack's gauge under stress.

label: Test relay failover and network redundancy
human_steps: Sit at the bridge ops console and open the relay failover screen.
Choose the primary relay on the list and press the take-offline key.
Watch the traffic counter shift to the backup route and confirm no packets are lost.
Walk the failover card's checklist: ping the bridge, ping the sickbay, ping the sensors.
Bring the primary relay back online and confirm traffic returns to it.
Log the failover time and any lost packets in the test book.
Mistake to avoid: failing over one relay and assuming the rest work without pinging each route.
what_makes_it_hard: Failover is untested until a real fault; the officer must confirm every route answers after the switch and back again.
ideal_interaction: Take the primary relay offline, watch the traffic counter shift to backup, ping each route on the card, then bring the relay back and confirm traffic returns.
fit_note: Decoding signals does not test failover by taking a relay offline and pinging each route.

label: Write the shakedown fault report
human_steps: Sit at the datacore console and open the shakedown report form.
Read the test results on the sweep card and the failover book for each system.
Type each fault as one line with its system, its code and the stack or relay number.
Mark each fault with a severity from the card: critical, major or minor.
Check the report's total count matches the faults listed on the cards.
Send the report to the ops officer and note the send time on the card.
Mistake to avoid: listing a fault without its code, so no one can find it again.
what_makes_it_hard: A report is only useful if every fault is listed with a code and a severity; vague lines leave the bridge with no list of what to fix.
ideal_interaction: Type each fault as a coded line from the test cards, pick its severity from the card, check the total count against the cards, then send the report.

label: Work the ops board
human_steps: Sit at the bridge ops console and open the board of open requests.
Read each request's department, power figure and urgency tag.
Compare the power asks with the current bus load shown in the side panel.
Call engineering on the handset to agree a rebalance when two asks clash.
Assign each comm or transport task to the matching officer on the board.
Update the bridge status line and clear each finished request.
Mistake to avoid: rebalancing power alone without asking engineering, which overloads the bus.
what_makes_it_hard: Several departments ask for the same power at once; the officer must rank asks against the bus load and confirm with engineering before committing.
ideal_interaction: Compare each power ask against the bus load panel, call engineering to agree any clash, then drag each task onto the officer who must act on it.

label: Check comm junctions
human_steps: Walk from the bridge to the datacore junction with the diagnostic kit.
Open the junction cover and read each relay's lamp in turn.
Clip the diagnostic meter to a relay test point and read the signal loss figure.
Write any relay whose signal loss is above baseline on the junction sheet.
Reseat a drifting relay card, then re-read its signal loss.
Walk back to the bridge and tell the comms officer by handset which relay drifted.
Mistake to avoid: reporting a relay as fine after reading only its lamp, not its signal loss.
what_makes_it_hard: A lamp can show green while the signal drifts; the officer must read the meter at each test point and reseat before reporting.
ideal_interaction: Open the junction, clip the meter to each relay's test point and read the signal loss, then reseat any drifting card and re-read it before reporting.
fit_note: Breaker flipping does not match reading relay signal loss with a meter and reseating cards.

label: Transporter readiness sign-off
human_steps: Walk to the transporter pad and meet the transporter chief at the console.
Ask the chief for the pattern buffer log and read the last entries.
Check each buffer entry's status against the readiness card.
Walk onto the pad and check the pad's ground line with a hand tester.
Sign the readiness sheet only if every entry reads clean and the pad line reads clear.
If any entry is marginal, press the lock-out key and tell the bridge at once.
Mistake to avoid: signing readiness without walking onto the pad to check its ground.
what_makes_it_hard: A signed readiness that was not walked is a bad beam later; the officer must check the log and the physical pad, and lock out on any doubt.
ideal_interaction: Read the pattern buffer entries against the readiness card, walk onto the pad to touch the ground line with the hand tester, then sign or press lock-out depending on what reads clean.

label: Supply and cargo tally
human_steps: Walk into stores and open the locker holding the critical spares.
Take the spares tally sheet from the clip on the locker door.
Count each critical spare on the shelf, pointing at each item as you say its number.
Compare each count against the manifest copy and mark any difference.
Flag each shortage on the sheet and walk it to the quartermaster's desk.
Hand the sheet over and wait for the quartermaster to initial the shortages.
Mistake to avoid: counting from the tally sheet instead of the shelf, which copies last week's number.
what_makes_it_hard: A tally is only true if counted off the shelf; copying the last count hides a shortage until a part is needed in a crisis.
ideal_interaction: Count each critical spare on the shelf by pointing and reciting, compare to the manifest copy, and mark only the differences you actually counted.

label: Confirm all ops systems nominal and report to bridge
human_steps: Sit at the ops console and open the systems status board when the bridge order comes in.
Read each system's status light in turn: power, comms, transport and computer.
Open any amber system and read its fault line before deciding it is nominal.
Tick each nominal system on the status form, writing the time beside it.
Read the completed form back to the bridge on the handset.
Wait for the bridge officer's acknowledgement before closing the form.
Mistake to avoid: reporting nominal for a system whose light is green but whose fault line is still open.
what_makes_it_hard: Small faults hide behind green lights; the officer must read the fault line of each system, not only its colour.
ideal_interaction: Read each system's status light, open any amber system to read its fault line, tick only truly nominal systems on the form, and read it back to the bridge before closing.

label: Walk the comm junctions and transporter pads
human_steps: Pick up the walk checklist at the datacore door and start with the nearest comm junction.
Open the junction cover and check each relay lamp, noting any dark or amber one.
Walk to the transporter pad and check the pad lamps and the ground line lamp.
Touch the pad's rail to feel for any heat or vibration that should not be there.
Tick each junction and pad on the checklist as you finish it.
Report any drift or heat to the bridge on the handset before leaving the route.
Mistake to avoid: ticking a junction without opening its cover, so a drifting relay inside goes unseen.
what_makes_it_hard: Drift builds slowly and is seen only by opening and touching; a ticked but unopened junction lets an anomaly grow unseen.
ideal_interaction: Walk the route in order, open each junction cover to read its relay lamps, touch the pad rail for heat, and tick each stop only after you have looked inside it.

label: Give sensors priority power and bandwidth
human_steps: Sit at the bridge ops console and open the power and bandwidth allocation screen.
Read the sensors' current draw and the bus headroom figure in the side panel.
Drag the sensor power slider up in small steps, watching the bus headroom figure.
Set the sensor bandwidth share so the sensors get priority without filling the bus.
Check the other departments' shares still show above their floors.
Confirm the allocation and note the new figures in the ops log.
Mistake to avoid: pushing sensor power until the bus headroom goes red.
what_makes_it_hard: Sensors need power and bandwidth, but pushing too far leaves the bus short for life support; the officer watches headroom as a limit.
ideal_interaction: Raise the sensor power slider in small steps while watching the bus headroom figure, stopping before it turns red and confirming other floors still show.

label: Reserve computer time for data processing
human_steps: Sit at the datacore console and open the processing timetable.
Read the open slots and the slots already reserved by other departments.
Select a block of time for sciences that does not overlap a medical or bridge slot.
Drag the block into the timetable and set its priority tag.
Check the timetable's conflict line reads clear before confirming.
Confirm the reservation and write its slot number on the request card.
Mistake to avoid: reserving a block that overlaps a medical slot, which blocks sickbay records.
what_makes_it_hard: Overlapping reservations silently block a department; the officer must check the conflict line against every other department's slot.
ideal_interaction: Pick an open block, drag it into the timetable, and confirm only when the conflict line reads clear against medical and bridge slots.

label: Keep the probe relay link open
human_steps: Walk to the datacore junction with the probe link kit.
Open the junction cover and find the probe relay card by its label.
Read the probe link lamp and the signal figure on its meter.
If the lamp is dim, reseat the card and tighten its retaining screw with the driver.
Clip the meter to the probe test point and watch the telemetry figure hold steady.
Log the telemetry figure and the time in the junction log.
Mistake to avoid: leaving the retaining screw loose, so the probe link drops again within minutes.
what_makes_it_hard: The link holds only if the card is physically seated and screwed down; a loose card looks fine on the lamp and then drops telemetry.
ideal_interaction: Reseat the probe relay card, turn its retaining screw until snug with the driver, then clip the meter to the test point and watch the telemetry hold steady.
fit_note: Tuning a link does not cover seating the card and tightening its retaining screw at the junction.

label: Check transporter and cargo handling are certified
human_steps: Walk to the transporter bench and collect the handling certificate and the test weight.
Place the test weight on the pad and set the handling rig's clamp on it.
Run the handling test and watch the rig's load gauge for any slip.
Check the clamp's grip mark on the test weight after the cycle.
Repeat the test for each handling rig on the certificate.
Sign the certificate only for rigs that passed both the gauge and the grip check.
Mistake to avoid: certifying a rig from its gauge alone when the grip mark shows slip.
what_makes_it_hard: A rig can read within load while still slipping; the officer must check the grip mark on the weight as well as the gauge.
ideal_interaction: Place the test weight on the pad, clamp it, run the handling cycle, then inspect the grip mark before signing each rig that holds on both gauge and mark.

label: Reconcile the manifest with the quartermaster
human_steps: Walk to the cargo desk and sit down with the quartermaster across from you.
Take the manifest copy and the quartermaster's inventory sheet side by side on the desk.
Read each crate line on the manifest and find the matching line on the inventory sheet.
Point at each crate on the cargo shelf to confirm its label matches the sheet.
Mark each match with a tick and each mismatch with a cross.
Agree each mismatch with the quartermaster and write the correction on both sheets.
Mistake to avoid: ticking a crate that was matched on paper but not checked on the shelf.
what_makes_it_hard: Paper can match while the shelf does not; the officer must point at real crates and agree each correction with the quartermaster.
ideal_interaction: Match each manifest line to the inventory sheet, walk to point at the crate on the shelf, then tick or cross it and write any agreed correction on both sheets.

label: Schedule transfer windows with the bridge
human_steps: Sit at the bridge ops console and open the transfer window grid.
Read the cargo delivery times from the manifest and the open dock windows on the grid.
Drag each cargo transfer onto a free window that matches its size and priority.
Check the window's conflict marker for any clash with a medical transfer.
Confirm the window with the bridge officer on the handset.
Write the confirmed window number on the manifest copy.
Mistake to avoid: booking a cargo transfer onto a window with a medical transfer, which blocks the sickbay pad.
what_makes_it_hard: Transfer windows are scarce and clash silently; the officer must match size and priority, and never take a medical window.
ideal_interaction: Drag each cargo transfer onto a free window, watch its conflict marker for any medical clash, and confirm by handset before writing the window number on the manifest.

label: Clear transporter for patient transfers
human_steps: Walk to the transporter pad with the patient transfer card.
Read the sickbay's destination coordinates from the card and enter them at the pad panel.
Read the coordinates back on the panel to check each digit.
Check the pad's lock light turns green and the buffer reads ready.
Stand clear of the pad and call the sickbay on the handset to confirm the coordinates.
Press the clear key only when the sickbay confirms the same numbers.
Mistake to avoid: clearing the pad with coordinates copied from an old card.
what_makes_it_hard: One wrong digit sends a patient to the wrong place; the officer must read every coordinate back and get the sickbay's confirmation before clearing.
ideal_interaction: Enter the sickbay coordinates digit by digit, read them back on the panel, wait for the lock light, and press clear only after the sickbay confirms the same numbers.

label: Prioritise comms with the receiving station
human_steps: Sit at the bridge comms console and open the receiving station channel.
Check the channel's priority flag and set it if it shows routine.
Confirm the handoff coordinates are saved in the channel's note field.
Send a short test line and wait for the receiving station's reply.
Read their reply aloud to confirm the channel is audible on both ends.
Log the priority time and handoff coordinates in the traffic book.
Mistake to avoid: leaving the handoff coordinates unsaved, so they are lost if the link drops.
what_makes_it_hard: Priority means nothing if the handoff coordinates are lost on a drop; the officer must save them in the channel and confirm the reply.
ideal_interaction: Set the priority flag, type the handoff coordinates into the note field, send a test line, and read the station's reply back before logging the channel as ready.
fit_note: A queue orders messages but does not cover saving handoff coordinates and confirming a live reply.

label: Divert power to sickbay on request
human_steps: Walk to the engineering power console and wait for the sickbay request to come through.
Read the sickbay's power request and the current draw on the bus panel.
Drag the sickbay power slider up to the requested level in steps.
Watch the bus voltage and the engineering alarm light while the draw rises.
Stop at the requested level and confirm the sickbay draw reads steady.
Log the diversion and its time on the engineering power sheet.
Mistake to avoid: raising sickbay power past the requested level and dropping engineering below its floor.
what_makes_it_hard: Diverting power is a trade: the requested level must hold without dropping engineering below its floor or tripping the alarm.
ideal_interaction: Raise the sickbay slider in steps to the requested level, watch the bus voltage and alarm light, and hold only where sickbay reads steady and the alarm stays off.

label: Run the full ops systems test sequence
human_steps: Walk to the datacore console with the test sequence card and open the sequence program.
Start the first test and watch its result line for pass or fail.
Walk to the matching system's panel and check its lamp matches the result line.
Move to the next test in the card's order and repeat the check.
Note each failed test and its system on the sequence card.
Re-run any failed test once after the fault is reset, and log the second result.
Mistake to avoid: reading only the result line and never checking the physical panel lamp.
what_makes_it_hard: A result line can say pass while the panel lamp disagrees; the officer must check each system's lamp against its line to catch hidden faults.
ideal_interaction: Run each test in card order, walk to the matching panel to check its lamp agrees with the result line, and note any mismatch before re-running.
fit_note: A trend graph shows numbers, not running a test sequence and checking physical panel lamps in order.

label: Log every fault found and assign tickets
human_steps: Sit at the ready room desk with the fault cards from the shakedown tests.
Take the first fault card and read its system, its code and its location.
Type the fault into the ticket form with the code and the location as written on the card.
Choose the assignee from the specialist list and set the ticket priority.
Attach the card's photo or note so the specialist can find the exact spot.
Tick the card as logged and move it to the done pile.
Mistake to avoid: assigning a ticket without the location, so the specialist searches the whole deck.
what_makes_it_hard: A ticket with no code or location costs the specialist time they do not have; every fault must be logged complete and assigned.
ideal_interaction: Take each fault card, type its code and location into the ticket form, pick the matching specialist and priority, then tick the card and move it to the done pile.

label: Engineering rounds
human_steps: Walk from the engineering corridor out onto the warp core access rail with the rounds tablet in hand.
Read the core temperature panel and the coolant inlet gauge, saying each number aloud.
Check the EPS load meter on the rail console and note the draw in megawatts.
Open the rounds log and pull up yesterday's readings for the same three gauges.
Compare each value against yesterday; a steady rise of several degrees across the lattice counts as drift.
Write the drifting gauge name and figure into the log, then close the round.
what_makes_it_hard: Judging whether a slow upward creep is normal warm-up or the start of a fault, and failing to notice drift because each reading looks fine on its own.
ideal_interaction: Walk the rail to each gauge and hold the cursor on the needle until the value settles, then drag that value onto the matching row of yesterday's log to see the change.

label: Work the repair queue
human_steps: Read the top ticket on the workshop board and note its priority tag and the named subsystem.
Walk to the parts rack and find the bin labeled with that subsystem's part number.
Lift the replacement part and check its serial sticker against the ticket.
Carry the part and a torque driver to the workbench and open the fault unit's access panel.
Swap the part, pushing each connector until it clicks, then tighten the mounting bolts in a star pattern.
Run the bench self-test and close the ticket only if the status light reads green.
what_makes_it_hard: Matching the exact part revision to the ticket and telling a truly seated connector from one that is only pressed, since a loose connector passes a quick look and fails under load.
ideal_interaction: Carry the part from the rack to the workbench, align the connector with the socket and press it in until the click, then tighten each bolt in a star pattern until the driver stops ticking.

label: Review reactor and env crews
human_steps: Walk to the plant junction and lift the crew work-order clipboard from its wall clip.
Ask the lead crew chief for status over comm and note which sections they say are finished.
Open the life support manifold cover and look at each valve handle for the paint mark that shows it was moved.
Check the pressure gauge needle against the value written on the work order.
Note any gap, such as a gauge still reading low or an unmarked handle, on the order.
Sign the order at the badge reader and hang the clipboard back on its clip.
what_makes_it_hard: Refusing to sign off a job on the crew's word alone, since the failure is signing a work order whose gauge value was never actually read at the junction.
ideal_interaction: Walk the junction and read each flagged gauge against the order's printed value, then press the sign button only after every gauge line has been checked by eye.
fit_note: The checklist covers the sign-off but not the physical junction walk and gauge check; the player never goes to the manifold.

label: Coolant and damper walk
human_steps: Walk the coolant run along the engineering bulkhead, following the orange floor line.
Read the coolant pressure gauge at each manifold tee and note its needle against the green band.
Stop at each damper housing and read the louver position indicator.
Press a fingertip to the damper actuator casing and feel for the buzz that means a louver is sticking.
Write each pressure and damper state into the wall terminal log.
Tag any gauge outside its band with a red tag before moving on.
what_makes_it_hard: Distinguishing a sticking louver from a normal one by feel before the position indicator shows any change, and spotting a slowly sagging needle inside the band.
ideal_interaction: At each damper, press and hold a finger on the actuator casing until the buzz pattern shows, then release and drag the pressure value you read at that tee onto the log row.
fit_note: Turning valves is the activity, but the job is reading pressure and damper position, not operating valves.

label: Run the routine maintenance sweep
human_steps: Walk the engineering deck clockwise, starting at the console beside the lift.
At each panel, read the status lamp color and the numeric readout, saying both aloud.
Compare each readout to the sweep card in the clipboard holder and note any value a few units off.
Wipe dust off each panel's sensor window with a lint cloth so the reading stays accurate.
Tug each cable gland lightly to confirm it is seated.
Record each drift on the console and mark the sweep complete.
what_makes_it_hard: Noticing a small drift that still sits inside the green band, and telling a real drift from a dusty sensor window that only fakes one.
ideal_interaction: Walk to each panel, stroke its sensor window with the cloth until it is clear, then drag the readout onto the matching line of the sweep card and see whether the numbers agree.

label: Catch up the repair backlog
human_steps: Pull the backlog ticket stack from the rack and sort the oldest tickets to the front.
Pick the oldest minor-fault ticket and read its symptom, such as a hum or a flicker.
Lift the faulty panel off its brackets with a flat driver and find the internal fuse.
Take a replacement fuse from the spares tin and match its amp rating to the one printed on the old cap.
Reseat the panel, screw it in, and power on to see whether the hum stops.
Initial the ticket, drop it in the closed tray, and repeat until the rack is empty.
what_makes_it_hard: Matching the fuse rating to the faulted circuit and knowing that a hum that stops for a minute is not a fix.
ideal_interaction: Pull the fuse from its holder, pick the matching one from the tin and push it home, then watch the status light stay steady for a full count before closing the ticket.

label: Divert extra power to sensors
human_steps: Read the bridge order on the console and note the target sensor array and requested power level.
Open the power distribution map and locate the sensor bus feeder lines from the EPS main.
Select the sensor feeder and raise its allocation in small steps while watching the bus voltage gauge.
Stop when the array load reaches the ordered level without the bus falling below its minimum.
Press the lock switch so the relay holds the new setting.
Report the new allocation to the bridge and log the time.
what_makes_it_hard: Feeding the sensors fast enough to meet the order without dropping the bus below the level other systems need.
ideal_interaction: Turn the sensor feeder knob in small steps on the bus map while the voltage needle climbs, and stop turning at the ordered level before the needle reaches the red zone.

label: Pre-check EPS for sensor load
human_steps: Walk to the EPS junction box on the engineering wall and open its cover with a hex key.
Read the load meter on each breaker branch and write its amperage on the pre-check sheet.
Flip each sensor-branch breaker off and on, feeling for a firm click and watching its trip light.
Add the sensor branch totals and compare them to the scan load printed on the sheet.
Flag any breaker above eighty percent or any breaker warm to the back of the hand.
Close the cover and report the pre-check total to the Chief.
tools: back of the hand heat test
what_makes_it_hard: Spotting a breaker near its trip point before it trips, and deciding whether the summed load leaves enough margin for the scan.
ideal_interaction: Flip each sensor-branch breaker, feel for the click and watch for a trip light, then copy each branch's amperage onto the expected-load line of the sheet.

label: Watch reactor margin during scans
human_steps: Take position at the warp core rail with the scan timer visible on the wall display.
Read the plasma flow and core temperature needles every few seconds and call out each value.
Watch for a needle that climbs faster than the slow creep seen during normal scans.
Check the coolant feed valve handle sits at the open mark on the rail.
If a reading crosses the red line, call the bridge to throttle the scan and say the value.
Hold position until the bridge confirms the throttle, then log the peak value.
what_makes_it_hard: Telling a fast but safe spike from a runaway rise, since a late call to the bridge lets the core run hot unnoticed.
ideal_interaction: Stand at the rail and press and hold the temperature gauge to track its needle; if the needle crosses the red mark, tap the throttle call before it reaches the top of the dial.
fit_note: A trend line is a read-only view; the real job is watching live core gauges at the rail and reacting to a spike with a throttle call.

label: Inspect cargo bay power and gravity
human_steps: Walk into the cargo bay and stop at the gravity plate control box mounted by the bay door.
Read the plate power indicator and the gravity setting, and note whether the plates cycle evenly.
Walk the bay floor and step on each plate in turn, noting any plate that feels light underfoot.
Open the junction box and look at the bay feed for scorch marks or loose lugs.
Lift a sample crate a few centimeters off the floor and set it down to confirm the gravity holds.
Report the bay status to the quartermaster over comm.
what_makes_it_hard: Feeling a weak gravity plate through a step or a small drift, and not blaming a sound junction box for a plate fault.
ideal_interaction: Walk the bay and step on each floor plate in order; when one feels light, pull the control box lever to test its pull and release it when the status light holds green.

label: Prep transporter power feed
human_steps: Walk to the transporter junction and unlock the feed cabinet with the cabinet key.
Read the feed voltage meter and compare it to the rated input on the transporter tag.
Trace the feed cable from the cabinet to the emitter housing, checking each cable clamp by hand.
Set the transporter main breaker to standby and wait for a steady light.
Bring the feed to full and listen for a hum that rises evenly.
Log the voltage and sign the feed sheet.
what_makes_it_hard: Telling a feed that holds voltage under load from one that only looks correct at idle.
ideal_interaction: Work the main breaker lever up through standby into full, pausing at each stop until the voltage needle settles, and leave it only when the needle sits inside the rated band.

label: Boost sickbay power and life support
human_steps: Walk to the sickbay junction and read the life support load on the wall meter.
Open the sickbay power distribution panel and find the medical bus line.
Turn the allocation knob toward the requested level while watching the bus voltage meter.
Look through the air handler grille and confirm the fan spins steadily.
Check the O2 percent and temperature readouts on the sickbay ops panel.
Log the new setting and tell the CMO the bus is ready.
what_makes_it_hard: Adding medical power without starving the air handler or diagnostic beds, a failure that shows up quietly as oxygen or temperature drift.
ideal_interaction: Turn the allocation knob toward the target in small steps and keep the O2 readout in view until it climbs back inside its band before you stop turning.

label: Ready quarantine environment controls
human_steps: Walk to the plant console and select the quarantine zone on the environment map.
Read the current pressure differential, temperature, and humidity values aloud.
Set the negative pressure dial to the required differential and wait for the needle to lock.
Turn the temperature and humidity dials to the setpoints marked on the quarantine card.
Check the airlock seal indicator reads green, meaning the lock holds.
Confirm zone status to the bridge and sign the card.
what_makes_it_hard: Keeping the negative pressure differential steady while the other two settings move, since a drop lets contamination leak into the corridor.
ideal_interaction: Turn the pressure dial to the target differential and keep it there until the needle locks, then nudge the temperature and humidity dials in turn while the seal light is watched.

label: Full systems stress test
human_steps: Receive the stress test script from the Chief's desk and read its step list.
Walk to the engineering console and load the test profile covering every engineering subsystem.
Start the ramp and watch each subsystem gauge rise toward its test load.
Stand at the junction and listen for pump or fan noise that changes pitch at each step.
Hold peak load for the scripted time and note any gauge that lags behind the others.
Ramp down, log each subsystem's peak value, and mark any fault found.
what_makes_it_hard: Spotting which subsystem lags or whines first under peak load, since a fault that surfaces later costs far more than one caught on the bench.
ideal_interaction: Step the ramp slider through each marked level on the bench console, and tap the subsystem gauge that lags to flag its peak before the ramp moves on.

label: Tune dampers and EPS after stress
human_steps: Walk to the damper housing at the junction and read each louver's current position.
Turn the handwheel one notch at a time, listening for the hull creak to ease.
Stop when the louver reaches the stress-test setting and lock the wheel with its pin.
Move to the EPS trim knob and nudge output back toward nominal.
Check the damper position indicator and the EPS voltage after each adjustment.
Sign the tuning sheet with the final positions.
what_makes_it_hard: Easing the dampers without overcorrecting, since a louver turned too far loads the hull in the opposite direction.
ideal_interaction: Turn the damper handwheel one notch at a time while watching the creak meter, and push the locking pin in once the meter needle falls back into the baseline band.

label: Compile fault list for the Chief
human_steps: Pull the fault tags from each test station's clip and lay them out on the desk.
Read each tag's system name, severity stamp, and the reading that triggered it.
Sort the tags into three piles: critical, minor, and cosmetic.
Write each critical fault onto the list with its system, reading, and originating station.
Check the list against the test log for any tag that has no line on the list.
Place the finished list in the Chief's tray and confirm receipt.
what_makes_it_hard: Sorting faults by real severity instead of by how loud they are, so a quiet drift is not buried under a loud alarm.
ideal_interaction: Drag each fault tag from the pile into its severity column, and let go only after the tag reading matches the test-log line you are placing it against.

label: Pad and emitter diagnostic
human_steps: Walk to the transporter pad and stand on the marked alignment spot.
Lower the alignment scanner arm over the pad and set it to the three-point sweep.
Read the scan trace on the arm's display and check each emitter coil's reading in turn.
Look at the coil housings for scorch discoloration or cracked insulation.
Tag any coil reading outside the green band and mark the pad.
Log the pad result and tell the bridge the pads are green.
what_makes_it_hard: Catching one emitter drifting out of alignment while the pad as a whole still reads green, which a rushed sweep misses.
ideal_interaction: Lower the scanner arm and drag the three-point sweep across the pad, pausing at each emitter until its trace locks into the band.

label: Pattern buffer and biofilter check
human_steps: Walk to the transporter console and open the pattern buffer log.
Check the residual pattern count against the purge threshold.
Open the purge valve and watch the count fall to zero on the buffer gauge.
Pull the biofilter cartridge from its housing and inspect the mesh for clogging.
Reseat the cartridge and confirm the biofilter status light is green.
Sign the buffer log with the time and your initials.
what_makes_it_hard: Judging whether a clogged biofilter mesh is slowing the purge, since residual patterns left in the buffer raise the error rate on the next beam.
ideal_interaction: Pull the biofilter cartridge out and hold it up to the light, then tap the mesh with the cleaning brush until light passes through it evenly.
fit_note: Verify covers the log check but not the physical cartridge removal and mesh inspection.

label: Process beam requests
human_steps: Read the incoming beam request on the console and note the target coordinates and person count.
Enter the coordinates into the targeting grid and read them back against the request.
Check the shield status and transporter lock indicator on the panel.
Look through the pad window to confirm the pad is clear.
Energize the beam with the two-hand switch and watch the transfer indicator.
Verify arrival on the sensor readout and report the transfer complete to the bridge.
what_makes_it_hard: Reading coordinates back correctly, since one transposed digit sends a person into a wall.
ideal_interaction: Type each coordinate digit into the grid and read it back aloud, then hold the two-hand switch until the transfer indicator shows arrival.

label: Drill the technician
human_steps: Pick a drill scenario card from the training rack, such as a lock failure or a misaligned pad.
Walk to the pad with the technician and set the scenario marker on the pad side panel.
State the scenario aloud and have the technician walk the pad in order, pointing at each part.
Stop the technician at the first wrong move and have them repeat it with the emitter in view.
Run the scenario to the end while watching the technician's hands on the controls.
Debrief at the console, writing each mistake and its correction on the training sheet.
what_makes_it_hard: Knowing when to interrupt a learner and when to let a small error happen, since a correction that comes too late teaches the wrong habit.
ideal_interaction: Tap the scenario pause on the pad panel during the technician's run, and release it only after they name the correct control and its fix aloud.
fit_note: Calibrate is a solo tuning game; drilling a technician means teaching a second person and watching their hands on the pad.

label: Routine pad diagnostics
human_steps: Walk to the pad with the diagnostic kit and kneel beside the pad base plate.
Open the base plate and check the emitter grease seal for wear marks.
Run the handheld quick scan across the pad and read the alignment offset.
Wipe the pad surface with a dry cloth to clear scuffs and dust.
Compare the offset against last week's log entry and note any creep.
Close the base plate and log the routine diagnostic complete.
what_makes_it_hard: Telling a slow creep in the alignment offset from a normal reading, which a single scan cannot show without the previous week's log.
ideal_interaction: Kneel at the base plate and run the handheld scan around the pad's marked ring, then tap the offset value and compare it against last week's line in the log.

label: Clean pattern buffer
human_steps: Walk to the buffer console and power the buffer down to service state.
Open the buffer housing and lift out the contact board with gloved hands.
Wipe each contact pin with a lint-free swab dipped in contact cleaner.
Look for a dark residue ring around each pin and rework any pin that still shows one.
Reseat the board and confirm the latch clicks shut.
Power up and confirm the buffer error counter reads zero.
what_makes_it_hard: Cleaning every pin fully without bending one, since residue left on a pin raises the error rate on every beam after it.
ideal_interaction: Dip the swab, then stroke each pin on the contact board in turn until its residue ring is gone.
fit_note: Calibrate is a tuning game; cleaning a buffer means wiping contacts and clearing residue by hand.

label: Prep away team pads and tricorder lock
human_steps: Walk to the away team pads with the tricorder and read its lock beacon ID.
Set each pad's alignment marker over its floor target and check the marker light.
Set the tricorder to the pad's beacon channel and hold it at the center of the pad.
Turn the pad position ring until the tricorder reads locked.
Confirm all team pads show matching lock IDs on the board.
Report the pads ready to the bridge.
what_makes_it_hard: Holding the tricorder still over the right spot long enough for the beacon to lock, since a shifted pad sends the team to a different place.
ideal_interaction: Step each pad marker onto its floor target and turn the position ring until the board's lock light goes steady, then tap the tricorder beacon channel to confirm it.

label: Hold transporter lock on team
human_steps: Read the away team beacon roster on the console and confirm each name is on the lock list.
Place the lock on the first beacon and watch its signal strength bar.
Listen to the comm for the team's position reports and note any hesitation.
If a signal dips, nudge the lock gain up one small step at a time.
Keep the lock steady through the mission window without touching other controls.
Write each signal dip into the lock log with the time it happened.
what_makes_it_hard: Holding the lock steady without overreacting to every small dip, since overcorrecting can drop the team mid-beam.
ideal_interaction: Leave the gain control at its set point and let the signal bar ride; only when it falls below the marked floor, press the gain up a single step.
fit_note: Calibrate suggests tuning; the real job is steady monitoring of a lock and reacting to signal loss.

label: Recover samples and team
human_steps: Read the return request and the pad coordinates for the team's beacon.
Clear the pad of loose equipment, looking under the marker for any dropped tool.
Enter the return coordinates and check the beacon ID matches the team.
Confirm the sample case is strapped to the marker and its hatch is closed.
Start the return and watch the pad sensor's arrival count.
Count the arrivals against the roster and call the team and samples aboard.
what_makes_it_hard: Making sure every person and sample arrives, since a missing sample case is found only after the beam is finished.
ideal_interaction: Type the return coordinates, then hold the recall switch while the pad sensor counts each arrival, and let go only when the count matches the roster line by line.

label: Calibrate for bulk cargo
human_steps: Walk to the cargo pad with the calibration weight set and read the mass limit on the pad frame.
Place the weight at the pad center and read the load cell display.
Turn each leveling foot in small steps until the bubble sits in the center ring.
Check each corner of the pad for clean seating under the weight.
Lift the weight off and confirm the load cell returns to zero.
Sign the calibration card and note the alignment offset.
what_makes_it_hard: Getting the pad level to a fine tolerance, since an uneven pad shifts crate mass and drops containers in transit.
ideal_interaction: Set the calibration weight on the pad, then turn each leveling foot until the bubble sits in the center ring and every corner reads the same load on the display.

label: Beam cargo to hold
human_steps: Read the cargo manifest's batch number and the hold deck coordinates.
Load the batch crates onto the pad and count them against the manifest.
Enter the hold coordinates and read each grid digit back aloud.
Check the bay camera for a clear landing zone in the hold.
Start the batch transfer and watch the crate count on the pad tally.
Log the batch as landed once the bay confirms the crate count.
what_makes_it_hard: Counting crates on and off the pad correctly, since one crate caught in the pattern beam can land on the wrong deck.
ideal_interaction: Type the hold coordinates into the console grid, then press batch start and keep the pad tally in view until it shows zero crates left.

label: Verify manifest and buffer purge
human_steps: Pull the completed manifest from the console tray and read the batch totals.
Compare each line's crate ID with the crate tag on the cargo bay list.
Open the buffer purge screen and run the purge cycle.
Confirm the buffer error counter reads zero after the purge.
Mark any mismatched line in red and hold the batch for a recount.
Sign the manifest with the final count and purge result.
what_makes_it_hard: Catching one crate ID that does not match between manifest and bay, since a mismatch can hide an unlisted item in the hold.
