Run the spectrometer scan and watch the peak list for unknown organic signatures.
Match each unknown peak against the hazard library, marking any match above the threshold line.
Swab the bench well and streak the swab onto a culture plate, timing the incubation.
Classify the sample safe, quarantine or hazard on the containment form before releasing the tag.
what_makes_it_hard: The judgement is reading an unfamiliar signature and deciding where the threshold sits; failure is clearing a sample that carries a contaminant nobody has catalogued.
ideal_interaction: Player places the sample into the bench well and reads the spectrometer peaks, matching each unknown signature to the library; a match above the threshold must be tagged quarantine before the classification can be submitted.

label: Post-survey decontamination check
human_steps: Strip the away team's returning suits in the decon bay and bag them in order of exposure.
Pass the handheld scanner over each person's hands, face and boots, watching the count meter.
Wipe a swab across the boot soles and suit seals, then seal each swab into its tube.
Run the swabs through the bench analyser for any live organism growth.
Spray the bay floor and seats with decon foam and let it sit for the full dwell timer.
Record a clean decon only once every scan reads under the limit and the dwell time has run out.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is tracing contamination to a hidden seam or sole; failure is a clean record while a carrier is still on a boot.
ideal_interaction: Player runs the handheld scanner over each returning suit's seams and boot soles, then sprays decon foam and waits out the dwell timer; a boot left unscanned or a timer skipped leaves the bay marked unclean.

label: Inspect cargo for biohazard
human_steps: Walk to the cargo bay door and read the crate manifest against the stencilled numbers.
Pull on gloves and unseal the first crate, checking the inner liner for tears or weeping.
Run the biohazard wand along the seams and into the packing foam, listening for a rising tone.
Read the air sensor clipped to the crate lid and log any reading above the baseline line.
Reseal the liner with the heat sealer and tag any flagged crate with a yellow quarantine tag.
Sign the manifest line for each crate passed and leave flagged crates on the hold list.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is catching a leak or a rising reading early in a crate that looks sealed; failure is a contaminated crate that slips onto the manifest.
ideal_interaction: Player unseals each crate and runs the biohazard wand along its seams, following the rising tone to a leak; a crate passed with a tone above the line or a missed seam fails the inspection.

label: Brief cargo crew on lifting injuries
human_steps: Walk to the cargo door and stand where the loaders can see your hands and face.
Hold up the lifting chart and point to the posture diagram showing bent knees and a straight back.
Demonstrate the lift with an empty crate, showing where the weight goes into the legs.
Ask a loader to lift a sandbag while you watch the spine line, correcting any twist.
Name the three signs of strain: a catch in the lower back, numbness in the fingers, a locked shoulder.
Pin the chart by the door and ask the crew lead to pull any tired lifter for rest.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is spotting a poor lift in a moving crew and correcting it without slowing the load; failure is a briefing nobody follows once the crates are moving.
ideal_interaction: Player stands at the cargo door and corrects a loader's lift by watching the spine line during a sandbag demonstration, then pins the lifting chart; a twisted-back lift left uncorrected fails the briefing.
fit_note: A counselling dialogue does not show a lift or a posture; the real work is demonstrating and watching technique.

label: Treat injuries from loading
human_steps: Bring the injured loader to the biobed and ask which hand or back hurts first.
Feel along the fingers and wrist for crepitus or a swollen joint, watching the patient's face.
Clean the cut with antiseptic gauze, flushing from the centre outward to the edge.
Select the dose from the hypospray menu for the pain level and check the weight entry first.
Press the hypospray to the arm and count two seconds before lifting it off.
Splint the wrist with the moulded splint and tell the patient to keep it still for twelve hours.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is choosing a safe dose from weight and not over-treating pain; failure is a dose that masks a fracture or stacks on a prior drug.
ideal_interaction: Player presses the hypospray to the patient's arm after setting the dose from the menu, then holds a moulded splint on the wrist; a dose set without checking weight or a loose splint fails the treatment.

label: Set up triage and isolation in sickbay
human_steps: Walk the sickbay and clear the aisle between biobeds to two metres, shifting crates against the wall.
Pull the isolation curtain from its ceiling track and hang it between the two beds nearest the door.
Set each biobed's field to isolation mode and check the panel shows green before moving to the next.
Mark the triage zones on the floor with coloured tape: red beds near surgery, green beds by the door.
Stock each bed with a sealed kit, an oxygen mask and a labelled chart clip.
Flicker-test the isolation field on the last bed; a bed reading amber is redone.
what_makes_it_hard: The judgement is laying out zones that work under pressure before anyone arrives; failure is a red bed placed far from surgery or an isolation field left amber.
ideal_interaction: Player walks the sickbay laying coloured tape zones and sets each biobed's field to isolation mode, stopping at any amber reading; a red bed placed away from surgery or an amber field left set fails the setup.

label: Receive and triage arriving patients
human_steps: Meet the transporter team at the arrival bay and count the stretchers as they come in.
Read each patient's breathing and bleeding at a glance, sorting them into red, amber or green.
Put a sensor cuff on each red patient and read the pressure and oxygen figures out loud.
Move the most critical patient to the surgery bed while the others wait on the zone tape.
Assign a nurse to each red bed, naming the patient, the injury and the next check time.
Re-triage the amber group every five minutes, because a patient who looked stable can turn in minutes.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is sorting many casualties fast by survivability and re-sorting as they change; failure is a patient who turns critical while parked in the green zone.
ideal_interaction: Player receives each stretcher in turn, tagging red, amber or green, and places a sensor cuff on each red patient; a critical patient left in green when the cuff reads low fails the triage.
fit_note: A single-patient vitals read does not capture a rapid multi-casualty sort and re-triage.

label: Brief captain on capacity and supplies
human_steps: Walk up to the bridge and wait at the rail until the captain's attention is free.
Read the bed count, the surgery queue and the oxygen reserve off your slate.
State capacity as beds left and how long oxygen lasts at the current draw.
Say how many more patients sickbay can hold before triage must start refusing transfers.
Recommend one specific request, such as a transporter pod or a cargo nurse, and name its cost.
Ask the captain to confirm the decision aloud, and note the time on the slate.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is giving a hard capacity number under pressure without rounding it up; failure is accepting more patients than sickbay can hold.
ideal_interaction: Player stands at the bridge rail and gives the captain a bed count and oxygen figure, then picks one request from the options; a capacity number rounded up or no spoken confirmation fails the brief.
fit_note: A form records the numbers, but the real work is a spoken capacity call and a recommendation.

label: Request transporter and cargo support
human_steps: Go to the sickbay console and pull up the staffing roster for transporter and cargo crew.
Note which crew are free, excluding anyone still on rest after a shift.
Fill in the support request with the number of people and the task each one needs.
Specify the time window and the lift load, writing the heaviest crate weight in kilograms.
Send the request to ops and wait for the reply code on the console.
Write the reply code in the log before leaving the console.
what_makes_it_hard: The judgement is asking for the right people for the actual lifts without draining another ward; failure is an underfilled request or one that pulls off-shift crew.
ideal_interaction: Player picks available crew from the roster, leaving out anyone on rest, and enters the crate weight and time window before sending; an unrested crewman or an underweighted lift fails the request.
fit_note: Form-filling captures the request but not the staffing judgement of who is actually free.

label: Stand ready for injuries during drills
human_steps: Stand at the biobed with the hypospray charged and the trauma kit open beside your hand.
Watch the drill feed on the wall screen for the moment a simulated casualty is called.
Step in when the call comes, moving the casualty onto the bed without waiting for the nurse.
Assess the airway by looking for chest movement and listening for a breath sound.
Give a drill dose from the hypospray only when the simulated dose order is read out.
Hold position and watch the monitor until the casualty is passed to the next station.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is staying alert through a long wait and reacting fast when the call comes; failure is a late response or a dose given without an order.
ideal_interaction: Player waits at the biobed with the hypospray in hand and taps the casualty within the call window once the drill alarm sounds; a late tap or a dose given before the order fails the standby.
fit_note: Holding a hypo ready and reacting to a call is a waiting-and-response task, not a single injection.

label: Check crew fatigue after drills
human_steps: Pull the drill roster on the sickbay console and list the crew who ran the longest shifts.
Call each crewman in by name and ask for their hours of sleep in the last two days.
Run each crewman through the reaction board, pressing the lit key as the panel flashes.
Compare each reaction time to baseline and note any delay above one-fifth of a second.
Mark the fatigue score on their chart and set a rest order for anyone over the threshold.
Send the rest list to the bridge so the duty roster changes before the next shift.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is separating fatigue from simple disinterest; failure is clearing an exhausted crewman who makes errors at the next watch.
ideal_interaction: Player runs each crewman through the reaction board, pressing the lit key as the panel flashes, and flags anyone whose delay passes the threshold; a crewman cleared with a slow reaction time fails the check.
fit_note: The job is a timed reaction measure against baseline, but the counsel activity is a conversation.

label: Report medical readiness to captain
human_steps: Walk to the bridge console and wait for the captain to acknowledge your presence.
Pull the sickbay readiness board and read the bed, staff and supply lines aloud.
Rate each line green, amber or red against the thresholds on the wall card.
State the single biggest gap, such as one nurse short on the night watch.
Type the readiness report on the console, attaching the staffing count and the date.
Submit the report and confirm the captain has it on screen before you leave.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is an honest colour rating of each line against thresholds; failure is a red gap painted green so the captain approves an unsafe drill.
ideal_interaction: Player rates each readiness line green, amber or red against the wall card thresholds, then submits the form; a red line reported green or an unconfirmed submission fails the report.
fit_note: A form only records the status; the real work is a verified colour rating and a spoken gap.

label: Wellness walkabout
human_steps: Leave the counselling office and walk the mess deck, stopping at each table to see who is sitting alone.
Sit beside one withdrawn crewman and set down a cup of tea without asking them to move.
Ask about their sleep and meals rather than duty, and listen for a long pause before the answer.
Note whether they eat, how many words they give, and whether they keep looking toward the door.
Offer to walk them to the next shift briefing, leaving the choice open.
Move on after twenty minutes and jot a one-word note in the pocket pad before the next table.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is getting someone to talk about sleep and meals rather than duty; failure is a conversation that feels like an interrogation and shuts them down.
ideal_interaction: Player sits beside a crewman at the mess table, asks about sleep and meals in turn, and watches for a withdrawn reply; pushing duty questions too early or leaving the table with no note costs the walkabout.

label: Scheduled counselling sessions
human_steps: Call the next name from the appointment list and invite the crewman to the chair facing the window.
Listen without interrupting for the first minute, nodding and leaving gaps for them to fill.
Ask one open question about what changed since the last session, writing only key words.
Reflect back what they said in their own words, then check that the reflection was right.
Agree one small plan with a date, such as sleeping before midnight for a week.
Close the confidential note with the plan and a review date, then lock it in the counsel drawer.
what_makes_it_hard: The judgement is reflecting accurately and noticing what the person avoids; failure is a session that hears the words but misses the real problem.
ideal_interaction: Player listens through an opening minute of dialogue, picks reflective replies in turn, and agrees a dated plan; a reply that interrupts or a plan left undated ends the session badly.

label: Crew morale report to the captain
human_steps: Collect the week's observation notes from the pocket pad and the mess walkabout log.
Sort the observations into groups by shift and by department, setting aside anything that names a person.
Anonymise each line by swapping names for roles, such as a junior engineer on gamma shift.
Walk to the bridge and wait for the captain's attention at the rail.
Read the morale summary aloud and raise a safety concern only if it needs action.
Confirm the captain has heard the summary before leaving, then close the log.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is summarising honestly without leaking identity or softening a real trend; failure is a report that names a confidant or paints good news over a fraying shift.
ideal_interaction: Player sorts the observation cards into shift groups and strikes out every name before reading the summary to the captain; a leaked name or a softened trend fails the report.
fit_note: A form records the summary, but the job is the anonymising and an honest spoken brief.

label: Fitness-for-duty review
human_steps: Pull the flagged crewmen's sleep logs from the console and read the hours for the last three nights.
Sit the crewman on the biobed and ask them to describe a recent mistake in their own words.
Check the pupil response with the penlight and the grip strength with the hand dynamometer.
Compare the grip and pupil readings with the baseline card, noting any drop below forty percent.
Co-sign the review sheet with the physician, reading each reading aloud for them to confirm.
Recommend rest or duty on the form and send the bridge a one-line summary with the reason.
what_makes_it_hard: The judgement is separating a tired officer from one who is genuinely impaired; failure is clearing someone whose grip and recall have both dropped.
ideal_interaction: Player takes the penlight to the crewman's eyes and reads the grip dynamometer against the baseline card, then co-signs the review; clearing someone whose grip drops below forty percent fails the review.
fit_note: The job is a physical and log-based fitness judgement; the vitals activity reads numbers but not sleep logs or the interview.

label: Open-door hours in the mess
human_steps: Set the chairs in a loose ring and put the tea urn on the sideboard.
Sit where the door is visible and watch who comes in and who stays at the edges.
Greet each arrival by name and ask how their watch went, keeping it light.
Notice two crew whose argument is building and sit between them without taking sides.
Offer a game of chess and watch whether the tension eases after two moves.
Leave the door open and note the names of anyone who did not come in at all.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is staying unobtrusive while noticing tension before it becomes a feud; failure is a quarrel that starts in the room while you are watching the urn.
ideal_interaction: Player moves between tables greeting crew and sits between two arguing people, then offers a chess game and waits for the tension to ease; ignoring an escalating quarrel for too long fails the open hours.

label: Check on crew on lonely posts
human_steps: Walk the engineering corridor to the isolated post and tap the access panel to announce yourself.
Ask the crewman how long they have been alone and when they last spoke to someone.
Look at their hands and face for shakes, skipped shaving or a sour smell from the cup.
Listen for flat or repeated answers and ask a second question about a pleasant memory.
Offer to swap a shift or send a relief runner, and set a time for the next check-in.
Record the post, the time and the mood in the pocket pad before moving on.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is reading isolation stress from small signs without alarming the person; failure is a withdrawn crewman whose decline goes unrecorded.
ideal_interaction: Player walks the corridor to the lonely post, reads the crewman's appearance and answers, and sets a check-in time on the rota; leaving before the check-in is logged or skipping a sign fails the visit.

label: Watch for fatigue in the science shift
human_steps: Stand at the back of the lab where you can see every console without blocking the sensor line.
Watch the scientists for slow blinks, long pauses between readings and repeated re-entered numbers.
Read the science shift log and compare entry times with the sensor-data timestamps.
Ask the lead analyst one question about the last hour, listening for a delayed or vague answer.
Call a rest break if two or more analysts show slow typing or repeated mistakes.
Note the names and signs on the shift board before leaving the lab.
what_makes_it_hard: The judgement is telling exhaustion from concentration in people who are working hard; failure is a rest call that is missed while bad data gets logged.
ideal_interaction: Player watches the analysts' consoles and clicks any re-entered reading or long pause on the timeline, calling a rest break when two show the pattern; missing a rest call while data errors pile up fails the watch.
fit_note: Conversation at a console does not show the fatigue signs (blinks, pauses, repeated entries) the real watch relies on.

label: Debrief the sensor team after a long scan
human_steps: Gather the sensor team at the lab table and sit down with them rather than standing over them.
Ask each person what they saw in the last scan, in their own words, before offering your reading.
Replay the scan timeline together and point to the moment the signal went strange.
Listen for guilt or self-blame, and name it back as something they can put down.
Agree one handover step for the next scan, such as a fixed tea break every two hours.
Log the debrief and send the bridge only the handover step, leaving out the personal remarks.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is letting people voice a mistake without turning it into a blame session; failure is a debrief that hardens guilt into a grudge.
ideal_interaction: Player sits with the sensor team and replays the scan timeline, asking each person what they noticed first; a debrief that blames one analyst or skips the handover step leaves the team worse off.

label: Visit the cargo handlers during loading
human_steps: Walk the cargo corridor between the loading bays and greet the handlers by name as you pass.
Stop beside the lift rig and ask the handler whether the rota gives them any rest.
Look at the crew's hands and back for splints, bandages or a limp on the rig walk.
Pass round water from the cooler and ask who skipped their last break.
Carry a crate for one minute if a handler asks for help, then return to the questions.
Report any flaring tempers to the cargo supervisor, naming the schedule as the cause.
what_makes_it_hard: The judgement is reading tension in a noisy, moving crew; failure is missing a flare-up or ignoring a handler who is hurting.
ideal_interaction: Player walks the corridor passing water to handlers and asks each one about their break, carrying a crate when asked; a handler left unbroken all shift or a flared temper left unreported fails the visit.

label: Report load-crew exhaustion to the quartermaster
human_steps: Walk to the cargo desk and wait for the quartermaster to finish the manifest call.
Read out each handler's hours in the last twenty-four from your notes, using crew names.
Name any handler who has been lifting for more than eight hours without a break.
Recommend a specific change, such as a two-hour rotation or an extra pair of hands on the rig.
Fill the exhaustion form with the names, hours and recommendation, then ask for a signature.
Hand the form to the quartermaster and note the signed time on your pad.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is making an honest case for relief without blaming anyone; failure is a report the quartermaster can wave away.
ideal_interaction: Player reads each handler's hours from the notes into the exhaustion form and picks a rotation change before handing it over for signature; a form submitted without a recommendation fails the report.
fit_note: The form captures the record, but the job is a spoken case for relief and a specific change.

label: Counsel the evacuees on arrival
human_steps: Walk to the biobed where the evacuee is sitting and kneel to their eye level.
Introduce yourself by role, not rank, and ask whether they know where they are.
Hold a cup of water and let them drink at their own pace while you speak.
Ask what they need right now, such as a blanket or a call to family, and fetch it.
Tell them what happens next in three short sentences, avoiding technical terms.
Check the wristband with the nurse and note the evacuee's name on the arrivals sheet.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is calming a frightened person in shock with short, plain sentences; failure is overload or panic spreading through the ward.
ideal_interaction: Player kneels beside the evacuee, offers water and a blanket, and speaks three short next-step sentences in turn; an overloaded explanation or a skipped name check lets panic spread through the ward.

label: Support medical staff through triage
human_steps: Walk to the triage desk and stand where you can see both the queue and the nurse's face.
Watch the nurse's hands for a pause or a shake before the next patient is called.
Take the next clipboard from the stack and read the patient's name aloud so the nurse can see it.
Hand over a water cup or a hot drink when the nurse's hands are free for a moment.
Quietly tell the physician when a nurse has been on the floor for four hours without a break.
Note on the desk board which nurse has had the longest stretch without relief.
what_makes_it_hard: The judgement is knowing when a staff member needs to step away and when they can keep going; failure is a nurse who breaks under the load in the middle of triage.
ideal_interaction: Player stands at the triage desk, takes the next clipboard for a nurse who is pausing, and passes a drink over; a nurse left at the desk past four hours without a break fails the support.
fit_note: Support here means reading the staff and taking the load off them, which a counselling dialogue does not show.

label: Debrief the medical team after the relief
human_steps: Gather the sickbay team at the desk and ask them to sit rather than stand.
Ask each person in turn to name the worst moment of the relief, without the others interrupting.
Repeat back the most painful moment in their own words so they know it was heard.
Name one thing the team did well and one thing that cost them, in plain words.
Offer a quiet room and a counselling slot to anyone who wants to talk alone.
Log the debrief and pass the team's named concerns, not the personal detail, to the CMO.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is letting staff voice trauma and sorting out what needs follow-up; failure is a team that leaves with its worst memory unspoken.
ideal_interaction: Player sits the medical team at the desk and asks each member for their worst moment in turn, then offers the quiet room and a counselling slot; skipping a member or passing personal detail upward fails the debrief.
fit_note: The debrief conversation is right, but the job also carries a logged referral that the dialogue does not capture.

label: Calm new crew during systems trials
human_steps: Walk to the mess table and sit with the new crew where they can all see the exit.
Ask each new crewman what their first alarm sounded like and what they thought it meant.
Show them the alarm chart, pointing to the colour bands and the matching sound.
Let one crewman press the alarm test button while you coach their breathing until the shaking stops.
Pair each nervous crewman with an experienced crewman for the next trial.
Note who froze and who fled, and give the trial lead the pairings by name.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is calming a startled crewman without making them feel tested; failure is a frozen or fleeing crewman at the next real alarm.
ideal_interaction: Player sits the new crew at the mess table, walks them through the alarm chart, then has one press the test button while breathing is coached; a crewman who flees the real alarm after this fails the calming.

label: Check on the engineering crew after a fault
human_steps: Walk the engineering corridor to the fault panel and wait for the crew to finish the reset.
Stand beside the crew lead and ask what the fault looked like from where they stood.
Look for a hand braced on the wall, a clenched jaw, or someone avoiding the lead engineer's eye.
Ask the junior crewman whether they think the fault was theirs, and listen to the answer.
Say plainly that the fault was a system problem, and point to the log entry that shows it.
Set a debrief time for the crew and note in the pocket pad who needs a private word.
what_makes_it_hard: The judgement is spotting self-blame early and separating it from the real fault cause; failure is a junior crewman who takes the blame and freezes at the next repair.
ideal_interaction: Player walks to the fault panel and asks the junior crewman whether the fault was theirs, then points to the reset log entry showing the system cause; blaming the junior or skipping the log leaves the tension rising.

label: Ward rounds
human_steps: Walk to the first biobed and scan the patient's wristband to bring up their chart.
Press two fingers to the wrist and count the pulse against the second hand of the pulse watch.
Ask the patient where it hurts and listen for the word that changes the diagnosis.
Lift the blanket to check the wound dressing, looking for redness and a wet edge.
Type the vitals and any change into the chart with a short clinical note.
Tell the nurse on duty about any change in dose or dressing before moving on.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is hearing a changed symptom in a patient who says they are fine; failure is a deterioration written up as stable.
ideal_interaction: Player scans each patient's wristband, lifts the blanket to inspect the dressing for redness, then types the observed change into the chart; a wound marked stable when the dressing is wet fails the round.

label: Walk-in clinic and fitness checks
human_steps: Call the next name from the queue and stand as the crewman walks in.
Look at their eyes and skin colour under the desk lamp, noting any yellowing or unequal pupils.
Take the temperature with the forehead probe and wait for the steady beep.
Ask two questions about pain and the last meal, writing the answers on the intake form.
Decide treat, refer or fit, then stamp the fitness line on the duty sheet.
Log the decision in the clinic register with the time and your initials.
what_makes_it_hard: The judgement is deciding fitness for duty from a short exam; failure is stamping someone fit who is carrying an infection or a concussion.
ideal_interaction: Player calls each walk-in to the desk, shines the lamp on their eyes, takes a probe reading, and stamps the duty sheet treat, refer or fit; stamping a feverish crewman fit fails the clinic.
fit_note: A ward activity does not show the walk-in exam, where the job is a quick hands-on look, a probe reading and a decision stamp.

label: Medicine and supply count
human_steps: Open the locker and lift out the hypo tray, sliding each cassette forward to read it.
Count the regenerator packs by tapping them into rows of five on the count tray.
Turn each sterile pack under the lamp and check the seal for a pinhole or a dent.
Log each count on the stores sheet and circle any line below the resupply mark.
Move any pack with a broken seal to the reject bin, not back onto the shelf.
Initial the sheet and file it; a shortfall past the mark gets a resupply line.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is counting accurately and catching a small seal fault; failure is a broken pack counted as sterile and shelved for an emergency.
ideal_interaction: Player tallies regenerator packs into rows of five on the count tray and turns each sterile pack under the lamp to spot a pinhole; a broken-seal pack returned to the shelf fails the count.

label: Check the holographic medic and scanners
human_steps: Walk to the scanner rack and power up the first unit, watching the boot light turn from red to green.
Place the calibration block on the scanner plate and read the reference value on the screen.
Turn the gain dial until the block reading sits within the tolerance band on the card.
Move to the hologram alcove and ask the medic a simple recall question about dosage.
Note any delay in the answer or any mispronounced drug name in the fault log.
Tag the scanner pass or fail, and pull any unit that fails to the bench.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is turning a dial to the exact tolerance band and hearing a lag in a voice answer; failure is a scanner tagged as passing while reading high.
ideal_interaction: Player places the calibration block on the scanner plate and turns the gain dial until the reading sits in the tolerance band; a unit tagged pass while outside the band fails the check.

label: Routine physicals and rounds
human_steps: Pull the physicals list from the desk slate and pick the first crewman by department.
Ask the crewman to step onto the scale and read the weight aloud to the slate.
Take a blood pressure reading with the cuff and write both numbers on the form.
Ask about any new medication and cross-check the answer against the medicine list.
Note any abnormal reading in the red column and recheck it after five minutes of rest.
Sign the physical as complete only when every column is filled and cross-checked.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is following a routine checklist while catching the one reading that is off; failure is a rote physical that clears someone with a rising pressure.
ideal_interaction: Player moves the crewman through the scale and blood pressure cuff, then rechecks a red reading after a rest timer; signing off a physical with an elevated pressure left unrechecked fails the round.
fit_note: The job is a sequence of measurements at a desk; a bedside ward activity does not capture the cuff and scale steps.

label: Weekly stores count
human_steps: Carry the weekly count sheet to the stores locker and unlock the top shelf.
Count the sealed blood analogue bags by lifting each out and reading its serial number.
Compare the serial sequence with the sheet to catch a bag logged twice or missing.
Check the expiry dates on the shelf label, pulling anything within thirty days to the front.
Write the final count in the box and circle any line that differs from last week.
Hand the sheet to the ops clerk and keep the carbon copy in the locker log.
what_makes_it_hard: The judgement is catching a duplicate or missing serial that a simple total hides; failure is a bag logged twice and a shortage nobody sees.
ideal_interaction: Player lifts each blood analogue bag, reads its serial and ticks it against the sheet, circling any serial logged twice or missing; a duplicate ticked through fails the weekly count.

label: Screen away team for exposure after sensor sweeps
human_steps: Bring each away-team member to the biobed and ask them to step onto the exposure mat.
Pass the dosimeter wand across the chest, back and hands, watching the needle for a rise.
Take a blood sample from the arm with the draw kit and label the tube with the crewman's name.
Ask whether the suit seal ever felt loose or whether any sensor alarm sounded on the sweep.
Compare the dosimeter reading with the sweep log, flagging any gap above the limit line.
Stamp the exposure card and send the flagged names to the bridge with the reading attached.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is catching a latent exposure that shows no sign at the moment of screening; failure is a crewman cleared while radiation builds up in the blood.
ideal_interaction: Player moves the dosimeter wand over each team member's chest and hands, then draws a blood tube and compares the reading to the sweep log; an exposure above the limit line stamped clear fails the screen.

label: Review lab samples for biohazard
human_steps: Walk to the lab console and pull the sample from the cold box with the tongs, not the hands.
Read the sample label and check the seal against the chain-of-custody form.
Place the sample in the microscope tray and bring the lens up to focus on the cell layer.
Look for any colour change or unusual cell shape, and note it in the sample record.
Run the sample through the reagent test strip and read the colour against the chart.
Mark the sample biohazard, safe or hold on the custody form before passing it along.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is reading a faint cell change or colour shift that a rushed look would miss; failure is a hazard marked safe and shipped to the lab.
ideal_interaction: Player focuses the microscope on the cell layer, then compares the reagent strip colour to the chart and marks the custody form; an unusual cell left unnoted or a hazard marked safe fails the review.

label: Prepare sickbay for survey injuries
human_steps: Walk the sickbay and pull the spare biobeds out from the wall into the working row.
Plug each biobed into the power bus and wait for its status light to show ready.
Count the bandages and splint packs on each bed tray against the kit list.
Lay a fresh sheet on each bed and test the restraint strap for a secure click.
Stock the wall cabinet with oxygen masks and label each shelf by injury type.
Walk the row once more and log the bed numbers that are ready for the survey team.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is making every bed ready before the first casualty falls; failure is a bed whose strap or power fails during the first emergency.
ideal_interaction: Player rolls each spare biobed into the working row, plugs it into the power bus, and clicks the restraint strap; a bed left unplugged or a strap that does not click fails the setup.

label: Inspect cargo handlers for strain injuries
human_steps: Walk the cargo corridor and stop each handler coming off the lift rig for a quick look.
Ask the handler to lift a light box from the floor and watch how the back and knees bend.
Press along the lower spine and the shoulder, noting any flinch or rise in pain.
Check the grip and wrist for swelling or a hand held in a protective posture.
Give a strain score from one to five on the card and write the handler's name beside it.
Pull any handler scoring four or higher from the rig and send them to sickbay for a second look.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is spotting strain before it becomes an injury by reading posture and flinch; failure is a handler scored low who ends the shift with a slipped disc.
ideal_interaction: Player watches each handler lift a light box and presses along the spine to score any flinch, then sends any score of four or higher to sickbay; a low score given to a visibly bending lift fails the check.
fit_note: A vitals reading does not capture a posture watch or a flinch under pressure, which is what strain scoring needs.

label: Check cargo manifest for medical supplies
human_steps: Take the cargo manifest from the stores clip and walk to the medical crate pile in cargo.
Read each crate's stencilled number and match it to the manifest line for medical supplies.
Open the crate lid and count the drug pallets against the quantity on the line.
Check the expiry dates on the drug labels, rejecting any pallet past its date.
Mark the manifest line received, short or rejected, initialling each change.
Return the signed manifest to the quartermaster and log any shortfall with its crate number.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is matching stencilled crate numbers and counts exactly against the manifest; failure is a crate of drugs marked received when it was misrouted.
ideal_interaction: Player matches each crate's stencilled number to its manifest line, opens the lid and counts pallets against the quantity, then marks received, short or rejected; a misrouted crate marked received fails the check.

label: Triage incoming patients
human_steps: Stand at the arrival door and take the patient list from the transporter as each stretcher comes in.
Look at each patient's colour, breathing and responsiveness before touching them.
Clip the pulse oximeter to a finger and read the oxygen level aloud to the nurse.
Assign a red, amber or green tag and place the patient in the zone that matches the tag.
Call for the surgery team if a red patient's oxygen drops below ninety percent.
Re-sort the amber patients every five minutes, moving any worsening patient up a zone.
what_makes_it_hard: The judgement is weighing a quiet patient who is in worse trouble than a loud one; failure is a silent, dying patient placed in a low zone.
ideal_interaction: Player meets each stretcher at the door, reads the oximeter for each patient, and tags them into red, amber or green zones; a quiet patient with low oxygen left in green fails the triage.
fit_note: Single-patient vitals cannot show the rapid multi-patient sort and re-tagging that triage requires.

label: Prepare treatment batches and quarantine bay
human_steps: Pull the batch recipe from the console and set out the drug vials for the first treatment run.
Draw each dose into the syringe and read the volume against the batch sheet in millilitres.
Label each syringe with the dose, the time and the batch number before it leaves the bench.
Seal the quarantine bay door and set the air filter to the closed setting.
Lay the treatment batches on the trolley by patient bed, with the most urgent at the front.
Confirm the quarantine light is green and log the batch count on the console.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is drawing exact doses and sealing the bay correctly under time pressure; failure is a wrong volume or a bay left open while supplies run low.
ideal_interaction: Player draws each dose into a syringe to the millilitre line on the batch sheet, then seals the quarantine door and sets the filter to closed; a dose drawn off the line or an open bay fails the batch.

label: Daily status to bridge on casualties
human_steps: Walk to the desk and pull the casualty count from the sickbay board.
Read the count of red, amber and green patients and any deaths since the last report.
Note the bed occupancy and the oxygen figure against the morning reading.
Type a short status with the numbers first, then one sentence on the most serious case.
Read the status aloud to the bridge officer and confirm they have the figures right.
Submit the status to the bridge log, timestamped, with the patient count attached.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is telling the bridge the true patient load in a few clear figures; failure is a flattened count that makes the bridge plan for fewer casualties than there are.
ideal_interaction: Player reads the red, amber and green counts from the sickbay board, types the status with the numbers first, and reads it aloud to the bridge officer; an unconfirmed or understated casualty count fails the report.
fit_note: A form records the figures, but the job is a spoken, confirmed status that names the most serious case.

label: Be on standby during drills
human_steps: Stand at the biobed with the vitals monitor on and the probe ready in your hand.
Watch the drill timer and the wall screen for the moment the casualty is announced.
Clip the probe to the casualty's finger as soon as they are on the bed and read the oxygen level.
Call out the pulse and breath rate to the nurse every thirty seconds while the drill runs.
Stop the drill and announce the casualty's condition when the timer reaches the end.
Wait by the bed for the debrief and record the time each casualty was first seen.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is holding attention through a long quiet stretch and reading the monitor the moment it changes; failure is a casualty whose drop goes unnoticed for a minute.
ideal_interaction: Player stands at the biobed watching the drill timer and clips the probe onto the casualty when the call comes, calling out the oxygen figure every thirty seconds; a drop missed for a full call interval fails the standby.
fit_note: Standing by and reacting to a drill call is a sustained watch, and a single vitals reading does not carry that.

label: Test emergency medical systems
human_steps: Walk to the emergency console and power up the defibrillator, watching the self-test lights.
Connect the test load to the defib pads and press the charge button, reading the energy figure.
Compare the delivered energy with the set value on the console, noting any gap above tolerance.
Test the emergency suction unit by sealing the tube end and watching the vacuum gauge.
Check the oxygen regulator by opening the valve one turn and reading the flow rate on the dial.
Log each system pass or fail and tag any faulty unit with the red out-of-service label.
what_makes_it_hard: The skill is reading a small gap in delivered energy or flow before a real emergency; failure is a defibrillator that passes its self-test but delivers too little in a cardiac arrest.
ideal_interaction: Player connects the test load to the defib pads, charges the unit and reads the delivered energy against the set value; a delivered energy outside the tolerance band passed as good fails the test.

label: Count and verify cargo against manifest
human_steps: Pick up the manifest tablet at the console and note the bay row numbers on its header
Walk row one and scan each crate tag with the handheld until it beeps, reading the ID aloud
Compare each scanned ID against its tablet line and tick the matched rows
Count stacked crates from the top down, since a crate hidden behind a pallet is the classic shortage
Where a count is off by one, walk that stack from the other side to rule out a miscount
Write each confirmed shortage on the clipboard with crate ID, slot and count
Carry the sheet to the console and file the discrepancy report to the quartermaster
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is telling a real shortage from a miscount caused by a hidden or stacked crate; failure is filing a false shortage or missing a real gap.
ideal_interaction: Player walks the rows and scans each crate in a fixed order against a manifest list, tapping to tick matches and recounting any stack that shows a mismatch before filing a shortage.

label: Check straps, seals and nets
human_steps: Walk the bay with a tension gauge clipped to the belt, starting at the pallets nearest the lift
Grip each ratchet strap and pull it hand-tight, then read the gauge needle against the green band
Tug each net corner and inspect the seal crimp on bonded containers for splits
Re-seat any pallet that rocks under a boot push, shimming its base with a wedge block
Move heavy crates down to the lowest tier so the stack centre of mass sits low
Chalk-mark hazardous containers with an orange tag and turn the placard outward
Radio the bridge that bay one is secured and wait for the acknowledgement
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is knowing how much tension is enough without crushing a seal; failure is a strap that looks tight but slips in a hard turn, or a heavy crate left high.
ideal_interaction: Player stands at each pallet and drags a tension gauge onto each strap, ratcheting until the needle locks in the green band; a slack or over-tight strap is marked wrong.

label: Stage cargo for the pads or shuttlebay
human_steps: Load the crate ID list on the padd and confirm the destination pad number
Pull the first crate from the bay onto the grav sled and check its lift point
Ease the sled through the bay door, keeping the load centred so it does not tip on the ramp
Walk the sled to the transporter pad and set it inside the marked footprint
Read the weight display on the sled and tell the transporter tech the figure out loud
Wait for the tech's nod, then step off the pad and set the sled brake
Clear the pad of boots and tools, checking the floor marks are visible before the beam-out
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is placing a load so its mass sits centred in the pad footprint; failure is an off-centre crate that misses the transfer window or a wrong weight reading.
ideal_interaction: Player drags a loaded sled along a ramp to a pad, steering so the load stays centred, then sets it inside the footprint and reads the weight from the sled gauge before the pad is cleared.

label: Restock galley and replicator stores
human_steps: Read the shortage list on the wall screen and note which galley items are on it
Walk to the bay shelf for the first item, reading the lot code on each carton
Check the expiry stamp and set aside any carton past its date
Carry a stack of cartons to the stores hatch with the heavy ones at the bottom
Shelve each carton by item, labels facing out, with the oldest lot at the front
Tick the matching manifest line for each item shelved
Strike the shortage line once the shelf count matches the carton count
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is shelving the oldest lot forward and rejecting outdated stock; failure is an expired carton hidden behind fresh ones, or a tick for a shelf that is still short.
ideal_interaction: Player pulls cartons off bay racks, reads each lot date, sets out-of-date ones aside, then slots the rest onto stores shelves oldest-forward before ticking the matching shortage line.

label: Routine inventory and stores top-up
human_steps: Open the inventory console and pick the stores category to count
Walk to the bay shelving and read each bin label against the console list
Count loose items by hand in each bin, separating sealed packs from opened ones
Enter the counted number for each bin and correct any typo before saving
Top up any bin under its minimum by pulling stock from the reserve shelf
File the top-up slip and tag the bin with today's date
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is spotting a bin that reads full on the console but is really short; failure is a count typed into the wrong bin so the galley runs short unseen.
ideal_interaction: Player moves down the shelving with a hand counter, sorting sealed packs from opened ones into two trays per bin, then refills any bin below minimum from the reserve shelf.

label: Re-secure loose pallets
human_steps: Hear the slide or spot a pallet shifting and walk over to it at once
Plant your feet and push the pallet by its base to find where it rocks
Lift one corner with the pry bar and slide a wedge block under the runner
Run the strap over the top crates and ratchet it until the gauge reads green
Test the stack by leaning a shoulder into it to confirm it holds
Note the pallet number on the sheet and recheck the adjacent stack
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is knowing a wedge alone will not hold a top-heavy stack; failure is a re-secured pallet that moves again in the next lurch.
ideal_interaction: Player nudges a rocking pallet until its wobble stops, then wedges and straps it with a ratchet, testing the stack by pushing against it and watching whether it creeps.

label: Stage sensor drones and sample cases at the shuttlebay
human_steps: Get the survey manifest from the lab tablet and note the drone and case count
Take the first drone case from the racks, holding it level with both arms
Walk the case to the shuttlebay door and set it in the marked staging bay
Check the foam insert on each case so the sample tubes do not rattle
Stack the cases with padded corners up and labels facing the door
Call the lab tech on comm to confirm your count matches the lab list
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is knowing how far a case can be tilted without shaking a sample; failure is a cracked sample tube or a drone case staged backwards.
ideal_interaction: Player carries a case from the racks to the shuttlebay door while keeping it inside a tilt band on screen, then sets it inside the staging marks; tilting past the band cracks the sample tube.

label: Clear a sample storage rack in the bay
human_steps: Read the rack label and the dependency note to see which samples come off
Pull each sample case off the rack, checking its seal tag before it leaves the shelf
Set each case on the trolley, not on the floor, and keep them upright
Log each case ID on the clear sheet with its shelf and slot
Wipe the empty rack shelf with a dry cloth and look for residue or spilt powder
Push the trolley to the lab hatch and hand over the case count to the lab tech
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is spotting a broken seal tag before a case leaves the rack; failure is a breached sample loaded onto the trolley and never logged.
ideal_interaction: Player empties a rack shelf by lifting each case and checking its seal tag, then places it upright on the trolley; a case lifted with a broken seal triggers a hold on the sheet.

label: Move returned specimen cases to the lab
human_steps: Collect the returned cases from the shuttlebay door and read each return tag
Check the temperature strip on each case, since a warm one has spoiled
Carry cases one at a time to the lab, keeping them flat on the trolley
Place each case on the lab intake shelf in the order the tags list
Scan each case tag at the lab console so intake logs the arrival time
Flag any warm strip for the lab tech to see before anyone opens the case
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is noticing a warm case before its contents are lost; failure is a spoiled specimen logged as received in good condition.
ideal_interaction: Player collects cases from the shuttlebay, reads each temperature strip for a colour change, and moves a case to lab intake only once its strip reads cool, flagging warm ones on the console.

label: Verify manifest and tie-down for outbound load
human_steps: Pull the outbound manifest up on the console and read the destination and crate count
Walk the outbound stack, scanning each crate tag against its manifest line
Check every crate is strapped to its pallet and the strap reads tight on the gauge
Confirm hazardous placards face outward and mark the manifest for each one
Sign the manifest sheet with the bay number and time
Send the verified manifest to the quartermaster and wait for receipt
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is matching a scanned tag to the right line when two crates look alike; failure is a wrong crate beaming out with a strap that looks fine.
ideal_interaction: Player checks each outbound crate by scanning its tag against the manifest line and then testing the strap tension; a wrong crate or a loose strap blocks the verified stamp.
fit_note: Lashing covers only the tie-down half; the scan-against-manifest check, which decides whether the right crates leave, has no matching activity.

label: Stage crates on the transporter pads
human_steps: Take the staging ticket from the transporter tech and note the pad and transfer window
Haul the first verified crate from the bay on the grav sled
Position the sled on the pad with the crate centre over the pad mark
Check the crate lock and straps are still in place before transfer
Confirm the weight with the tech out loud so the beam gets the right mass
Step clear of the pad and signal the tech that it is ready
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is placing the crate so the transporter reads a clean lock; failure is an off-mark crate that misses the window and jams the pad.
ideal_interaction: Player rotates a crate on the sled until its lock indicator turns green over the pad mark, then waits out a short transfer timer; a crate set off-mark stalls the pad.

label: Receive inbound load and shelve in bay
human_steps: Collect the inbound crates from the pad as the transporter tech lands them
Read each crate tag and match it to the inbound manifest sheet
Check each crate for dents or wet patches before it goes near the shelf
Carry the crate to the rack bay and read the rack code stencilled on the upright
Slide the crate onto the shelf, pushing it back so its front lip sits flush
Write the rack and slot number on the inbound sheet
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is spotting a damaged crate before it sits on a shelf; failure is a dented or leaking crate shelved where it blocks the next load.
ideal_interaction: Player takes each inbound crate, checks its tag and surface, then carries it to the rack named by its code and slides it into the slot; a wrong rack or a crate left proud of the lip raises a toppling warning.

label: Close out manifest and report totals
human_steps: Open the closed-out manifest and read the totals for each section
Add the received count and the shipped count in separate columns
Compare each sum against the bay count and note any gap in pencil
Enter the final figures on the report form, one line per section
Attach the signed inbound and outbound sheets to the report
Submit the report and confirm the bridge has received it
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is reconciling a gap and deciding whether it is a real loss or a clerical slip; failure is totals submitted with the gap left out, so the bridge trusts a wrong number.
ideal_interaction: Player fills a report form by entering received and shipped counts per section; a total that does not reconcile with the bay count must be explained in a notes field before submit is allowed.

label: Pull medical supply crates from the bay
human_steps: Take the medical order from the nurse and note crate IDs carrying a red medical tag
Walk the bay racks to the medical section, found by its red stripe
Lift each crate with knees bent and the load close to the chest
Check each crate seal and lot label as it comes off the rack
Stack crates on the grav sled with the heaviest at the base
Confirm the count with the nurse before the sled moves
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is spotting a crate with a broken seal among sealed medical stock; failure is a compromised drug crate sent to sickbay as good.
ideal_interaction: Player walks the racks finding red-striped crates and lifts each onto the sled, keeping it level; a crate with an unsealed flap is caught at the seal check and must be set aside.

label: Haul crates to sickbay and shelve them
human_steps: Pull the sled along the corridor to the sickbay door and wait for it to open
Wheel the sled into sickbay, watching the floor for bumps that could tip a crate
Ask the nurse which cabinet or shelf each crate class belongs in
Unload each crate and check its lot against the order before placing it
Shelve drugs in the locked cabinet and dressings on the open shelf
Tick the order slip and hand it to the nurse for signature
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is sorting controlled drugs from dressings and locking the right items away; failure is a controlled drug left on an open shelf.
ideal_interaction: Player wheels a loaded sled through the corridor and shelves each crate into its marked cabinet or shelf; a controlled-drug crate left on an open shelf triggers a reshelve prompt.

label: Clear a quarantine corner in the bay
human_steps: Read the quarantine notice and find the corner marked by yellow floor paint
Pull on gloves and check each item for visible residue before touching it
Bag each contaminated item in a sealable sleeve and seal the zip fully
Place the bagged gear on the quarantine shelf with the tag facing out
Wipe the bay rail and the corner floor with a disinfectant cloth
Hang the quarantine tag and log the corner as sealed on the sheet
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is deciding what counts as contaminated and sealing it fully; failure is a half-sealed bag or a missing tag, so someone uses gear they should not touch.
ideal_interaction: Player walks to the yellow-marked corner, bags each contaminated item and drags its zip shut, then wipes the rail and hangs the tag; an unsealed bag leaks a warning.
fit_note: Clearout moves stock off a rack; quarantine needs bagging, sealing, wiping and tagging, which this activity does not cover.

label: Strap down everything in the bay before maneuvers
human_steps: Hear the shakedown alert and walk the bay to find what is still loose
Work along each crate row, pulling each strap end through its ratchet
Check every gauge needle sits in the green band, not the red slack zone
Lash loose crates to the bay ring anchors and tug each one to test its hold
Shim any rocking crate with a wedge block under its base
Walk the far wall last to check the nets, then report to the bridge
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is knowing which crates need an anchor and which can sit on a wedge; failure is a loose crate that goes airborne in a hard turn.
ideal_interaction: Player sweeps the bay row by row with a shake test on each crate; a crate that rattles past a threshold forces an anchor placement before the all-clear.

label: Test the cargo lift and sled
human_steps: Read the lift's last inspection tag and the sled's load rating on its placard
Walk the lift car and check the cable guide for grit or fraying
Load a test weight onto the sled and secure it with two straps
Run the lift up one level and back, listening for a stutter at each stop
Park the sled at the top of the ramp and check its brake holds
Log the test weight, run time and any noise on the lift sheet
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is hearing a stutter or grind before it becomes a stall; failure is a sled that fails under a live load in an emergency.
ideal_interaction: Player loads a test weight onto the sled, starts the lift, and balances the load on a distribution gauge while it runs; a lopsided load or brake creep forces a stop.
fit_note: Load balancing checks weight distribution only; it misses the cable inspection, brake hold and stutter listening that define a real lift test.

label: Post-maneuver inspection for damaged crates
human_steps: Start at the bay door and walk the racks in order, looking for crates tipped or split
Run a hand along each crate edge to feel for cracks or bowed panels
Check each tag and seal, noting any broken seal
Open a dented crate and look inside for shifted or broken contents
Tag each damaged crate with a red mark and note its rack slot
Enter each damage record on the console and file it to the quartermaster
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is spotting a hairline crack or bowed panel that is not obvious at a glance; failure is breakage that goes unlogged and a damaged crate shipped on.
ideal_interaction: Player inspects each crate by zooming along its edges on the console and tapping flagged panels, then opens a crate to check its contents; missed cracks surface on a re-scan.

label: Sterile field sweep and tray check
human_steps: Glove up from the dispenser and check the fingertips for tears
Wipe the biobed surface and rails in a fixed pattern, top to bottom
Check the scanner calibration light is green before using it on the field
Count hypos in the tray against the tray card, touching each to confirm the seal
Count dressings and sponges by sealed pack, noting any with torn corners
Log the stock counts and tray status, then reset the field drape
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is noticing a breach in the sterile field before it reaches a patient; failure is a contaminated tray used on a patient.
ideal_interaction: Player wipes the biobed rails in order with a cloth and taps each hypo in the tray to confirm its seal; a pack opened out of order or a missed rail marks the field unsterile.

label: Vitals round on occupied beds
human_steps: Walk to the first occupied bed and read the monitor's heart and oxygen numbers aloud
Check the IV line for air bubbles and confirm the drip rate on the pump
Look at the patient's colour and breathing before touching anything
Ask the patient how they feel and note the answer word for word
Check the dosing chart against the pump setting and the nurse's order
Chart any change and tell the nurse, not the bridge
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is telling a slight change in a patient from normal noise; failure is a drifting reading charted as stable.
ideal_interaction: Player moves bed to bed reading each monitor, checks the IV drip for bubbles and compares the pump rate against the chart; a drift must be caught before the patient's line flags.

label: Carry samples to the lab
human_steps: Collect labelled sample tubes from the sickbay rack and read each label
Seal each cap with the sealing clip, pressing until it clicks
Set tubes upright in the transport case, padded side down
Carry the case to the lab, keeping it level and away from the lift's shake
Load the tubes into the analyser tray in order, matching chart IDs
Log each result on the chart and recheck the ID before saving
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is keeping each sample's ID tied to the right patient; failure is a swapped label that gives a wrong result on a live patient.
ideal_interaction: Player seals each tube with a click, then loads it into the analyser slot matching its chart ID; a tube loaded against the wrong ID is rejected.

label: Check sickbay power and medical hologram readiness
human_steps: Open the power panel and read each bed's supply light, top to bottom
Press the test switch on each biobed and watch its monitor boot
Check the medical gas gauges and note any reading below the red line
Fire the emergency hologram trigger and confirm the emitter lights come up
Read the emitter self-test light and log any fault
Report any fault to the nurse first, then to Ops
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is telling an intermittent power dip from a real fault; failure is a bed that loses power while a patient is on it.
ideal_interaction: Player reads the bed lights and gas gauges, presses each bed's test switch until its monitor boots, and sets the hologram trigger so every emitter light goes green.
fit_note: Calibration covers the hologram emitter only; the bed power lights, gas pressure reading and trigger test that make up this check have no matching activity.

label: Restock hypos, dressings and trays
human_steps: Take the restock list from the locker door and read the low-stock items
Pull hypo cases, dressing packs and trays from the locker one item at a time
Check each pack's sterile seal and expiry date before shelving it
Put the oldest pack at the front of each shelf and the newest at the back
Load sterile trays on the cart and fill each slot to its marked line
Tick the list and tell the nurse which items are low for the next order
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is catching a broken seal and an expired pack in the same glance; failure is an expired hypo in the tray the next time it is needed.
ideal_interaction: Player fills each tray slot by dropping in one pack at a time until the marked line; a pack from a broken-seal slot is rejected by the expiry check.

label: Run baseline scans on duty crew on request
human_steps: Take the scanner from its cradle and check the battery and lens for smudges
Ask the crew member to stand still on the marked spot by the biobed
Pass the scanner over the crew member's face, chest and palms in a slow sweep
Read the baseline figures off the screen and note any out-of-band reading
Compare the figures to last month's baseline on the chart and mark any drift
Tell the crew member the result and file the scan to their chart
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is weighing a small drift against that person's own baseline; failure is missing fatigue or early illness that shows only as a slight shift.
ideal_interaction: Player sweeps the handheld scanner over a standing crew member in a slow arc, holding at each marked point until the reading locks; a sweep done too fast forces a re-scan.
fit_note: The ward activity is bedside monitoring; a baseline scan is a handheld sweep over a standing crew member, which that activity does not give.

label: Prepare isolation bed and decon kit in case of sampled contaminants
human_steps: Take the decon kit from its locker and check each item against the kit list
Strip the biobed and fit a fresh sheet, tucking the corners tight
Lay the isolation curtain across the bed frame and clip each fastener
Set up the decon shower head and check the water and drain
Stock the bed with a sealed gown, gloves and a biohazard bag
Log the bed as ready on the isolation board and tell the nurse
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is knowing a bed is safe to seal and a kit is complete; failure is an isolation bed with a missing clip or drain, letting contaminants escape.
ideal_interaction: Player makes up the biobed, fits the curtain clips in order and sets the decon shower head until its drain light turns green; a missing clip leaves the curtain open to a warning.

label: Screen away-team members on return
human_steps: Meet the away team at the transporter door and count heads against the roster
Run the handheld contamination sensor slowly over each person's boots, hands and hair
Ask each person about cuts, rashes, or any unusual taste or smell
Take a swab from anyone whose sensor reading goes amber
Bag the swab, label it with name and time, and send it to the lab
Mark each cleared person on the roster and hold anyone flagged for the doctor
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is deciding whether an amber reading is real or a sensor artifact; failure is contamination that gets past screening and spreads through the crew.
ideal_interaction: Player moves along the returning crew with the contamination sensor, sweeping boots, hands and hair, then takes a swab from any amber reading; a skipped sweep leaves that person unscreened.
fit_note: The ward activity is bedside monitoring; screening returning people needs a handheld sweep over each person, which that activity does not provide.

label: Inspect incoming medical stores and log expiry
human_steps: Walk to the cargo locker and take the incoming medical stores manifest
Open each carton and read the expiry date printed on each vial
Hold each vial to the light and check the liquid is clear, not cloudy
Set any expired or damaged vial in the red-marked bin
Log the expiry date and lot code for each good vial on the stores sheet
Report the count of expired items to the nurse before shelving
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is noticing a near-expiry or cloudy vial that looks fine at a glance; failure is degraded drugs shelved for treatment.
ideal_interaction: Player picks each vial from its carton, reads the expiry with a tap, holds it to the light for cloudiness and drops expired or cloudy ones into the red bin; a missed one blocks the shelf.

label: Prepare for lifting injuries and strains
human_steps: Pull the strain kit from the cabinet and check the splints and supports are all there
Set the biobed height to waist level for a patient coming off the sled
Lay out cold packs, support belts and a sling on the tray, grouped by use
Check the pain relief stock and the dose sheet clipped to the tray
Make up the bed with a clean sheet so the patient can be lifted without a shift
Tell the nurse which support sits on which side of the bed
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is picking the right support for a strain versus a fracture; failure is a patient moved on a bed with the wrong support, making the injury worse.
ideal_interaction: Player sets the biobed to waist height and then picks supports from the tray to place in their slots; a belt or splint placed on the wrong injury type is flagged.
fit_note: Tray arrangement covers laying items out, but not setting bed height or matching a support to a strain versus a fracture, which this job needs.

label: Set up triage beds and sort incoming patients by urgency
human_steps: Count open biobeds and check each bed's power light before assigning anyone
Read the incoming patient list on the nurse's tablet for injury type
Sort patients by triage tag colour, red first, then yellow, then green
Walk to the first red patient and move them to the nearest bed with a clear airway
Move a green patient to the waiting bench, keeping beds free for critical cases
Call out bed numbers to the nurse as each patient is placed
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is ranking a patient whose injury looks minor but whose vitals say otherwise; failure is a critical patient left on the bench behind minor cases.
ideal_interaction: Player drags each incoming patient tile to a bed slot, ranking red first, yellow next and green last; a critical tile left waiting past its timer flashes as a failure.

label: Run rapid scans and bloodwork for the doctor
human_steps: Collect the doctor's scan order and note which patients need bloods first
Walk to the lab and prime a fresh draw kit with saline
Tie the tourniquet above the elbow and feel for a vein
Draw the blood into the correct tube colour and seal the cap
Load the tube into the analyser and start the rapid scan
Read the output and send the figure to the doctor's display
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is hitting a vein on the first attempt and keeping the sample clean; failure is a haemolysed or mislabelled sample that gives a false result.
ideal_interaction: Player lines the needle up on the vein and draws back until the tube fills, then loads the tube into the analyser; a jerky needle path ruins the sample.
fit_note: Vitals reads bedside monitor numbers; this job is drawing blood and running the analyser, which the vitals activity does not cover.

label: Move stable patients to recovery and chart handoff
human_steps: Confirm the doctor's sign-off note on the chart before moving anyone
Unclip the monitor leads and cap the IV line
Help the patient sit up, then guide them onto a stretcher or wheelchair
Wheel the patient to the recovery bay and set the stretcher brake
Give the recovery nurse a verbal handoff with the last set of vitals
Chart the transfer time and last readings on the handoff form
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is deciding a patient is truly stable enough to move; failure is an unstable patient moved and then deteriorating in recovery.
ideal_interaction: Player unclips the monitor leads and caps the IV line, then wheels the stretcher to recovery and gives the handoff; moving a patient with leads still attached snags them and causes a fault.
fit_note: A form covers the charting but not the unclipping, lifting and wheeling of a patient, which is most of this job.

label: Test sickbay power, bed monitors and hologram trigger
human_steps: Go to the sickbay power panel and read each bus voltage on its display
Power each biobed monitor in turn and watch its self-test finish
Check the monitor alarm tone at low and high volume
Fire the hologram trigger and time how long the emitters take to come up
Log each bed's pass or fail on the shakedown sheet
Report any failing bed to the nurse before the drill starts
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is telling a slow emitter from a broken one; failure is a bed that passes its test but drops out under a real patient load.
ideal_interaction: Player steps through each bed's self-test by pressing its power and listening for the alarm tone, then fires the hologram trigger and times the emitter rise; a late or missing tone marks a fail.

label: Treat shakedown bumps and burns on the engineering crew
human_steps: Look at each engineer's burn or bruise under good light before touching it
Wash hands and glove up, then clean the wound with saline
Press the skin beside the burn and watch how fast the colour returns
Spray regen dressing evenly over the burn from a fixed distance
Wrap the area in a non-stick pad and tape the edges flat
Log the treatment on the chart and tell the engineer when to come back
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is grading burn depth and deciding whether regen alone is enough; failure is a deep burn treated as superficial and left to become an infection.
ideal_interaction: Player cleans each wound with saline, presses the skin to read how colour returns, then sprays regen at a set distance and applies a pad; a spray too close or an untaped pad forces a re-dress.

label: Patient rounds
human_steps: Wash hands at the sink and dry them before touching any patient
Walk to the first biobed and read the monitor's pulse and blood pressure
Check the patient's wrist and face colour and listen to their breathing
Take the temperature with the ear probe and record it
Give scheduled meds from the tray, checking name and dose against the chart
Chart each reading and report any change to the bridge at watch start
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is telling a patient who looks tired from one who is deteriorating; failure is a slow decline missed between rounds.
ideal_interaction: Player moves bed to bed reading each monitor, probing the ear thermometer and checking the med tray against the chart; a dose given to the wrong patient or a skipped reading flags the round.

label: Pharmacy and controlled meds count
human_steps: Open the controlled cabinet with the key and read the drug log on its door
Take out each controlled tray and count the ampoules or tablets in it
Compare each count to its log line and note any mismatch in pencil
Check the seal and expiry on each sealed pack before counting it
Restock from the replicator for any item below minimum, checking the batch code
Relock the cabinet and sign the log with the time and count
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is catching a small count mismatch that could mean diversion or a miscount; failure is a missing controlled drug signed off as present.
ideal_interaction: Player opens the cabinet and counts each drug tray by tapping items into a tally, then compares the tally to the log line; a mismatch cannot be signed until the count is redone.

label: Sterilise instruments and surgical bay
human_steps: Collect used instruments from the trays and sort them into soiled and clean piles
Rinse each instrument under the basin tap to clear blood and debris
Scrub joints and serrations with a brush until no residue shows under the lamp
Load instruments into the steriliser basket and close the lid
Start the steriliser cycle and wait for the pressure gauge to read full
Reset the surgical bay with a clean drape and a tray laid out in order
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is seeing residue hiding in a joint; failure is an instrument that goes through the cycle still dirty and is used on a patient.
ideal_interaction: Player brushes each instrument's joints under the inspection lamp and loads the basket; a residue spot still visible under the lamp blocks the cycle from starting.

label: Check medical hologram matrix
human_steps: Open the hologram matrix console and read the loaded program name
Run the emitter self-test and watch each emitter light come up in turn
Confirm the matrix version matches the sickbay program file in the log
Check each emitter for a dim or flickering light
Log the self-test result and the position of any dim emitter
Report any emitter failure to Ops
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is telling a dim emitter from one that is about to fail; failure is a hologram that drops out during a patient consult.
ideal_interaction: Player runs the self-test and watches each emitter light come up, flagging a dim or flickering one as a fault; a version mismatch must be corrected before the self-test can pass.
fit_note: Calibration covers a single dial; the emitter self-test, version check and fault log that make up this job have no matching activity.

label: Routine rounds and charting
human_steps: Pick up the chart pad and read the due-time list for each bed
Go to each biobed in order and check the patient is breathing normally
Read the bed monitor and compare the number with the last chart entry
Ask each patient one question about pain or sleep and write the answer down
Chart each bed's reading, time and any change on the pad
Initial each entry and move to the next bed
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is catching a small change against the last entry; failure is a trend missed because each single chart entry looks normal alone.
ideal_interaction: Player works down the chart pad bed by bed, comparing each reading against its last entry; a trend change prompts a note before the next bed opens.

label: Wellness walk to quarters
human_steps: Leave sickbay and walk the corridor to the crew quarters deck
Stop at each crew door and listen for music, raised voices or silence
Look at each crew member's face when they answer the door
Ask how sleep and meals have been this week and listen for a short answer
Offer a counselling referral or a check-in time and write it on the wellness list
Walk back to sickbay and log the names of anyone to follow up
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is hearing a flat or evasive answer for what it is; failure is someone slipping into withdrawal while everyone assumes they are fine.
ideal_interaction: Player walks the quarters corridor knocking on each door and reads a short exchange, choosing a supportive reply from a few options; a dismissive reply lowers that crew member's morale.
fit_note: Counselling is a talk-based exchange; the wellness walk is mostly walking doors and reading moods on the way, which a talk does not cover.

label: Prep radiation and sensor-exposure screening kit
human_steps: Take the exposure kit from the wall cabinet and check the dosimeter badges against the roster
Test each dosimeter by holding it near the test source until its read-out ticks up
Check the sensor wand battery and its calibration seal
Lay badges, wand and blank forms on the tray in roster order
Write each crew member's name on a badge before it goes on the tray
Log the kit as ready and tell the doctor it is on the tray
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is spotting a dead badge before a crew member leaves; failure is an away team sent out with a badge that reads nothing.
ideal_interaction: Player checks each dosimeter by holding it near the test source until its read-out rises, then lays it on the tray in roster order; a dead badge flags red and must be replaced.

label: Screen returning survey team
human_steps: Meet the survey team at the sickbay door and count them against the roster
Read each member's dosimeter badge and note the reading on the roster
Ask each member about headache, nausea or a metallic taste
Look at each person's skin and eyes for redness or swelling
Send anyone with a high reading or a symptom to a biobed for a closer look
Mark each person's screen result on the roster and inform the doctor
