what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is deciding whether a faint reading needs a closer look; failure is a delayed exposure that shows up as illness days later.
ideal_interaction: Player walks the returning team past a sensor reading each dosimeter, then asks the symptom questions; a reading above the line sends that person to a biobed, and a skipped questionnaire leaves them unscreened.
fit_note: The ward activity is bedside monitoring; screening a returning team is a walk-past reading and symptom check, which the bedside activity does not provide.

label: Treat crush and strain injuries from cargo bay
human_steps: Take the handler's history and ask where the weight came down
Feel along the limb for swelling, a cold spot and any grating
Ask the handler to move the fingers or toes and note any loss of feeling
Fit a splint or sling to the injury and check circulation below it
Give a pain dose from the tray only after the chart shows no allergy
Set a recheck time on the chart and tell the handler when to return
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is sorting a sprain from a fracture and a compression injury from a crush; failure is a crushed limb left unsplinted and worsening through the shift.
ideal_interaction: Player probes the injured limb, then picks a splint from the tray and fits it over the injury; a splint fitted over swelling or with circulation blocked triggers a recheck warning.
fit_note: Dosing covers medicine only; treating a crush injury means examining the limb and splinting it, which the dose activity does not include.

label: Stock splints and burn gel
human_steps: Count the splints left on the shelf by size, from small to large
Pull a fresh splint from the replicator tray and check its sterile seal
Stack the splints by size with the largest at the base
Check each burn gel tube for cracks or leaks at the cap
Shelve the gel by the sink with the lot code facing out
Tick the stock list for each size and each tube
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is keeping every splint size stocked so a small injury does not get a large splint; failure is a shelf that runs out of the size a handler needs mid-run.
ideal_interaction: Player fills each splint size slot from the replicator tray, stacking largest at the base; an empty size slot turns red so the player knows which to replace.

label: Prepare biobeds and isolation bay
human_steps: Count the biobeds and check each bed's power and monitor lights
Strip used sheets and bag them in the biohazard bin
Make each bed up with a fresh sheet, tucking the corners tight
Set the isolation bay door to seal and check the seal light
Stock each isolation bed with gowns, gloves and a sealed sharps box
Mark the beds ready on the bay board before the transport arrives
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is knowing which beds are free and which only look it; failure is a bed marked ready that has a fault the arriving patient finds.
ideal_interaction: Player makes up each biobed, strips used linen into the hazard bin and seals the isolation door until its light goes green; a door left unsealed or a bed missed flags on the board.

label: Triage incoming patients
human_steps: Take the incoming patient list and note injury type and arrival time
Walk to each arriving patient and check breathing and bleeding first
Read the pulse and oxygen figures off the pocket monitor for each patient
Tag each patient red, yellow or green on the wrist strap
Call the doctor for any red tag and point to the nearest free biobed
Chart each patient's tag, time and first figures before moving on
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is assigning the right tag colour under pressure; failure is a red patient tagged yellow and left waiting.
ideal_interaction: Player checks each arriving patient's breathing and bleeding, reads the pocket monitor, then taps a red, yellow or green tag onto their strap; a critical patient tagged yellow triggers a late-deterioration event.

label: Dispense meds and update patient list
human_steps: Open the patient list on the desk and read each patient's next dose time
Take the drug from the cabinet and check its name against the order line
Measure the dose into a cup or draw it into a syringe at the labelled line
Give the dose to the patient and ask them to say their name back
Tick the dose as given on the list with the time and your initials
Update the list with any new medication or changed dose
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is matching the drug, dose and patient together; failure is a wrong dose to the wrong patient that the list still shows as given.
ideal_interaction: Player takes a drug from the cabinet, checks its name against the order, draws the dose to the correct syringe line and gives it to the right patient; a dose drawn past the line or given to the wrong bed is caught.

label: Stage trauma kit near bridge-deck lift
human_steps: Take the trauma kit off the locker shelf and check the seal on its lid
Carry the kit to the bridge-deck lift and set it on the floor marking
Check the kit contents against the kit list inside the lid
Squeeze the bag valve once and check the oxygen mask seal
Set the lid latch and check it opens with one hand
Log the kit location and time on the shakedown board
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is knowing the kit is complete without unpacking all of it; failure is a kit that opens to find the bag valve missing during a drill.
ideal_interaction: Player carries the trauma kit to the lift floor marking, then checks the bag valve squeeze and the lid latch; a kit set down outside the marking or a missing item leaves the stage marked incomplete.
fit_note: Restock is shelving stock; staging a trauma kit by the lift means carrying it, checking its contents and testing the bag valve, which that activity does not cover.

label: Treat drill injuries and bruises
human_steps: Look at each drill casualty's bruise and note its size and colour
Press gently around the bruise to find the tender edge
Ask the crew member which movement hurts most and watch them do it
Give a cold pack and a pain relief dose from the tray, after checking the chart
Bandage any split skin with a dry pad and tape it flat
Tell the crew member which signs of worse injury to watch for and when to return
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is knowing when a bruise hides a deeper injury; failure is a bruise that is really a fracture going untested.
ideal_interaction: Player presses along the bruise edge to find the tender point, applies the cold pack and dose from the tray and bandages any split skin; missing a deep tenderness triggers an X-ray recommendation.

label: Cook and serve the meal
human_steps: Walk to the dry-stores hatch, read the tally card on each bin, and load a sack of rice, two tins of tomatoes and two onions onto the trolley.
At the stove, look inside the pot for old residue, then light the burner and wait for a steady blue flame before adding oil.
Dice the onions on the board, scraping them into the pan with the flat of the knife until they turn translucent.
Add rice and stock, cover, and set the kitchen timer; lift the lid each few minutes and press one grain between thumb and finger.
Ladle portions into the bowls on the counter and wipe any drip from the rim with a cloth before it reaches the tray.
Slide the tray onto the serving line and hand each bowl across with a spoon, calling the next name from the queue.
what_makes_it_hard: Timing several dishes so everything lands hot at the line while judging doneness by texture and smell; failure is a cold or scorched meal with a queue waiting.
ideal_interaction: The player stirs rice on the stove with a drag motion that keeps grains off the base, lifts the lid to press-test a grain, then ladles and plates portions onto bowls before the queue timer runs out.

label: Check galley replicator base stock and feed lines
human_steps: Walk to the replicator alcove and crouch at the access panel, reading the base-stock gauge against the paper chart taped inside the door.
Open the feed-line cover and trace each line with a fingertip to find kinks, frost or a loose clamp.
Unlatch the base cartridge, lift it out with both hands, and check its seal ring for cracks before fitting the spare.
Run a sample plate of plain rice and watch the output for grey streaks or a sour smell while the pattern buffer cycles.
Write the cartridge serial and gauge reading on the clipboard, circling any value inside the red band on the chart.
Close the panel and press the test button twice, confirming the status light goes green rather than amber.
what_makes_it_hard: Telling a slightly low gauge or a hairline seal crack apart from normal wear before it becomes a fault; failure is a contaminated batch or a replicator that quits mid-service.
ideal_interaction: The player opens the feed-line cover, drags the cursor along each line to find the bad clamp, swaps the cartridge by matching its seal-ring colour, then reads the gauge and logs any value that falls in the red band.
fit_note: Fresh is an expiry-date sort; the real job is reading a gauge, swapping a cartridge and tracing feed lines by hand.

label: Check cold store and dry stores
human_steps: Walk the corridor to the cold store, carrying the clipboard and a probe thermometer on its lanyard.
Read the wall display, then push the probe into a tub of milk and wait for the needle to settle before writing the number.
Walk the dry-goods shelves and count each crate of flour and tinned beans, lifting the lid to check for weevils or damp.
Pull any bag with a torn seam, sniff it, and drop it in the spoilage bin marked with a red tag.
Write each count beside the par level on the sheet, flagging any line that falls below half.
Tap the flagged line on the clipboard so the Galley Chief sees the shortage on the way out.
what_makes_it_hard: Spotting a slow temperature drift and a small amount of damp or pests before they spread; failure is a wasted delivery or a missed shortage that surprises the galley next week.
ideal_interaction: The player walks the stores, pushes a thermometer probe into a tub until the reading settles, then opens crates one at a time to count stock and tags any bag with a torn seam.
fit_note: Only the date-expiry part mirrors the work; temperature reading and crate counting are not modelled.

label: Scrub and sanitise the galley
human_steps: Clear the serving line by carrying pans and utensils to the sink, leaving only the wipe cloths on the counter.
Fill the sink with hot water and sanitiser, testing the temperature with a wrist before scrubbing.
Scrub the hot plates in circles with a green pad, working toward the grease trap so you never push grime onto clean metal.
Wipe every counter and handle with a sanitiser cloth, then count to thirty so the surface stays wet for the full contact time.
Load the dish rack, running each pan through the hot rinse and setting it upside down to drain.
Lift the bin liner from the waste bin, tie it off, and carry it to the chute, checking the floor for drips on the way.
what_makes_it_hard: Working in the right order so clean surfaces are not recontaminated, and holding sanitiser on the surface long enough; failure is a hidden film of grease or a dirty counter that makes someone ill.
ideal_interaction: The player works the cursor over each surface in a set order, scrubbing with a drag that removes grime only when the path runs toward the grease trap, then holds a wipe on each counter for a count of thirty.

label: Cook the ordinary meal and keep the line moving
human_steps: Check the hot plate by holding a palm an inch above the surface, then set the first pot on the front burner.
Cut bread into slices on the board and stack them on the cooling rack, nudging any crust that falls off back into the bin.
Stir the stew in a slow figure of eight so the bottom does not catch, and taste one spoon-tip for salt.
When the queue is long, add a second pot of rice and ladle portions faster, dropping a spoon when a bowl is overfilled.
Call out each dish to the line so the crew knows what is coming before it reaches the counter.
Wipe the spill at the front of the counter as soon as it happens so nobody slips on the way to a tray.
what_makes_it_hard: Keeping several pots moving while the queue grows and not letting one dish burn; failure is an empty line of hungry, grumbling crew and a scorched bottom on the stew.
ideal_interaction: The player moves between two pots, stirring each in a figure-of-eight so the base stays clear, and dispenses portions onto bowls as the queue fills, with spills appearing on the counter that must be wiped.

label: Stock check and shopping list for the Galley Chief
human_steps: Walk to the stores locker and take the stock card from the hook, noting the last date it was signed.
Go shelf by shelf, reading each tin and sack label for the quantity and the best-before date.
Compare each count with the par sheet and write the gap for every item that is under par.
Add the gaps to the shopping list in order of how soon the mess will run out, with the most urgent item first.
Tick off items already on the pending order slip so nobody is charged twice for the same bags.
Leave the list in the Galley Chief's tray with a note on any date that is closer than a week away.
what_makes_it_hard: Turning raw counts into an accurate, prioritised list without double-ordering stock already on order; failure is a shortage nobody saw coming or a duplicate order.
ideal_interaction: The player reads each shelf's labels, matches the count against the par sheet to build a list, then drags the most urgent gaps to the top of the order slip while ticking off items already pending.
fit_note: Writing the shopping list and checking pending orders are missing; the game only sorts dates.

label: Prepare a sealed, easy meal for the science crew at consoles
human_steps: Pick a sealed pouch of soup and a flat bread roll from the stores tray, checking the seal for pinholes.
Heat the soup in its pouch in the warm-water bath, timing it with the wall clock.
Cut the bread roll open and spread a thin layer of paste, keeping the knife clear of the crew's napkins.
Pack both into a covered tray with a cup of water and a fork, so the crew can eat one-handed at a console.
Carry the tray through the corridor, keeping it level, and set it down on the console shelf without spilling.
Watch the lab crew eat and note whether anyone is still hungry, then clear the tray when it comes back.
what_makes_it_hard: Choosing meals that can be eaten one-handed without mess near sensitive gear; failure is a spill on a console or a meal the crew cannot eat during the shift.
ideal_interaction: The player picks pouches off a shelf after checking each seal, warms one in the bath to a set timer, then packs a covered tray and carries it to a console without tilting it past a marked line.

label: Deliver coffee and sandwiches to lab and sensor stations
human_steps: Load the coffee flask and sandwich box onto the carry tray in the mess, checking the lids are clipped.
Walk to the lab door, shifting the tray to one hip so you can use the door panel without tipping it.
Find each analyst at the bench by sight, asking which mug they want and passing it across with the handle toward them.
Walk to the sensor station and lift a sandwich out of the box with tongs, placing it on a napkin next to the keyboard.
Pick up each empty mug from the bench and stack it on the tray, avoiding the cables on the floor.
Return to the mess and drop the empties into the wash bin, noting which station asked for more.
what_makes_it_hard: Getting drinks and food to the right person without interrupting their readings or spilling near equipment; failure is a broken mug, a stain on a console or an analyst left without food.
ideal_interaction: The player carries a tray through the lab, steps between stations and taps each bench to hand over a mug, then uses tongs to lift sandwiches onto napkins without bumping any console or cable.

label: Receive and shelve incoming food crates
human_steps: Meet the cargo handler at the dock hatch and sign the manifest, checking each crate number against the sheet.
Open the first crate and look inside for dents, damp or a broken seal on the bags before you lift anything out.
Stack the dry goods on a sack trolley and wheel it to the stores aisle, keeping your back straight on the ramp.
Shelve each sack on the bin marked with its label, turning the best-before date toward you so older stock sits in front.
Discard any split or wet bag into the spoilage bin, tagging it with the crate number.
Close the crate and stack it flat by the door so the handler can collect it on the next run.
what_makes_it_hard: Checking each crate fast enough that perishables do not sit on the dock while still spotting damage; failure is spoiled food nobody noticed or a mismatched manifest.
ideal_interaction: The player opens each crate, inspects bags for damage, then drags sacks onto a trolley and places each on the correct shelf bin, discarding any wet bag with a click before the dock timer runs out.

label: Cook big batch meal for the loading crews
human_steps: Lift two heavy pots onto the back burners and fill them with stock, checking the level against the marked line.
Add a sack of beans and a pack of rice, stirring with a long paddle so the bottom does not scorch.
Test one spoonful for salt, then add a handful more salt if the taste is flat, tasting again after stirring.
Check the lid seals and set the timer for the full batch, leaving a note on the counter with the time it will be ready.
Ladle portions into tall containers, leaving a finger's width at the top so the lids clip on.
Carry the containers to the dock hatch on the trolley and hand them to the loading crew, counting each one out.
what_makes_it_hard: Cooking enough food for a crowd without scorching the bottom of the pot or running short partway through; failure is a burnt pot or a loading crew eating cold rations.
ideal_interaction: The player stirs two large pots with a paddle along the bottom to keep beans from scorching, tastes to adjust salt, then fills containers to the fill line before wheeling a trolley to the dock.

label: Cook bland, high-calorie meals for patients and sickbay staff
human_steps: Read the diet card for the day in the sickbay tray book, noting which patients need soft food.
Weigh out oats, butter and milk on the scale, writing the grams on the card beside each patient's name.
Cook the oats slowly in a small pan, stirring constantly and watching for lumps that would be hard to swallow.
Add butter and a pinch of sugar, tasting a spoon and rejecting any batch with a burnt edge.
Divide the porridge into labelled bowls, one per patient, and cover each with a lid.
Carry the covered bowls and card to sickbay and check each name against the card before setting it down.
what_makes_it_hard: Matching each patient's diet card exactly while making food smooth and calorie-dense; failure is a patient given the wrong food or porridge that is too thick to swallow.
ideal_interaction: The player weighs each ingredient to the number on the card, stirs the pan to clear lumps, then matches each covered bowl to the patient name on the card before it goes on the sickbay tray.

label: Carry trays to sickbay
human_steps: Pick up the stacked trays at the mess hatch and check each cover is secured with the clip.
Walk down the corridor to sickbay, keeping the tray at chest height so the lids do not slide.
At the door, shift the stack onto one forearm and press the door panel with the other hand.
Find the biobed by its number, leaning in to match the patient's name against the tray label.
Set the tray on the bedside table and lift the cover so the nurse can see it is still warm.
Return to the mess with the empty trays, leaving any uneaten food in a bin for the nurse to report.
what_makes_it_hard: Matching each tray to the right patient bed in a busy ward while keeping food hot and balanced; failure is a patient left unfed or a tray set on the wrong bed.
ideal_interaction: The player carries a stacked tray down a corridor without letting it tilt past a marked line, then matches each tray label to the biobed number before setting it down and lifting the cover.

label: Make extra water and broth in bulk
human_steps: Fill the large kettle at the tap, checking the reading on the purification gauge before you close the lid.
Put the kettle on the high burner and watch the steam until a rolling boil starts.
Pour a measured sachet of stock powder into the second pot, stirring it in with the paddle until the granules dissolve.
Use the ladle to fill the water jugs, counting each jug on the rack and marking it with a strip of tape.
Cool the broth by standing the pot in the cold-water bath, stirring to bring the temperature down evenly.
Carry the labelled jugs to the sickbay hatch and hand them over, recording the count on the supply sheet.
what_makes_it_hard: Keeping water safely purified and broth at the right strength while the volume grows; failure is weak or unsafe drinks handed to a crowd.
ideal_interaction: The player fills and boils a kettle while watching the purification gauge, adds stock powder by stirring to dissolve it, then ladles and labels jugs by filling each to its line before the bulk count completes.
fit_note: Batch volume, purity gauge and cooling are not modelled; the cook game covers one plate at a time.

label: Test all galley equipment, hot plates and replicator lines
human_steps: Walk the length of the counter and switch on each hot plate in turn, placing a palm above it to feel the heat rise.
Check each plate's thermostat dial against the setpoint card, noting any plate that runs hot or cold.
Crouch at the replicator panel and run a test plate, watching the output for colour and texture changes.
Open the feed-line cover and press each clamp to confirm it holds, writing any loose one on the test sheet.
Load a sample of water and a dry sample into the replicator, timing how long each takes to cycle.
Switch every plate and replicator off, writing the final status on the sheet before you leave.
what_makes_it_hard: Telling a slow or drifting plate from a fully working one before service starts; failure is an equipment fault that shows up in the middle of a live meal.
ideal_interaction: The player turns each hot plate's dial to a setpoint and waits for the indicator to settle in the target band, then runs a timed test cycle on the replicator and marks any plate that drifts.

label: Report any galley faults to the bridge and Replicator Tech
human_steps: Open the fault log on the galley console and find the form for faults with a status code.
Type the plate or line number, the symptom you saw, and the time, reading each entry back before saving.
Select the addressee: the bridge for any safety issue, and the Replicator Tech for any replicator fault.
Attach the sample plate photo or note so the tech can see the grey streak or the faulty dial reading.
Press send and wait for the acknowledgement, then tap the notice to check it lists your report number.
Write the report number on the galley board so the next cook knows the fault is already being handled.
what_makes_it_hard: Describing a fault precisely and routing it to the right person; failure is a fault that stays hidden until a plate fails in service.
ideal_interaction: The player fills in the fault form by choosing the equipment from a list, selecting the symptom and the correct addressee, then attaches a sample note and sends it before the acknowledgement timer runs out.

label: Cook a quick meal under drill conditions
human_steps: Hear the drill call and grab a pot and a pack of rice from the nearest shelf without looking away from the stove.
Light a burner, fill the pot with water from the tap, and set it on the flame.
Measure rice by eye into the water, stirring with the spoon so it does not clump at the bottom.
Cover the pot and set the drill timer, checking the lid every thirty seconds for steam.
Serve each bowl onto the tray, calling the drill crew's names as each one lines up at the hatch.
Wipe the spoon and set it on the rack so the next cook can reach it.
what_makes_it_hard: Working fast under drill noise and pressure without skipping the boiling or the rest time; failure is undercooked rice and a line of crew fed late and griping.
ideal_interaction: The player grabs ingredients under a drill timer, pours rice into boiling water while stirring to stop clumps, then serves bowls onto a line of crew before the drill timer runs out.

label: Plan, cook and serve a meal
human_steps: Stand at the menu board and compare tonight's dishes with the stock sheet, crossing out anything the pantry cannot cover.
Walk to the cook's station and brief the cook on portions, timing and which dish to start first.
Watch the counter from the queue end, counting how many crew are waiting and signalling the cook to fire the next pot.
Walk the line with the portion scoop, checking each bowl's weight against the card and correcting an overfilled one.
Stand at the serving hatch and call names as the queue moves, pointing a late crew member toward the next free seat.
Write the portion count and any leftovers on the meal log before the next sitting.
what_makes_it_hard: Judging how many portions to cook and the right moment to start each dish so the queue never waits; failure is a missed meal or a half-empty mess after overcooking.
ideal_interaction: The player reads a stock sheet to cross out dishes the pantry cannot cover, then watches a queue meter and taps to fire each pot at the right time while the portion scoop checks bowl weight.
fit_note: Menu planning, briefing the cook and reading the queue are missing; the cook game only covers the hands-on cooking.

label: Cold store and pantry inventory
human_steps: Enter the cold store and read the temperature display, noting any reading above the red mark on the wall card.
Walk the shelves and count each carton of produce, lifting the leaves to check for rot or slime.
Open the dry-goods locker and count each sack and tin, comparing the number against the stock card.
Pull any soft or mouldy item into the spoilage bag, tying it and tagging it with the date.
Write each count on the pantry sheet, circling any line that dropped below the reorder mark.
Hand the sheet to the quartermaster's runner and confirm the reorder slip has the circled items.
what_makes_it_hard: Telling a slightly bruised item from a spoiled one while counting quickly; failure is stock that rots unseen or a reorder that is missed.
ideal_interaction: The player walks the shelves, lifts each produce carton to inspect it, drags soft items into the spoilage bag, and types counts into the sheet before the reorder slip is sent.

label: Replicator and galley equipment round
human_steps: Walk to the replicator panel and open the cover, reading the matter-stock gauge against the chart on the inside of the door.
Put a test plate in the tray and press start, watching it cycle until the output shows its texture and colour.
Check each feed clamp by pressing it, then listen for any hiss that would point to a leak.
Switch on a hot plate and read the thermostat, waiting for the dial to settle in the green band before moving on.
Write each reading and any fault on the equipment log, underlining the ones that need the tech.
If a value is off-spec, call the replicator tech from the wall handset and read out the gauge and the test plate result.
what_makes_it_hard: Telling a normal drift in a gauge from a true off-spec reading and describing it clearly to the tech; failure is a bad batch of food or a fault reported too late.
ideal_interaction: The player runs a test plate on the replicator and checks the gauge against the chart band, presses each clamp to listen for a leak, and calls the tech with the reading when a value is off-spec.

label: Sanitation and waste sweep
human_steps: Start at the counter's far end and wipe each surface with a cloth, moving toward the sink so no grime is spread back.
Scrape any crumbs from the floor into a dustpan, then sweep the corners behind the serving line.
Open the recycler lid and empty its tray into the chute bag, checking the seal before you move on.
Walk the mess floor and look under tables and along the walls for pests droppings or spilled liquid.
Mop any puddle with the bucket, wringing the mop until it drips no more than a few drops.
Set a wet-floor sign at each spot still drying and log the sweep time on the board.
what_makes_it_hard: Spotting pests and small spills in corners that are easy to miss; failure is a hidden infestation or a slip hazard left on the floor.
ideal_interaction: The player wipes each counter from the far end toward the sink, scrapes crumbs into a dustpan, then walks the floor looking under tables for droppings and mops any spill to a dry shine.

label: Serve the regular meals on time
human_steps: Stand at the serving counter and pick up the next bowl from the hot shelf, checking its label against the queue slip.
Ladle a standard portion, scraping the scoop once on the rim so the weight stays even.
Hand the bowl across with one hand and call the crew member's name, making eye contact as they take it.
Watch the queue and pull a second bowl forward when a crew member is waiting, checking the time on the wall clock.
Clear a dirty tray from the counter and wipe any splashed gravy so the next person does not slip.
Note the portion count on the tally slip and send a runner to the cook if the hot shelf runs low.
what_makes_it_hard: Keeping portions even and the queue moving while noticing when the hot shelf is running low; failure is a long wait, cold food or a short portion that angers the crew.
ideal_interaction: The player takes each bowl off the hot shelf, fills a standard portion using a scoop that levels off the rim, and hands it to a waiting crew icon while watching for a low-shelf warning.

label: Cold-store and pantry inventory
human_steps: Check the cold-store display for temperature, then walk the racks and read each date stamp on the cartons.
Pull the older cartons forward on the rack so the freshest goods sit behind them.
Count the sacks in the dry locker, ticking each one on the pantry sheet as you pass it.
Set aside any carton past its date into the spoilage crate and mark it on the sheet with a red pen.
Compare the count with the reorder mark and circle any line that is below it.
Carry the sheet to the galley office and leave it on the desk for the quartermaster's runner.
what_makes_it_hard: Reading small date stamps quickly and remembering which items are older; failure is spoilage that goes unnoticed until a meal is ruined.
ideal_interaction: The player reads each carton's date stamp, drags the oldest cartons forward on the rack, and moves any expired carton into the spoilage crate before the rack is counted.

label: Deliver night-shift plates to the bridge
human_steps: Stack the covered plates on the carry tray in the mess, checking each lid is clipped so the food stays hot.
Walk the corridor to the bridge hatch, holding the tray level and shifting it to one hip for the door panel.
Find the watch officer at the console by sight, and set down the plate closest to their hand without touching the controls.
Wait while the officer lifts the cover, then pass each remaining plate to the next watch station along the rail.
Lift the empty plates and stack them back on the tray, checking for cutlery left in the bowls.
Return to the mess and drop the empties in the wash bin, noting any station that asked for more coffee.
what_makes_it_hard: Getting plates to the right station on the bridge without interrupting a watch officer or touching a console; failure is a cold plate or a spill near the helm controls.
ideal_interaction: The player carries a covered-plate tray down a corridor and places each plate in front of a watch station, keeping the tray steady past a marked line and avoiding the console buttons.

label: Prepare extended-hours field rations for science teams
human_steps: Take a box of sealed ration packs from the stores shelf and check each pack's seal for pinholes.
Lay out the packs on the counter in a row, sorting them by meal type into labelled compartments.
Add a heat pad and a spoon to each pack, pressing the seal closed with the sealer clip.
Write the pack's batch number and the time it was packed on the field label, pressing it down so it sticks.
Stack the packs in the case by team name, placing the heaviest at the bottom to keep the case from tipping.
Close the case, strap it down, and log the count on the field sheet before it goes to the science lab.
what_makes_it_hard: Packing enough complete meals for a long survey without missing a spoon, heat pad or label; failure is a team that finds a pack with no heat source or a box that comes open in transit.
ideal_interaction: The player sorts ration packs by meal type into compartments, drops a heat pad and spoon into each pack, clips each seal shut, and stacks the packs into a case with the heaviest at the bottom.

label: Send hot meals to the lab
human_steps: Load the covered plates onto the carry trolley in the mess, checking each lid so the heat stays in.
Wheel the trolley down the corridor, slowing at the door and pressing the panel with an elbow.
Find each analyst by the workbench, asking whether they want the plate now or in a few minutes.
Set each plate on a heat mat next to the instrument, moving the cables aside so nothing gets knocked.
Check each plate with the back of a hand to be sure it is warm and not hot enough to burn.
Return to the mess with the trolley and tip the leftovers into the waste bin, logging which bench asked for more.
what_makes_it_hard: Serving hot food next to delicate instruments without knocking cables or sensors; failure is a spilled meal on the bench or a plate that goes cold before it is eaten.
ideal_interaction: The player wheels a trolley to the lab, lifts each covered plate onto a heat mat beside an instrument without touching the cables, and returns the trolley before a cooling timer on the plate runs out.

label: Restock the mess before the second sweep
human_steps: Open the stores locker and check the pantry sheet, noting which items the mess will run out of first.
Pull the sacks and tins for the first item from the nearest shelf, checking each best-before date.
Load the trolley with the newest stock and wheel it to the mess, pushing carefully over the threshold.
Shelve the items in the mess cupboard with the oldest at the front, turning the labels outward.
Tick each item on the restock sheet, adding any gaps to the reorder slip.
Leave the empty crates by the door for the runner to collect before the sweep begins.
what_makes_it_hard: Putting the right items back in the right order while keeping the oldest stock to the front; failure is a menu that runs out mid-survey or stock that spoils out of sight.
ideal_interaction: The player reads the pantry sheet, pulls items from locker shelves onto a trolley in order of urgency, then places each item on the mess shelves with the oldest date to the front before the second sweep timer runs out.

label: Draw fresh stock from incoming cargo
human_steps: Walk to the cargo bay and check the incoming crate list against the number stencilled on each box.
Open the first crate with a crowbar and look inside for bruised fruit, leaking seals, or wet packaging.
Lift each sealed item out and check its date stamp before setting it on a trolley.
Load the trolley with the freshest items first, keeping perishables in the insulated bin.
Wheel the trolley to the galley lift and send it up, watching the lift indicator reach the mess deck.
Mark each crate on the crate list with a tick or a cross and sign the receipt at the bay hatch.
what_makes_it_hard: Judging which items are fresh enough to keep before they spoil in the hold; failure is perishables left sitting in the hold until they rot.
ideal_interaction: The player opens each crate with a crowbar, inspects and lifts out each item to check its date, then drags perishables into an insulated bin and loads a trolley before the lift timer closes.

label: Rotate stores: use older stock first
human_steps: Walk the stores aisle and read the date on the front carton of each shelf, noting which ones are oldest.
Pull the older cartons to the front of each shelf, sliding them forward so they are picked first.
Move the newest cartons to the back, turning the labels outward so the dates can be read at a glance.
Pick out any carton past its date and set it in the spoilage crate with a red tag.
Update the rotation card on the shelf with the date of the new order.
Close the locker and log the rotation on the sheet, leaving the spoilage crate by the door for collection.
what_makes_it_hard: Telling which carton is oldest when several share the same shelf; failure is old stock used last and wasted, and an overfull cold store.
ideal_interaction: The player reads each carton's date on a shelf and drags the oldest one to the front, moving any expired carton into the spoilage crate, until the shelf is in date order.

label: Feed the loading crew double shifts
human_steps: Check the double-shift list and count the loading crew who are coming to the mess for the extra meal.
Ladle portions into bowls, adding a cover to each so the food stays warm on the walk to the dock.
Hand each bowl to a loader at the hatch, calling their name off the list and ticking them as they take it.
Watch the queue and fill the next bowl immediately when a crew member is waiting, keeping the line moving.
Wipe any splash from the counter and stack empty bowls on the trolley.
Note the number served on the crew list and tell the cargo supervisor if the queue is still long.
what_makes_it_hard: Keeping a long queue moving without dropping portion size or running out; failure is a crew that works hungry and the cargo schedule slips.
ideal_interaction: The player fills bowls from a ladle as crew icons queue at the hatch, ticks each name off the list when served, and refills the counter before the queue meter empties.

label: Prepare special-diet and soft-food trays
human_steps: Read each patient's diet card in the tray book, noting which items are soft, low-salt or thickened.
Measure the cooked rice and mash into the right portion using the small scoop, then soften it with broth.
Check each tray's texture by pressing a spoon into the food, rejecting any lumps that would be hard to swallow.
Set each tray in the order of the diet cards, pairing each cover with the matching patient label.
Clip the lid on each tray and write the patient's name and diet code on the sticker.
Stack the finished trays on the sickbay cart with the labels facing out so the nurse can check them quickly.
what_makes_it_hard: Matching each diet card exactly and getting the texture right for patients who cannot chew well; failure is the wrong food reaching a patient or lumpy food that is unsafe to eat.
ideal_interaction: The player reads a diet card, scoops the correct portion, then presses a spoon into the food to check the texture before sticking the matching patient label onto the lid.
fit_note: Reading diet cards and checking food texture by hand are missing; the cook game does not model dietary rules.

label: Deliver trays to sickbay
human_steps: Pick up the trays from the mess hatch and check each label matches the sickbay list.
Walk down the corridor with the cart, keeping the trays level so the covers stay put.
Enter sickbay and find each biobed by its number, reading the patient label against the tray.
Lift the cover to confirm the food is warm and the portion looks right, then set the tray on the bedside table.
Tell the nurse which patients have eaten and which need a second tray, writing it on the sickbay board.
Return the cart to the mess, sorting the empty trays into the wash rack.
what_makes_it_hard: Finding the right patient in a busy ward and checking the food before it goes on the table; failure is a patient left unfed or a meal set on the wrong bed.
ideal_interaction: The player wheels a tray cart down the corridor and matches each tray label to a biobed number before lifting the cover and placing the tray on the table.

label: Sanitise the galley against contamination
human_steps: Clear the counter of food and move any open containers into the cold store before cleaning starts.
Spray the counter with sanitiser and wipe it in one direction, starting from the clean end and moving toward the bin.
Scrub the handles and tap heads with a brush, reaching into the crevices where germs gather.
Rinse each utensil in hot water, then leave it to dry on a clean rack instead of a cloth.
Mop the floor from the back wall forward, changing the mop water when it looks grey.
Set a wet-floor sign at the door and log the sanitising time on the board before the next meal.
what_makes_it_hard: Making sure no surface is missed and the sanitiser has time to work; failure is contamination that spreads illness through the crew.
ideal_interaction: The player sprays and wipes each counter section in one direction from clean to dirty, brushes the tap heads and handles, and holds the surface for a sanitiser timer before it turns green.

label: Keep the mess open through drills
human_steps: Stand at the mess door and check the drill schedule on the wall screen, noting which crews are arriving first.
Call the cook and sort the pans so the first dish can be started without waiting.
Walk the counter, watching the queue and the hot shelf, and calling out which dish needs to be replenished next.
Take a bowl from the queue to the drill crew who are standing by, checking they can eat while they wait.
Wipe the counter when a bowl is set down and shift the trays to keep the line clear.
Log the number of crew served and any gaps on the drill board for the bridge to see.
what_makes_it_hard: Coordinating a cook, a queue and a drill schedule at once; failure is crew who go hungry during drills and a line that stops moving.
ideal_interaction: The player watches a queue and a hot-shelf gauge while calling the cook to start dishes at the right time, and serves bowls to crew icons before the drill timer on the line runs out.
fit_note: Running the room and the line under drill pressure is not modelled; the cook game only tests one meal.

label: Test galley backups: manual stoves and spare stock
human_steps: Find the manual stove in the back cupboard and pull it onto the counter, checking the gas valve is closed.
Connect the gas cylinder, open the valve slowly, and light the burner with a striker, watching for a steady blue flame.
Set a small pot on the stove and boil water, timing how long it takes to reach a rolling boil.
Open the spare stock crate and check each sack and tin against the spares list for damage.
Log the boil time and stock count on the test sheet, marking any valve that leaks or any tin that is dented.
Shut the valve, disconnect the cylinder, and store the stove back in its cupboard with the spares crate beside it.
what_makes_it_hard: Lighting and running an unfamiliar manual stove safely while timing it accurately; failure is a gas leak, a burner that will not light, or a backup that fails in an emergency.
ideal_interaction: The player connects a gas cylinder, opens the valve slowly while watching a pressure gauge, strikes the burner to light it, and times a boil on the pot before shutting the valve.

label: Stage emergency ration packs by the lifeboats
human_steps: Carry a box of emergency ration packs from the stores locker to the lifeboat bay, checking the seal on each pack.
Stack the packs by the lifeboat hatch in groups of ten, keeping the labels facing out.
Check each group's count against the stage list and tick them off as you go.
Strap the packs down on the shelf to stop them shifting, leaving a clear path to the lifeboat hatch.
Tag the stack with the date and the lifeboat number so the crew knows which stack is theirs.
Write the total count on the emergency board and report it to the bridge when the stage is complete.
what_makes_it_hard: Getting an accurate count and keeping packs sealed and clear of the lifeboat path; failure is a shortage of rations in an evacuation or a blocked hatch.
ideal_interaction: The player carries ration packs from a locker to the lifeboat bay, stacks them in groups of ten, and ticks each count off the stage list before straps are fastened to keep the hatch path clear.

label: Safety interlock and emitter sweep
human_steps: Walk to the holocube and crouch by the interlock panel, reading the status light on each door.
Check the interlock readout on the wall screen against the green band, noting any door that shows amber.
Stand at each boundary emitter in turn and tap its casing with a test probe, listening for the right tone.
Move the test probe slowly across the emitter face, watching the grid line on the handheld for any gap.
Write each emitter's reading and any amber light in the safety log, underlining the ones that need attention.
Sign the safety log at the bottom of the page with the time and close the cover.
what_makes_it_hard: Telling a faint flicker from a real gap in the boundary grid, and catching an interlock that is drifting before it locks; failure is a program that breaks containment during use.
ideal_interaction: The player walks to each emitter, taps the casing with a probe until the tone matches, sweeps the probe across the face to check for gaps, and logs every amber interlock before signing off.

label: Audit the program archive
human_steps: Open the new-program list on the datacore console and read the file names, noting any with unfamiliar tags.
Select the first program and start the integrity scan, watching the progress bar for any corrupted segment.
Open the scan report and read each flagged block, comparing its checksum with the one on the manifest.
Mark each mismatched block in the quarantine list, dragging it into the holding folder so it cannot be loaded.
Run a second scan on the quarantined files to confirm the corruption is not just a read error.
Save the audit result and sign the archive ledger with your access code.
what_makes_it_hard: Spotting a single corrupted block among thousands that look identical; failure is a corrupted program loading during a live session and endangering users.
ideal_interaction: The player compares program blocks against their checksums, flags each mismatched block, drags the corrupt program into the quarantine folder, and runs a second scan to confirm.

label: Reset a booked session
human_steps: Walk onto the holodeck and check the room for stray items, lifting props and moving any loose furniture to the wall.
Purge the matter residue by running the purge cycle at the console, watching the matter counter reach zero.
Open the next booking on the console and read the program name and the number of guests.
Load the program, confirming the parameters match the booking card and correcting any mismatch in the field.
Check the safeties on the console, confirming each interlock shows a green armed status.
Step out, close the door, and tell the booking desk the room is ready.
what_makes_it_hard: Making sure the room is empty and the safeties armed before the next guests walk in; failure is leftover matter or an unarmed safety that puts guests in danger.
ideal_interaction: The player clears props from the floor, runs the purge cycle until the matter counter hits zero, and dials in the booking parameters before confirming each interlock turns green.
fit_note: Clearing the room and walking through the booking is missing; the calibrate game is a dial-tuning task.

label: Request cleaning stock from stores
human_steps: Walk to the emitter cabinet and count the boxes of emitter wipes, noting how many are left in each stack.
Check the wipe count against the reorder sheet, circling any box that is below the minimum mark.
Walk to the stores counter and fill in the request form, choosing the item and quantity from the drop-down list.
Attach the form to the quartermaster's tray and check it has the holodeck tag on the top corner.
Wait for the quartermaster to sign the acknowledgement slip and read it back to confirm the quantity.
Write the request number on the emitter cabinet door so the next person knows a restock is on its way.
what_makes_it_hard: Counting the wipes accurately and picking the correct quantity so the holodeck does not run out; failure is dusty emitters or a restock that is never requested.
ideal_interaction: The player counts each box of wipes on a stack, circles low stock, and fills in a request form by choosing the item and quantity before sending it to the quartermaster tray.

label: Open bookings and run the standard grid sweep
human_steps: Open the booking board on the wall console and read each slot for the day, noting which programs are booked.
Walk to the holocube and crouch by the grid panel, checking each emitter's status light for amber.
Tap the boundary emitters one by one with the test probe, listening for the right tone and feeling for any drift.
Set the grid to the standard sweep pattern and watch the readout climb to full power, stopping at any dip.
Open each booking slot on the board so guests can book, confirming the room is clear first.
Log the sweep time and any amber light on the safety log before you leave.
what_makes_it_hard: Telling a grid that is drifting from one that is merely noisy and noticing it before a guest does; failure is an interlock fault that goes unseen during a booked session.
ideal_interaction: The player walks the grid panel, taps each emitter with a probe until its tone matches, and opens booking slots on the board only after the sweep readout reaches full power.
fit_note: The physical emitter and grid sweep is missing; the schedule game covers only the bookings.

label: Audit the archive for corrupted programs
human_steps: Open the archive index on the datacore console and pick the oldest programs first.
Run the integrity scan on each file, watching the progress bar until it reports a complete pass.
Read each flagged block and compare its checksum against the value on the manifest line.
Drag any corrupt file into the quarantine folder, checking its name so it does not get loaded by mistake.
Look for any file that has a missing tag or a broken header and mark it for review.
Save the audit result and sign off the log with your access code.
what_makes_it_hard: Finding a few corrupt blocks in a large archive without skipping files; failure is a bad program loading at the worst time.
ideal_interaction: The player runs the integrity scan on each file, compares flagged blocks against their checksums, and drags any corrupt file into the quarantine folder before it can be loaded.

label: Limit sessions to low-power programs so sensors keep power
human_steps: Open the power budget on the holodeck console and read the current draw against the sensor allowance.
Scroll the program list and mark each program's power rating, highlighting any above the allowance.
Set the session limit to low-power programs only, confirming the cap appears on the booking screen.
Walk to the holocube and check the emitters are running at the reduced setting, watching the draw meter.
Tell the booking desk which programs are now off the list so guests do not try to book them.
Log the new limit and the time it was set on the power log.
what_makes_it_hard: Choosing programs that keep the draw under the allowance without making the room boring; failure is sensors losing power or guests booking a program that starves them.
ideal_interaction: The player reads the draw meter against the allowance, marks each program's power rating, and sets the cap so the draw meter stays under the limit line.

label: Run a calm relaxation program for off-shift survey crew
human_steps: Read the survey crew's request card, noting the preferred setting and how many people will be in the room.
Browse the calm program list on the console and open each candidate's preview to check its scenery and sound.
Select a program that matches the request, then set the scenery brightness and background sound to the level on the card.
Walk to the holocube and check the emitters are set for a low-intensity scene, watching the readout settle.
Step into the room and check the scenery is clear of hazards, moving any object that could catch a foot.
Leave the room and confirm the program has started on the console before closing the door.
what_makes_it_hard: Matching a program to a crew's mood and checking it is safe before anyone enters; failure is a program that feels wrong or a hazard left in the scenery.
ideal_interaction: The player previews calm programs, matches scenery brightness and sound to the request card with sliders, and confirms the emitter readout settles into the low-intensity band before the room is opened.
fit_note: Previewing and matching a program to a crew request is missing; the calibrate game is a dial-tuning task.

label: Close the playroom during cargo transfers and give the space to stores
human_steps: Walk to the holodeck door and read the cargo transfer schedule posted on the frame.
Check the room is empty by peering through the window and calling out once before entering.
Shut the holocube down at the console, watching the emitter lights go out one by one.
Walk the room and lift any remaining props or furniture to the wall so the floor is clear for crates.
Lock the door at the panel and tape a notice on it stating the room is closed until the transfer ends.
Tell the stores lead the room is clear and hand over the key card.
what_makes_it_hard: Making sure nobody is inside before shutting down the emitters and that every light goes out; failure is a crew member caught in a live program or a locked room no one knows about.
ideal_interaction: The player shuts the holocube down by switching off each emitter in order, checks the room through the window, and locks the door at the panel once the room is empty.

label: Help the cargo handlers stack crates in the playroom
human_steps: Meet the cargo handlers at the playroom door and read the crate list to confirm which boxes are going in.
Lift the first crate with the handler on the other side, bending at the knees and keeping your back straight.
Walk the crate to the wall stack, setting it down on a pallet and checking it is level with the crate below.
Move the next crate onto the stack, aligning the corners so the pile does not lean toward the door.
Strap the stack with a cord and tug each knot to check it holds before moving to the next pile.
Tick off the crate list and tell the handler the stack is ready to be counted.
what_makes_it_hard: Stacking heavy crates so they stay level and do not block a corridor; failure is a stack that tips and blocks the doorway.
ideal_interaction: The player lifts crates onto a pallet and aligns each one with the crate below before strapping the stack, with a warning if a pile leans toward the doorway.
fit_note: Lifting and aligning physical crates is missing; the load-balance game abstracts the stacking.

label: Switch grid emitters to a calm recovery program for patients' families
human_steps: Read the family visit card at the holodeck door, noting the number of visitors and any patient restrictions.
Walk to the holocube and crouch by the emitter panel, checking the interlock lights are green.
Select a calm recovery program on the console and read its preview of scenery and sound.
Adjust the scenery brightness and background sound on the sliders until they match the card's request.
Watch the emitter readout settle into the low band, tapping any emitter that flickers to reset it.
Confirm the program is running, then tell the nurse the room is ready for families.
what_makes_it_hard: Setting a gentle program that is safe for sick patients' families; failure is a harsh scene or a flickering emitter that upsets the visitors.
ideal_interaction: The player previews a calm recovery program, sets brightness and sound with sliders to match the card, and taps any flickering emitter until the readout holds in the low band.
fit_note: Previewing and matching a program to a family card is missing; the calibrate game is a dial-tuning task.

label: Stand by with the grid in case the medical hologram needs emitter help
human_steps: Sit at the holodeck console and check the grid power readout, noting the baseline draw.
Open the medical channel on the console and listen for a call from the medical hologram.
Watch the readout and the emitter status while you wait, looking for any dip or spike.
When the medical hologram asks for emitter help, switch the requested emitter to full power and watch its response.
Confirm the emitter holds the setting, then return it to the baseline and log the time of the change.
Stay at the console until the medical call ends, then close the channel and write the outcome in the log.
what_makes_it_hard: Staying alert for a call that may not come, then reacting in time without overloading the grid; failure is a late or wrong emitter change that spoils the medical program.
ideal_interaction: The player watches a grid power readout and waits for a call marker, then raises the requested emitter to full power and holds it steady while keeping the draw inside the limit line.
fit_note: The job is standing by and reacting to a call; the power game is a timed draw-limit task with no waiting on a channel.

label: Test the safeties at full power and log the result
human_steps: Walk to the holocube and check the interlock lights are green before raising the emitter power.
Raise the grid power to full at the console, watching the readout climb to the top mark.
Walk around the holocube and tap each boundary emitter with the probe, listening for the tone that shows it holds.
Trigger each interlock test in turn, watching the door lock and the emitters drop out on command.
Note any interlock that fails to drop, marking it red on the test sheet.
Return the grid to standby, sign the test sheet, and log the safety result.
what_makes_it_hard: Pushing the grid to full power while watching every interlock respond; failure is a safety that does not cut power and a program that runs unsafe in front of guests.
ideal_interaction: The player raises the grid to full power, taps each boundary emitter until its tone holds, and triggers every interlock test to confirm each emitter drops out on command.

label: Cycle the emitters through every program class
human_steps: Open the program class list on the console and read the name of each class, from scenery to combat.
Load the first class's sample program and watch the emitter readout for dips or spikes.
Walk the holocube and check each emitter's glow and tone while the sample plays.
Move on to the next class, leaving the sample running long enough to see any weak emitter.
Mark any emitter that dims or stutters on the test sheet, circling its number.
Shut the sample down and write the class result on the sheet before moving to the next class.
what_makes_it_hard: Spotting a weak emitter that only shows up under one program class; failure is a visibly weak emitter that ruins a public program.
ideal_interaction: The player loads each program class in turn, walks the emitters to check their glow and tone, and circles any emitter whose readout dips while the sample runs.
fit_note: Walking the emitters to check glow and tone is missing; the calibrate game is a dial-tuning task.

label: Audit food and spares stores
human_steps: Walk to the stores depot with the ledger slate and a tally counter clipped to the belt.
Check the cold store door gasket by running a gloved finger along it and reading the wall thermometer.
Pull the bin ledger printout for aisle A and start at the top-left bin.
Count each tin or pack in the bin by touching it, one at a time, and tap the counter per item.
Compare the bin total to the ledger line; a shortfall means the count is lower than the printed figure.
Read the best-before stamp on any dry goods pulled forward to confirm nothing is past date.
Write shortfalls on the slate and mark any line under two days of supply for a resupply call.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement lies in counting every item behind the front row and spotting a shortfall before it becomes a crisis; failure is copying last watch's figures or counting a stacked bin as full.
ideal_interaction: Aisle walk with the tally counter: the player moves along a shelf grid, sweeping each bin and tapping per item, and a bin skipped or double-counted shows as a mismatch to fix against the ledger line on screen.
fit_note: fresh is a generic console screen; a shelf-by-shelf physical count against a ledger does not come through.

label: Replicator feedstock and queue
human_steps: Walk to the mess replicator bay and read the four feedstock canister gauges on the panel.
Note any gauge below the 20 percent mark and record the canister ID on the handheld.
Open the replicator touch queue and scroll down the list, reading each job tag for corrupt or stuck entries.
Select the jammed entry, confirm the tag matches a dead job rather than a live meal order, then press purge.
Pull the pattern cartridge from the faulty slot, wipe the reader contacts with a dry cloth and reseat it.
Enter a refill request from stores for every low canister and get the signature from the galley.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is telling a stuck job from a live meal order before purging; failure is purging a valid lunch order and leaving the galley with nothing to serve.
ideal_interaction: Tag match and purge: the player reads queued job tags on the replicator screen and purges only the corrupt ones, while a hold-and-release on the refill button fills each low canister until its needle enters the green band.
fit_note: fresh does not involve reading job tags, reseating cartridges or topping up gauges.

label: Cargo manifest and lashing check
human_steps: Walk to the cargo workbench and pick up the manifest slate for the current bay.
Read the manifest line by line and note the pallet count and each pallet's lashing class.
Walk the pallet row and check each pallet's ID tag against its manifest line.
Crouch at each pallet's lashing points and pull the strap by hand to feel for slack.
Press each buckle until it clicks home and look for fraying on the cargo net edges.
Enter the pallet count on the slate; any mismatch means the load is held until Ops is told.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is telling a strap that looks tight from one that actually holds; failure is missing slack on a rear pallet, which later shifts in transit.
ideal_interaction: Strap tension: the player walks the pallet row and holds the tension trigger on each strap until the gauge needle enters the marked band, releasing early leaves the strap slack and the load flagged.

label: Requisition round
human_steps: Walk to the stores door and collect the requisition pad from the rack beside it.
Read each request slip and check the signature field against the officer roster.
Walk to the bin named on the slip and pull the item and the quantity requested.
Check the item's expiry or serial tag matches the request before handing it over.
Have the requester sign the pad on the screen with their finger.
File the signed slip in the ledger tray and log the issue time.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is refusing an unsigned or mismatched request calmly; failure is issuing against a forged signature or handing over the wrong serial.
ideal_interaction: Signature gate: the player picks each requested item from its bin, then checks the slip's signature field and rejects an unsigned slip before the item can be handed over.
fit_note: manifest matching does not cover checking signatures or the hand-over.

label: Full inventory count of cold and dry store
human_steps: Walk into the cold store and check the door seal and temperature panel before starting.
Pick up the tally clicker and a chalk stick, then start at the far corner of aisle one.
Count each stacked crate by pressing the clicker once per crate, moving crates aside to see hidden rows.
Chalk a tick on the bin label when a bin's count is finished so no bin gets counted twice.
Write each aisle total on the tally sheet and compare it to the last count.
Circle any aisle where the difference is larger than the usual spoilage allowance.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is seeing rows hidden behind stacked crates and stopping at the right tally; failure is a missed back row that makes the total look fine when it is short.
ideal_interaction: Crate shift and count: the player walks the aisles, shifts stacked crates aside to reveal hidden rows, and presses the clicker once per crate, with a missed hidden row showing as a gap in the aisle total.

label: Rotate expiring stock to the galley
human_steps: Walk to the mess table with the expiry list and the rotation cart.
Lift each tin from the expiring tray and read the best-before stamp on its base.
Sort the tins by date, placing the earliest-dated ones at the front of the galley shelf.
Move newer stock behind the old so the oldest item is the first reached.
Load the cart with the items near expiry and wheel it to the galley hatch.
Hand over the cart and mark the rotation line on the expiry list.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is reading the date on the base of each tin quickly and in the right order; failure is putting new stock at the front so old tins rot unused.
ideal_interaction: Date-order sort: the player lifts each tin, reads its date, and places it into the front-of-shelf slot for the earliest date, with a wrongly ordered placement counted as a mistake.

label: Issue probes and sample containers to science
human_steps: Walk to the stores locker and open the probe case on the shelf.
Check each probe's calibration tag and set aside any with an expired date.
Count sample containers into a tray, matching the number on the science request sheet.
Tick each item off the sheet as it goes into the tray.
Carry the tray to the lab hatch and hand it to the science officer.
Get the officer's initials on the sheet and file the copy.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is catching an expired calibration tag before the probe leaves the depot; failure is sending a probe that gives science wrong readings.
ideal_interaction: Kit assembly: the player picks each probe and container against the request sheet, rejecting any probe with an expired calibration tag before it can be loaded into the tray.
fit_note: manifest matching does not cover calibration tags or handing a tray to an officer.

label: Stage extra rations for long lab shifts
human_steps: Walk to the mess replicator and open the ration crate beside it.
Check the shift roster and count one ration bar and one water pouch per lab tech.
Pack each tech's items into a shift bag, reading the allergen card attached to each bag.
Seal the bag with the heat strip and press it until the strip is flat.
Write the shift number and the tech's name on the bag label.
Stack the bags on the cart by shift, lowest number at the front.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is matching the allergen card to the right bag and confirming the count per tech; failure is handing a tech a bag with the wrong allergen flag.
ideal_interaction: Pack and seal: the player drops one ration bar, one pouch and the matching allergen card into each shift bag, then presses the seal strip only when the bag count matches the roster.

label: Log consumed survey stock
human_steps: Walk to the stores desk and pick up the returned survey slips from the tray.
Walk to the returns bin and count the empty containers and used packs.
Match each empty container to a slip by its batch number.
Type each item and quantity into the ledger form, one line per item.
Compare the typed quantities with the original issue record and correct any mismatch.
Initial the slip and file it in the closed-survey folder.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is matching empties to the correct slip and correcting a quantity that does not balance; failure is entering a quantity from the wrong slip so the ledger drifts.
ideal_interaction: Slip matching: the player takes each returned slip, matches its batch number to the issue record line, types the quantity and fixes any entry that differs from the record before filing.

label: Clear space and verify the cargo manifest
human_steps: Walk to the cargo workbench and pick up the run manifest slate.
Clear loose tools and tote bins out of the marked transporter zone.
Lay floor tape along the edge of the clear zone and check the markings are straight.
Walk the bay and read the ID stencil on each crate in the zone.
Match each stencil to a manifest line and tick it off on the slate.
Flag any crate that is missing from the manifest or sitting in the transporter path.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is seeing which crate sits in the transporter path and which stencil does not match; failure is a stray crate blocking the hand-off or an unlisted crate going out.
ideal_interaction: Clear and check: the player drags clutter out of the marked zone to clear the transporter path, then walks the crates and scans each stencil against the manifest, flagging any crate not on the list.
fit_note: the manifest check fits, but clearing the transporter path is missing.

label: Supervise loading and lashing
human_steps: Walk to the pad edge and put on the headset linked to the loader crew.
Watch each pallet slide onto the pad and read its tag as it passes.
Call the loader to stop when a pallet's corner is flush with the pad edge.
Check the strap is fed through the ring and the buckle is set.
Signal the next pallet only when the previous one is fully lashed.
Walk the finished load and tug each strap to confirm it does not give.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is spotting a pallet sitting crooked before it is lashed; failure is a load that shifts in transit and damages the cargo.
ideal_interaction: Flush call timing: pallets slide onto the pad and the player presses call as each corner lands flush within the edge marker, with a call too early or too late leaving a crooked load.

label: Seal hazmat and secure cargo
human_steps: Walk to the hazmat locker, put on gloves, and check the seal date on the drum label.
Pick up a seal wire and the crimp tool from the locker shelf.
Set the drum on its cradle and check the secondary containment tray is in place beneath it.
Thread the seal wire through the lid eyelet and pull it snug.
Hold the crimp trigger until the click, then tug the seal to check it holds.
Tag the drum with the hazard placard and log the seal number on the slate.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is telling a seal that looks closed from one that is truly crimped; failure is an uncrimped seal that leaks hazardous material in transit.
ideal_interaction: Crimp and tug: the player threads the seal wire through the lid eyelet, holds the crimp trigger until the click, then tugs to test the seal before the placard can be applied.
fit_note: lash is strap tensioning; threading a seal wire and crimping a hazmat lid is a different hand action.

label: Final manifest report
human_steps: Walk to the stores console and log in with the officer ID badge.
Pull up the run manifest and read the loaded pallet count.
Enter the counts of loaded pallets and sealed hazmat drums into the report fields.
Compare the entries to the loading log printed at the pad and resolve any highlighted mismatch.
Tap the handover signature field only after both counts agree.
Print the signed report and carry it to the bridge.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is reconciling two counts that disagree and refusing to sign until they agree; failure is signing a handover the bridge later finds false.
ideal_interaction: Reconcile then sign: the player types the pallet and seal counts, a mismatch highlights the field, and the sign button stays locked until the numbers match the loading log.

label: Draw medical supplies and bedding to sickbay
human_steps: Walk to the stores locker and read the sickbay draw sheet.
Pull the folded bedding bales and the sterile dressing packs from the shelves.
Check each pack's seal and expiry stamp, setting aside any torn or past date.
Stack the linen bales on the cart with the heavy ones at the bottom.
Wheel the cart down the corridor to the sickbay door.
Hand the load to the nurse and get a signature on the draw sheet.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is spotting a torn seal or past-date pack before it reaches a patient; failure is a contaminated dressing going into a wound.
ideal_interaction: Stacked carry: the player loads sealed packs and linen bales onto the cart, keeping heavy bales low and sterile packs on top, and a dropped or crushed item costs the load.
fit_note: clearout is about removing items; drawing and loading stock is a carry-and-check job.

label: Prepare extra meals and water for evacuees
human_steps: Walk to the mess replicator and read the diet tag list from sickbay.
Select the bland meal pattern on the touch panel and set the batch count to the tag total.
Take one portion from the first batch and check its temperature with the probe.
Load the water pouches into the dispenser tray and check the seal on each pouch.
Lid each tray and write the evacuee's bed number on the label.
Stack the finished trays on the cart by bed number.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is matching the meal to the right diet tag and keeping the portion hot enough to eat; failure is a patient getting the wrong diet or a cold tray.
ideal_interaction: Tag-to-tray: the player reads each evacuee's diet tag, picks the matching meal, and taps the temperature probe on the portion before lidding; a wrong pick earns a complaint from the patient.

label: Open quarantine supply route through cargo
human_steps: Walk to the cargo door and read the quarantine signage and the hatch seal light.
Swipe the access card and wait for the lock light to go green.
Crank the hand wheel to open the bulkhead door fully.
Clear crates and loose straps off the floor along the route line.
Lay floor tape along the lane edge, checking it is wide enough for a stretcher.
Walk the lane and confirm no edge sticks out into it.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is judging the lane width for a stretcher and clearing a path before the bulkhead closes; failure is a blocked corridor that delays treatment.
ideal_interaction: Lane clearing: the player pushes each crate off the route line one at a time, and the lane must be wide enough for a stretcher to pass before the route can be marked clear.

label: Verify spares kits against the stress-test plan
human_steps: Walk to the stores locker and open the stress-test plan on the slate.
Open the first spares kit crate and take out the parts list.
Take each part from the kit and read its spec tag.
Place each part into its foam cutout and check it fits without force.
Mark pass or fail on the list for each part and note any missing item.
Repack the kit and report gaps to engineering.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is telling a part that fits the cutout from one that only looks right; failure is an engineer finding the wrong spare during a failed system.
ideal_interaction: Spec-tag fit: the player takes each spare, reads its spec tag, and drops it into its foam cutout, where a wrong or missing part fails the kit until fixed.
fit_note: manifest matching does not cover checking spec tags against the stress plan or testing physical fit.

label: Pre-position emergency rations and repair stock
human_steps: Walk to the stores door with the empty cart and read the bridge staging order.
Pick ration cases and repair kits from the racks, checking each emergency tag.
Load the cart with heavy cases on the bottom and light kits on top.
Wheel the cart to the marked staging spot outside the stores door.
Unload each case against the bulkhead, keeping the exit path clear.
Stamp the staging log with the time and count.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is placing stock without blocking the exit path or the bulkhead route; failure is a jam in the corridor during a crisis.
ideal_interaction: Staging run: the player loads cases onto the cart, wheels it to the marked staging spot, and sets each case down in its box while keeping the exit path clear.

label: Post-test inventory reconciliation
human_steps: Walk to the stores desk and pull the pre-test inventory sheet.
Walk the shelves and tally each returned item in its bin.
Write each count beside its pre-test figure on the sheet.
Mark any difference in red and check the test log for a relocation entry.
Confirm whether the item was moved or lost before recording a loss.
Sign the reconciliation and file it with the test report.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is telling a relocated item from a lost one by checking the test log; failure is writing a loss that was never a loss, or hiding a real one.
ideal_interaction: Tally and diff: the player counts returned items in each bin, and the on-screen diff flags any item count off the pre-test figure, where the player must choose relocated or lost after checking the log.

label: Pattern buffer diagnostics
human_steps: Walk to the mess replicator and kneel to unlock the service hatch with the panel key.
Plug the diagnostic probe into the buffer port.
Start the pattern check and watch the pass or fail light on the readout dial.
Press the flush key and hold it until the buffer lamp goes dark.
Re-run the check once to confirm the flush cleared the fault.
Close the hatch and log the result in the unit's book.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is deciding if a fault cleared or only paused; failure is closing the hatch while the buffer is still lit, leaving a corrupt meal on the next print.
ideal_interaction: Probe and flush: the player seats the probe in the buffer port, watches the readout needle, and holds the flush key until the lamp goes dark and the second check reads clear.

label: Matter stores count and refill
human_steps: Walk to the matter locker and pull the manifest sheet from the clip.
Lift each feedstock canister to judge its weight and read its label.
Tap the count for each canister on the manifest line.
Refill any hopper below the fill line with canisters from the locker.
Pour the canisters into the hopper until the fill line is reached.
Write a shortfall on the slate for the quartermaster if any hopper cannot be filled.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is telling an empty canister from a full one by weight, and deciding when a shortage is worth reporting; failure is counting an empty canister as full.
ideal_interaction: Weigh and pour: the player lifts each canister, feels its weight, and pours it into the matching hopper until the fill line, and an empty canister lifts too easily and is flagged.

label: Industrial replicator job queue
human_steps: Walk to the workshop workbench and read the request tickets on the clipboard rack.
Pick the ticket for the part to print and note its pattern code.
Load the matching pattern cartridge into the industrial replicator slot.
Start the print and watch the progress bar until it finishes.
Lift the printed part out and measure its critical dimension with calipers.
Deliver the part to the requester or tag it for the shelf.
what_makes_it_hard: Judgement is matching the cartridge to the ticket and catching an out-of-tolerance part before it leaves the bench; failure is delivering a part printed from the wrong pattern.
ideal_interaction: Ticket, print, caliper: the player matches the ticket's pattern code to the cartridge, starts the print, then measures the finished part and rejects it if it falls outside the tolerance band.

label: Routine pattern checks on all food units
human_steps: Walk the mess unit line in order, starting at the unit nearest the galley.
Open each unit's sample tray and take a pattern sample on the readout.
Compare the readout to the golden pattern card taped beside the unit.
